cards.key: Introduction and Motivation
cards.gist: The chapter asks one question: can worn sensors track how a museum visitor feels, second by second, for a visitor the system has **never seen**? It sets the scene (a VR museum, five paintings, free walking), poses five research questions and lists six contributions. Everything is tested **leave-one-subject-out (LOSO)**, because a guide always meets a new visitor.
steps: 1.1 sets the application: a VR guide that could read affect from eye tracking, EDA, HRV and speech and adapt its narrative.

1.2 sets the gap: lab datasets (DEAP, MAHNOB-HCI) are clean and seated; the nearest museum study (Marin-Morales 2019) used EEG + ECG and a two-class retrospective target, so its 71 to 77% is not comparable to a per-second CCC.
1.2 names three technical challenges: mismatched rates (120 Hz eye vs 4 Hz EDA), wrist movement noise, and intermittent speech.
1.3 poses the primary question and RQ1 to RQ5, each answered by one experiment (RQ1 by Exp 1 and 2, RQ2 by Exp 3, RQ3 and RQ4 by Exp 4, RQ5 by Exp 5).
1.4 lists six contributions, each delivered by one Methods/Results section pair (see the Contributions card).

numbers.what: Participants collected by van der Kaaden (rcea / retro)
numbers.from: Thesis - Final - Bas van der Kaaden.txt:2213

qa.q: In one sentence, what is your thesis about?
qa.a: I test whether eye tracking, skin conductance, heart-rate variability and speech can predict a museum visitor's second-by-second valence and arousal when the model has never seen that visitor. The answer on this cohort is no: every score sits at the chance-corrected floor.

qa.q: Why is 'unseen visitor' the constraint for every question?
qa.a: A museum guide meets each visitor for the first time and cannot collect training labels from them first. So I hold every visitor out in turn and train on the others. A within-person split would let the model learn that person's habits, which a real guide never has.

qa.q: Is this a replication of van der Kaaden?
qa.a: It uses his dataset and starts from his published configuration, but it asks a different question. He classified seven k-means regions with balanced accuracy. I predict the continuous 0 to 10 rating scored by CCC, then ordered levels scored by QWK, and add fusion, localisation, variance decomposition and personalisation, which he did not do.
qa.src: final_thesis_body.tex:189-201; Thesis - Final - Bas van der Kaaden.txt:2300,2525

qa.q: What is the headline result?
qa.a: No sensor and no combination rises above the chance-corrected floor for an unseen visitor. The ratings are mostly about the person (36.4 to 64.5% of variance) and barely about the painting (0.1 to 1.5%). Personalisation moves figures in the expected direction but no test survives correction.

traps: The chapter says eye tracking is 'recorded at 120 Hz'. That is the nominal rate. The achieved rate is a median 23 Hz over a session, and 18 Hz at the paintings, because the logger writes one sample per rendered frame (Results 4.1.2). If asked: 120 Hz is the specification; I measured the real rate and report it in Data Characterisation.

The intro promises to find what 'limits or improves' prediction. The honest answer is that nothing tested improves it; the limit is mainly the person-specific nature of the labels (RQ4). Say that directly rather than hunting for a positive.

cards.key: Introduction and Motivation > The Application Context
cards.gist: Museum visitors react to art, and those reactions leave traces in the body. The data come from van der Kaaden's VR version of the HERE exhibition: five paintings in one room, visitors walking freely and talking to a gaze-driven guide. Real conditions limit the sensors: no seated posture, no guaranteed skin contact, a short setup.
steps: Data source: van der Kaaden's recordings, raw per-participant files in raw_data_from_sensors/ (pupil 120 Hz nominal, EDA and BVP from a wristband, speech via push-to-talk and Whisper transcripts, RCEA 4 Hz joystick, RetroSketch 1 Hz).
The agent reacts to the painting and AOI the gaze settles on; the same gaze-and-behaviour log is reused in Exp 4 to define the attended painting.

Constraint listed here (sensors may fail) shows up in the data: EDA is unusable in 20 of 47 recordings, BVP is empty for M18 and M37, M28's eye recording starts after its annotation window (Results 4.1.1, 4.1.2).

qa.q: Who built the VR museum and collected the data?
qa.a: Bas van der Kaaden, for his MSc thesis at Twente, with the Rembrandthuis exhibition as the source. I did not collect any data. I rebuilt the processing from his raw sensor files.
qa.src: Thesis - Final - Bas van der Kaaden.txt; CLAUDE.md

qa.q: Which sensors were worn?
qa.a: An eye tracker in the headset giving pupil diameter and gaze direction, a wristband giving skin conductance, blood-volume pulse at 64 Hz, acceleration and skin temperature, and a push-to-talk microphone. Acceleration and temperature are never predicted from; acceleration drives the EDA motion mask.

qa.q: Why does the setting make the problem harder than a lab?
qa.a: Visitors walk, so wrist signals pick up movement. Nobody checks sensor contact during the visit, so some channels fail silently. Speech happens only when the visitor chooses to talk. And the art is calm and static, so the affect it evokes is weak compared with lab elicitation.

qa.q: Why do you say gallery studies used bodily traces?
qa.a: Troendle and Tschacher's eMotion project measured cardiac activity, skin conductance and locomotion in a real gallery and related them to aesthetic ratings. It shows the idea is not new; what is new here is predicting per second for an unseen visitor.

traps: Earlier drafts cited Wang2022 for 'museum visits are most meaningful when visitors connect emotionally'; the audit found that review has no museum content and removed it. The first sentence now carries no citation. If pressed, it is a framing sentence, not a finding.
The agent is described as 'falls silent when interest wanes'. That is the system design from van der Kaaden, not something this thesis evaluates.

cards.key: Introduction and Motivation > Research Gap and Technical Challenges
cards.gist: Most emotion recognition work uses clean, seated lab data. The closest museum study (Marin-Morales 2019) reached 71 to 77% accuracy, but on an easier question: two classes, rated once per room, with EEG and chest ECG. Three challenges follow here: sensors on different clocks, wrist movement noise, and long silences with no speech.
steps: Marin-Morales 2019: physical museum arousal 71.52%, valence 77.08%; virtual 75.00% and 71.08%, LOSO, two classes, SAM once per room/artwork.

Challenge 1 (rates): handled by fixed temporal windowing onto a 1 Hz label grid, with per-sensor windows (pupil 8 s, EDA searched, selected 3 s, HRV 60 s) and a searched direction/delay (Methods 3.3.2, 3.3.3). Exp 2 then compares DTW, DCCA and DCTW against windowing.

Challenge 2 (movement): EDA motion mask from the accelerometer, median + k x MAD with k searched in {2,3,5}, selected k=5 (key E_nk_k5_w3); HRV has no mask but carries repaired-fraction and motion-fraction columns (Methods 3.3.1).

Challenge 3 (intermittent speech): speech features are NaN outside utterances; every model is a Pipeline(SimpleImputer(median), StandardScaler, model) fitted on the training fold only; late fusion renormalises weights over sensors that produced a prediction (scripts/exp1_v2/families.py:122-133; Methods 3.1).

numbers.what: Marin-Morales 2019 LOSO accuracy, physical museum (arousal / valence)
numbers.from: final_thesis_body.tex:29 (MarinMorales2019, not in the citation audit files)

qa.q: Why can't you compare your CCC to Marin-Morales' 77%?
qa.a: They are different questions and different metrics. Their 77% is accuracy on two classes, where 50% is chance, for one SAM rating per room or artwork after the fact. My CCC measures agreement with a per-second trace, where 0 is chance and it punishes both wrong shape and wrong level. Being on the right half of a scale once per room is much easier than tracking every second.

qa.q: Why CCC and not accuracy or Pearson r?
qa.a: The target is continuous, so accuracy does not apply. Pearson r ignores bias and scale: a prediction that is always 2 points too high can still get r = 1. CCC = 2 cov / (var_true + var_pred + (mean difference)^2), so it drops if the mean or spread is wrong. It is the standard metric for continuous affect (AVEC, RECOLA).

qa.q: What does zero mean for CCC here?
qa.a: Zero is what a model with no information about the held-out visitor gets. It can go negative. I call it the chance-corrected floor, and a model is only useful if it rises clearly above it, by more than the 0.08 selection resolution.

qa.q: How is the CCC averaged?
qa.a: For Exp 1 and 2 I compute CCC on each held-out visitor's rows and then average over visitors. That is the mean CCC over LOSO folds named in RQ1. The ordinal QWK, by contrast, is pooled over all held-out predictions.

qa.q: How did you handle the 120 Hz vs 4 Hz mismatch?
qa.a: Every sensor is summarised over a fixed window that ends at, or is shifted around, each labelled second, so all sensors land on the same 1 Hz grid as the ratings. In Exp 2 I also tried learned and warping alignments; the four methods span only 0.006 CCC.

qa.q: How did you handle silent stretches with no speech?
qa.a: Speech features are simply missing outside an utterance. The median imputer, fitted on training participants only, fills them, and rows are never dropped for a missing feature. In late fusion a sensor with no prediction for a row is left out and the weights are renormalised.

qa.q: Is 'walking introduces noise' shown in your data?
qa.a: Yes, indirectly. EDA failed in 20 of 47 recordings, mostly from lost contact in the second collection wave, and the tonic level tracks skin temperature at median r = 0.89. For HRV, what the wrist gives is pulse-rate variability, and the beat detector was validated at rest on fingertips, not while walking.

traps: The Marin-Morales 2019 figures (71.52, 77.08, 75.00, 71.08, 15 of 60) are not in literature/citation_audit.md or citation_audit.csv, and the PDF is not in literature/_cited. Only the 2018 paper is audited (75.00% arousal, 71.21% valence, and it analysed only the fixed-viewpoint 360 stage; the free museum stage was analysed in the 2019 paper). If asked, say the 2019 figures were taken from the paper but I would re-check them before quoting exactly.

Their 77% is under LOSO, so it is subject-independent like mine. The difference is the target (two classes, one rating per room/artwork) and sensors (EEG, ECG), not the validation. Do not claim they cheated with within-subject splits.

Speech features are copied onto every second between a transcript segment's start and end, which includes pauses, so speech columns are present on about 71% of rows while voiced audio is a median 6.9% of a visit. 'Intermittent speech' is true of the audio, less so of the feature matrix. See the BRIEF note on speech broadcasting (scripts/independent_pilot/speech_sweep.py opensmile_aligned).

Kumar2025 was originally cited for 'labs where participants sit still'; the audit narrowed the sentence to what the paper says (typically lab, shift to real-world). Wu2025 was removed from this sentence as WRONG.

cards.key: Introduction and Motivation > Research Questions
cards.gist: One main question: how well can moment-to-moment valence and arousal be recovered for an unseen visitor, and what limits or improves it? It splits into five: sensors and fusion (RQ1, Exp 1 and 2), ordered levels (RQ2, Exp 3), the attended painting (RQ3, Exp 4), where the variance sits (RQ4, Exp 4) and personalisation (RQ5, Exp 5).
steps: RQ1 (Sensor contribution and representation) -> Methods 3.3 Exp 1 and 3.4 Exp 2 -> Results 4.2 and 4.3. Answer: no sensor separates from the floor (twenty sensor-by-slice CCCs span -0.072 to +0.084); no combination beats the best single sensor (both +0.0822); sensors, families and alignment methods each span less than the 0.08 selection resolution.

RQ2 (Target representation) -> Methods 3.5 Exp 3 -> Results 4.4. Answer: ordered levels do not lift agreement above chance at any level count swept (3 to 20; selectable 3 to 7); the two arms differ by 0.0123 against a 0.21 resolution; three levels carried.

RQ3 (Localisation) -> Methods 3.6.1 to 3.6.5 -> Results 4.5.1 and 4.5.2. Answer: no; none of 48 paired tests on identical rows survives correction; the only established differences are losses (painting B2).

RQ4 (Sources of shared variance) -> Methods 3.6.6 -> Results 4.5.3. Answer: person 36.4 to 64.5%, painting 0.1 to 1.5%, residual 35.4 to 62.1%. For the sensor part: EDA features carry the largest painting share (3.85%), speech acoustics (2.98%) and pupil (1.87%) exceed the rating's own share on rcea; HRV is the most person-locked (66.2% and 56.9%).

RQ5 (Personalisation) -> Methods 3.7 -> Results 4.6. Answer: not established; pooled figures rise in 21 of 24 cells but 0 of 48 tests survive (smallest q = 0.138); only the labelled warm-up grows with the amount of annotation.
Code: RQ1 scripts/exp1_v2/families.py, predictions.py, exp2_*.py; RQ2 exp3_binning.py; RQ3 exp4_localisation.py; RQ4 exp4_variance.py; RQ5 exp5_personalisation.py.

numbers.what: RQ1: range of twenty sensor-by-slice CCCs (Extra Trees)
RQ1: best fusion cell = best single sensor
RQ5: tests surviving / cells moving up

numbers.value: 180 s warm-up, rcea arousal, per-participant CCC +0.0217 to +0.0739, 16 of 22 improved, p = 0.0066, q = 0.138

qa.q: Which experiment answers RQ1, and what is the answer?
qa.a: Experiments 1 and 2. Exp 1 scores each sensor alone and Exp 2 combines them. No sensor separates from the floor: the twenty scores run from -0.072 to +0.084. Combining does not help: the best combination and best single sensor both reach +0.0822.

qa.q: RQ1 also asks how much the preprocessing choices change the figure. What is the answer?
qa.a: Very little. Five configuration parameters were searched and eight model families compared; the families span 0.0124 CCC and the alignment methods 0.006, both well inside the 0.08 resolution. So the null is not a tuning accident.

qa.q: Which experiment answers RQ2, and what is the answer?
qa.a: Experiment 3. Binning the ratings into equal-width ordered levels does not lift pooled QWK above chance at any count from 3 to 20. The trained-on-levels and post-hoc arms differ by 0.0123, far inside the 0.21 QWK resolution. The cohort supports at most seven levels, since above that some level holds under 1% of seconds; three is carried as the coarsest tied count.

qa.q: Which experiment answers RQ3, and what is the answer?
qa.a: Experiment 4. Restricting to the seconds a visitor attends a painting, scored on the same rows as the whole-session model, does not help. None of the 48 paired tests survives correction, and the only significant results are two losses on painting B2.

qa.q: Which experiment answers RQ4, and what is the answer?
qa.a: The variance decomposition in Experiment 4, a crossed mixed model fitted by REML on attended rows. Who is viewing explains 36.4 to 64.5% of a rating, which painting only 0.1 to 1.5%. It is computed on the self-reports alone, so it bounds any pipeline. Among sensors, EDA features carry the most painting share, and HRV is the most person-locked.

qa.q: Which experiment answers RQ5, and what is the answer?
qa.a: Experiment 5, with three levers: baseline-window calibration, a labelled warm-up of 30 to 180 s, and a person-relative target. Not established: 21 of 24 cells move up but none of 48 tests survives correction. Only the warm-up gets better with more annotation, and it needs the visitor's own ratings, which a museum cannot ask for.

qa.q: Why five sub-questions in this order?
qa.a: Each experiment settles a choice the next needs. Exp 1 fixes each sensor's configuration and the model; Exp 2 fixes the fusion; Exp 3 fixes the target and level count; Exp 4 tests scoping and bounds what is shared; Exp 5 tests personalisation on the result.

qa.q: Why does RQ1 use CCC but RQ2 to RQ5 use QWK?
qa.a: Exp 1 and 2 are regression on the continuous rating, and a continuous score separates candidate pipelines more finely. From Exp 3 the target is ordered levels, because the ratings have no shared scale across people, so the natural score is QWK, with balanced accuracy against 1/B as a cross-check. Exp 4 and 5 also report CCC beside it.

qa.q: RQ4 asks which sensors carry the painting-shared component. Doesn't the summary skip that?
qa.a: The one-line summary only gives the rating split. The sensor part is in Results 4.5.3: the EDA features have the largest painting share at 3.85%, and on retro every sensor category exceeds the ratings' 0.1%. That does not make those sensors more affect-informative; it means they respond to the painting, for example to its luminance or to walking up to it.

traps: RQ1 says 'leave-one-participant-out' while RQ intro and Methods say 'leave-one-subject-out'. Same thing. One fold per usable visitor, sklearn LeaveOneGroupOut with participant as group.

The +0.0822 'best single sensor' in the RQ1 summary is the Exp 2 figure (HRV-only subset, late_simple, retro valence, fixed hyperparameters). Exp 1's best for the same cell is +0.0841 because Exp 1 nested-tunes max_depth. Both sit just above 0.08 and are within 0.002 of each other; neither is separable from its neighbours at the 0.08 resolution. If asked why two numbers: one is nested-tuned (Exp 1), the other is a single fit of the standard model (Exp 2).

The best Exp 2 'combination' is literally a single-sensor subset (subset 'H', size 1) in fusion_summary.json. So 'combination = best single sensor' is by construction of which cell was best, not two separate models tying.

RQ2 pooled QWK and per-participant QWK can disagree in sign (Results 4.4.4: rcea arousal -0.0582 pooled vs +0.0130 per participant). If pressed on why pooled is headline: it was fixed in advance, and it avoids unstable kappas on visitors with few levels occupied.
RQ4 variance decomposition runs on attended rows only, so 20 rcea and 15 retro participants, not 22 and 16 (variance_ratings.csv n_participants).

RQ5 says 'visitor-specific calibration including a labelled warm-up'; the warm-up needs the visitor's own ratings, so it is not usable in a real museum. Say it shows what labels would be worth, not a deployable method.

cards.key: Introduction and Motivation > Contributions
cards.gist: Six contributions: a benchmark pipeline plus one controlled test per experiment. They are framed as a benchmark and tests, not a winning model, because every result is null.
steps: C1 Subject-independent benchmark, five sensors, two streams, all LOSO -> delivered by Methods 3.1 (protocol) and Results 4.2 and 4.3 (Exp 1 and 2), with per-cell tables in appendix_final_exp1.tex.

C2 Preprocessing pipeline with open parameters selected empirically under the evaluation protocol -> Methods 3.3.1 to 3.3.3 (five searched parameters: fixation rule, gaze-angle correction, window direction and delay, interbeat multiplier, EDA decomposition + mask + window) and Results 4.2.1 Parameter Sweep. Selected keys: pupil P_vt30_c0_t0, EDA E_nk_k5_w3, HRV H_m3_t0. Code scripts/exp1_v2/selection.py (Ridge scoring, rank vote inside training folds).

C3 Continuous vs ordinal target on identical rows -> Methods 3.5 and Results 4.4 (trained-on-levels arm vs post-hoc binned continuous predictions, same features and rows). Code scripts/exp1_v2/exp3_binning.py.
C4 Scoping to the attended painting -> Methods 3.6.1 to 3.6.5 and Results 4.5.1 to 4.5.2. Code scripts/exp1_v2/exp4_localisation.py.

C5 Crossed mixed-effects decomposition into visitor, painting, residual, extended to each sensor's features -> Methods 3.6.6 and Results 4.5.3. Code scripts/exp1_v2/exp4_variance.py (stage_ratings, stage_icc, stage_sensors).
C6 Three personalisation strategies tested visitor by visitor -> Methods 3.7 and Results 4.6. Code scripts/exp1_v2/exp5_personalisation.py (centre_by_baseline, warm-up, person_levels).

numbers.value: 8 (ridge, SVR, RF, Extra Trees, HistGB, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost)

qa.q: If every result is null, what is actually new?
qa.a: Three things. A clean subject-independent benchmark on a free-roaming VR museum, with every open preprocessing choice tested rather than assumed. A set of controlled tests showing the null is not caused by tuning, fusion, target form, scoping or simple personalisation. And the variance decomposition, which shows the ceiling comes from the labels themselves: most of a rating is the person, almost none is the painting.

qa.q: What does 'selected empirically under the evaluation protocol' mean in practice?
qa.a: For each open parameter I fixed a candidate set in advance. Inside each LOSO training fold, every training participant scores every candidate with ridge by CCC, the scores are ranked within participant, and the best mean rank wins. The held-out visitor never influences the choice.

qa.q: Contribution 3 says 'continuous and ordinal compared on identical rows'. How exactly?
qa.a: In Exp 3 the post-hoc arm takes the stored continuous predictions and bins them with the same fixed edges, and the trained-on-levels arm fits a classifier on the binned rating from the same features and rows. Both are scored by pooled QWK. Exp 4 and 5 also report CCC beside QWK on the same rows.

qa.q: Why is the variance decomposition a contribution if van der Kaaden computed ICC?
qa.a: He computed inter-rater ICC on painting windows, which asks whether visitors agree. I split the total variance into person, painting and residual shares with a crossed random-effects model, which asks how much of a rating each source explains, and I repeated it on each sensor feature. He did not do a variance decomposition.

In fact five are searched; some choices are fixed with a citation (pupil 8 s window, HRV 60 s window, 0.5 s blink bridge, 30 s rolling baseline) and some are inherited from the dataset's origin (SCR amplitude threshold 0.1 of max, swept only as a sensitivity check). If pressed: those are fixed because the literature gives one value or a hard validity floor, not a range.

C3 says 'comparison of continuous and ordinal target representations'. Both arms of Exp 3 are scored on QWK; the classifier in the trained-on-levels arm (ExtraTreesClassifier) treats levels as unordered, and no ordinal-specific model was fitted (Methods 3.5 says so). Honest framing: it compares training on levels vs binning a regressor, not an ordinal regression method.
C6 says three strategies; Chapter 2 describes more families (CORAL, few-shot fine-tuning, contrastive alignment) that were not tested. See the Personalising card.

cards.gist: The review follows the design decisions in order: how affect is represented and rated, whether to bin it, what each sensor measures, how to align and fuse sensors, and how to model a small cohort. It ends with van der Kaaden's findings on this dataset, shared versus personal response, and personalisation; most sections justify one Methods choice.

2.2 -> justifies the ordinal target, QWK, and sweeping level counts 3 to 20 (Methods 3.5).

qa.q: How did you check your citations?
qa.a: I kept a citation audit that records, per key, the claim it carries, what the paper actually says, a verdict (OK, WEAK, WRONG, CONTRADICTS) and how it was checked. Several were corrected or removed, for example Wang2022 (no museum content), and Wass2015 (it contradicted the original claim, so it is now used as a caution).

qa.q: What is the single most important prior result for your thesis?
qa.a: Van der Kaaden's: on this dataset, a classifier reaches about 0.84 balanced accuracy within people but falls to 0.20 to 0.24 on a new person. My thesis asks whether any better processing, target, fusion, scoping or personalisation can close that gap, measured on a continuous target.

Know each one's scope; the section cards list them.

Chapter 2 reviews convolutional and recurrent networks, but the final thesis trains no neural network. A raw-signal CNN arm and a fused-vector network arm existed in earlier drafts and were removed (literature/citation_audit.md:845). The review of networks justifies choosing tree ensembles.

cards.key: Literature Review > Dimensional Models of Affect and the Annotation Problem
cards.gist: Affect sits on two continuous axes: **valence** (unpleasant to pleasant) and **arousal** (calm to excited). Only the person can report it: RCEA rates live with a joystick and lags, RetroSketch rates afterwards from a replay and relies on memory. The two do not give one ground truth, so the thesis never pools them.
steps: Both streams are recorded on the 0 to 10 circumplex axes.

rcea: 4 Hz joystick reduced to 1 Hz by the per-second median, zero fixed label delay (scripts/exp1_v2/features.py:57 labels_v2 calls load_rcea_aligned with valence_delay_s=0, arousal_delay_s=0, reducer='median'). The lag is absorbed by the searched window direction and delay (Methods 3.3.3).
retro: native 1 Hz (load_retro_aligned).
The two streams are separate participant groups (22 rcea, 16 retro) and are analysed separately in every experiment (Methods 3.1).
Where the Mariooryad lag claim is used later: Methods 3.3.3 searches delays 0 to 6 s in each direction because lag varies by annotator and dimension.

numbers.what: Reaction lag in the paper itself
numbers.value: 1 to 6 s, by annotator and dimension

qa.q: Why a dimensional model and not discrete emotions?
qa.a: Both annotation tools record a point on the valence-arousal plane, so the data are dimensional to start with. A dimensional rating can also change gradually through a visit, which suits per-second prediction.

qa.q: What is RCEA and what is RetroSketch?
qa.a: RCEA is real-time continuous annotation: the visitor moves a joystick on the two axes during the visit, sampled at 4 Hz. RetroSketch is retrospective: after the visit the visitor watches a replay of their own session and sketches valence and arousal over it, at 1 Hz.

qa.q: Why keep the two streams separate and never pool them?
qa.a: They measure the same experience in different ways. RCEA is step-like and rests at 5 for about a fifth of the time; RetroSketch is smoother, wider, never exactly at 5, and shaped by memory. Van der Kaaden concluded they do not converge on one ground truth, and his cross-method models reached only 0.17 to 0.18 balanced accuracy. Pooling would mix two different targets.
qa.src: final_thesis_body.tex:108, 199; Thesis - Final - Bas van der Kaaden.txt:2565

qa.q: How did you handle the RCEA reporting delay?
qa.a: I did not apply a fixed delay to the labels. Instead the sensor window's direction (trailing or forward) and delay, 0 to 6 s, are searched inside each training fold, and for HRV a per-participant delay can be estimated. The held-out visitor gets the median of the training delays. Van der Kaaden instead applied a fixed 1 s for arousal and 2 s for valence.

qa.q: Why the median to go from 4 Hz to 1 Hz?
qa.a: The median of the four samples in a second is robust to one jumpy joystick sample and gives a value on the continuous scale. Van der Kaaden used the mode. The inherited 'modal' reducer is still the default in the loader; the thesis pipeline calls it with reducer='median'.

qa.q: Does RetroSketch really have no delay?
qa.a: It removes the in-the-moment delay between feeling and reporting during the visit. It still has its own timing error, because the visitor sketches while watching a replay and relies on memory. That is why the searched window delay is applied to retro as well, not only to rcea.

qa.q: Is arousal hard for people to rate?
qa.a: Larradet et al. name arousal as a concept untrained raters find unfamiliar, and in-the-wild annotation as an open problem. It is one reason I expect noisy labels.

traps: The text says 'roughly one to three seconds' citing Mariooryad2015; the paper's own words are 'this delay varies from one to six seconds, depending on the annotator, expressive dimension, and actual behaviors' (citation_audit.md:592). The Methods delay search (0 to 6 s) matches the paper's wider range. If pressed: 1 to 3 s is the typical figure; the search covers up to 6.

Potts2025 compares RetroSketch against experience sampling (ESM), not against RCEA specifically (citation_audit.md:147). The sentence says 'experience sampling', which is accurate, but do not claim Potts tested RCEA.
'Keeping them separate' is the thesis's decision built on van der Kaaden's finding, not his own recommendation. Section 2.6 says so explicitly.
Because streams are separate groups of people, the thesis cannot compare the two methods within a person.

cards.key: Literature Review > Ordinal Targets and the Discretisation of Continuous Affect
cards.gist: Much affect work bins ratings into levels, such as high versus low. One argument is that affect is ordinal: one visitor's 9 may be another's 7, but the order holds. Binning loses detail, needs a distance-aware score (QWK), and nobody agrees on how many levels, so the thesis sweeps the count.
steps: Exp 3 bins each axis into B equal-width levels on 0 to 10: np.digitize(np.clip(y,0,10), np.linspace(0,10,B+1)[1:-1]) (scripts/exp1_v2/exp3_binning.py:57). Edges are fixed, never fitted.
B swept from 3 to 20 (no consensus count, per Yang2026). A count is selectable only if every level holds at least 1% of seconds in both streams; only 3 to 7 qualify (Results 4.4.1).
Scoring: pooled QWK via sklearn cohen_kappa_score(weights='quadratic'), balanced accuracy vs 1/B as a cross-check (Doewes2023 caution about QWK alone).
Odd vs even counts matter for rcea because 20% of seconds sit at the midpoint 5 (joystick rest).
Person-relative levels (each visitor's own quantiles) are tested later as a personalisation lever in Exp 5 (exp5_personalisation.py:123-134).

qa.q: What is QWK and why use it?
qa.a: Quadratic weighted kappa is agreement between two sets of ordered labels, corrected for chance, where each disagreement is weighted by the squared distance between levels. Predicting level 1 when the truth is 3 costs four times as much as predicting 2. Zero is chance, one is perfect.

qa.q: Why also report balanced accuracy?
qa.a: QWK depends on how unevenly the levels are filled (Doewes 2023), so I do not rely on it alone. Balanced accuracy is the mean recall per level, read against its chance value 1/B, never across counts because 1/B changes with B.

qa.q: If affect is ordinal because people judge relative to their own reference, does fixed equal-width binning capture that?
qa.a: No, and I say so. Fixed cohort-wide edges keep the ordering but still assume a 7 means the same for everyone. That is why Exp 5 tests a person-relative target whose edges come from each visitor's own ratings.

qa.q: Did you expect binning to help?
qa.a: Not really. On bounded scales Wu et al. find the ordinal advantage is in tracking relative change, not in higher agreement, and binning throws away borderline information. The sweep was there to test whether any granularity lifts agreement above chance, not to find the best one.

qa.q: Why sweep 3 to 20 instead of using the usual binary split?
qa.a: There is no consensus count, and the biggest comparison (Yang 2026) finds reliability rising with finer scales. Sweeping every count means no one can ask why I chose a particular set. The 1% occupancy rule then limits what is selectable to 3 to 7.

qa.q: Why equal-width and not quantile bins?
qa.a: Equal-width edges on the known 0 to 10 scale are fixed by design and cannot leak information from the data. Quantile edges would have to be fitted, and fitted on whose data is a leakage question. The person-relative quantile version is tested separately in Exp 5.

traps: The literature argues levels are ordered, but the Exp 3 trained-on-levels classifier is an ExtraTreesClassifier, which treats levels as unordered categories (scripts/exp1_v2/exp3_binning.py:150). Methods 3.5 admits no ordinal-specific model was fitted. Honest answer: the post-hoc arm preserves order by construction, and both arms tie.

Yannakakis' ordinal argument is about relative (pairwise, rank) judgements. Binning absolute ratings into fixed levels is a weaker use of that idea. Do not claim the thesis implements preference learning.
DEAP splits nine-point ratings at the midpoint; MAHNOB-HCI uses a few ordered classes. Both are lab datasets, so the 'common practice' being cited is lab practice.
Mitsios2024 is text emotion prediction, not physiology; it supports the general point that not all misclassifications are equal.

cards.key: Literature Review > What Each Modality Measures
cards.gist: Each sensor reads a different body system. Pupil size rises with **arousal** but also with brightness; EDA tracks **sympathetic** sweating (slow tonic level, fast phasic responses); PPG gives heartbeats for HRV; speech carries affect in how it sounds (eGeMAPS) and what is said (VADER). The closest VR study (Szymanska 2025) found pupil prediction works coarsely but fails on finer targets.
steps: Pupil (Methods 3.3.1): invalid samples and diameters outside 1.5 to 9.0 mm dropped (Kret2019); eyes averaged; gaps under **0.5 s** interpolated (Mathot2022Methods, 'by default 500 ms'); 30 s rolling mean subtracted (Mathot2018); gaze vectors 5-sample median then angular velocity; fixation rule searched; selected 30 deg/s (P_vt30_c0_t0). Features 7: diameter mean, SD, slope, blink rate, fixation duration, saccade frequency, sample count. Pupil window fixed at 8 s.

EDA (Methods 3.3.1): recording dropped if at least half negative, or if the 5th to 95th percentile span is under **0.02 uS**, because the conventional minimum SCR is **0.01 to 0.05 uS** (BenedekDeconv2010, verified verbatim). Motion mask median + k MAD (k=5 selected); NeuroKit decomposition selected over convex (Greco2016); window 3 s selected. Features 10.

HRV (Methods 3.3.1 to 3.3.2): Elgendi dual-moving-average beat detector; intervals outside 40 to 180 bpm removed; successive-difference filter, multiplier searched (3 selected, H_m3_t0). Window fixed at **60 s**, the shortest where indices stay valid (Castaldo2019: 6 of 23 consistent to 1 min; 4 used: meanNN, SDNN, HF, SD2; RMSSD added per Laborde2017; LF and VLF excluded because they need 2 and 5 min per Shaffer2017). Features 8 including interval count, repaired fraction, motion fraction.
Speech: per-utterance openSMILE eGeMAPSv02 functionals (88 columns) and one VADER compound score on Whisper transcripts.
Total 114 columns across the five sensors (7 + 10 + 8 + 88 + 1).
Expected directions from this section are compared against within-participant Spearman correlations in Exp 1 (scripts/exp1_v2/relations.py; relations_literature.csv). 0 of 436 tests survive FDR.

qa.q: What does pupil size measure physiologically?
qa.a: Autonomic arousal, via the balance of sympathetic dilation and parasympathetic constriction. Partala and Surakka found it larger for both negative and positive stimuli than neutral, so it tracks arousal, not valence. But light dominates it: a bright painting constricts the pupil regardless of feeling, and I could not control scene luminance.

qa.q: What does EDA measure, and why could it fail at the wrist?
qa.a: Skin conductance from eccrine sweat glands, which are driven only by the sympathetic system, so it indexes arousal. At the wrist there are fewer active glands than on the palm (wrist-to-palm r = 0.31 tonic), the electrodes lose contact, and arm movement creates artefacts. In this dataset 20 of 47 recordings were unusable, and the tonic level partly tracks skin temperature.

qa.q: Why is EDA called slow?
qa.a: The deconvolved sudomotor impulse lasts under two seconds, but the measured skin-conductance response starts one to three seconds after the trigger and rises and decays over several more. So a phasic response lags the moment by seconds. That is why the EDA window only trails the rated second.

qa.q: What does HRV measure, and why could it fail while walking?
qa.a: Variation in time between beats, which reflects autonomic, mainly parasympathetic, control of the heart. From a wrist PPG it is strictly pulse-rate variability. Walking changes heart rate by itself, and motion corrupts the optical pulse, so beats are missed or doubled. The beat detector was validated on fingertips at rest, not on a walking wrist.

qa.q: Why a 60-second HRV window when affect changes faster?
qa.a: HRV indices need enough beats to be valid. Castaldo et al. show six of 23 indices stay consistent down to one minute, and I use four of them plus RMSSD. Frequency bands like LF need two minutes and VLF five, so I excluded them. The cost is that HRV cannot follow second-by-second changes.

qa.q: Why bridge pupil gaps only under 0.5 s?
qa.a: A blink lasts at most about half a second; 500 ms is the default blink ceiling in the pupillometry methods literature (Mathot 2022). Longer gaps are probably tracking loss, and interpolating across them would invent data, so they stay missing.

qa.q: Where does the 0.02 uS flat-recording rule come from?
qa.a: The conventional minimum amplitude for a skin-conductance response is 0.01 to 0.05 uS, quoted in Benedek and Kaernbach 2010. If a whole recording's 5th to 95th percentile span is under 0.02 uS, it cannot contain even one response, so it has no usable contact.

qa.q: Why eGeMAPS and not wav2vec2 or WavLM?
qa.a: Self-supervised embeddings do perform better on speech tasks, but they are hundreds of dimensions learned on huge corpora, and here voiced speech is a median 6.9% of a visit. eGeMAPS is a small, interpretable set designed to limit over-fitting on small data (Eyben 2016).

qa.q: Is VADER valid for spoken remarks?
qa.a: It was validated on tweets, reviews and news, short informal text. Spoken remarks are closer to that than to edited prose, but the transfer to speech is an assumption I state, not something I tested.

qa.q: What does Szymanska 2025 tell you?
qa.a: In a headset, with 105 people viewing standard emotional pictures, pupil and gaze gave F1 0.73 arousal and 0.64 valence on a binary split of extreme ratings, but only 0.31 and 0.28 on nine levels. So coarse pupil prediction in VR works but falls apart as the target gets finer. It was seated, static images, not free roaming.

traps: Partala2003 was once cited for 'pupil grows with arousal and with mental load'; the audit found the mental-load half is not the paper's finding (citation_audit.md:187). The current sentence only claims dilation to pleasant and unpleasant vs neutral, which is correct.

Gu2025 and O'Dwyer2019 were once cited together for 'time series beats summary statistics for continuous prediction'; audit: WRONG on both (Gu is three-class, O'Dwyer runs no such comparison). The current text splits them: O'Dwyer for continuous prediction, Gu for classifying levels. Do not merge them again when answering.

Szymanska2025 is a two-page abstract and reports no subject-independent evaluation (citation_audit.md:166). Its F1 scores are probably not LOSO, so they are an upper bound, not a comparable benchmark.

Valenza2014 measures brain-heart coupling (EEG plus heart rate), not HRV alone, and does find valence effects at intermediate arousal (citation_audit.md:191). The sentence was narrowed accordingly. The bibkey also points to a 2016 paper (citation_audit.md:174).

Methods trap on the pupil chain: the 5-sample median follows the Tobii I-VT filter (Olsen2012IVT), which is specified for 2D screen gaze coordinates, while the thesis applies it to 3D direction vectors; Methods says so. Also 30 deg/s is the default for seated screen viewing, yet it won the search over the 240 deg/s rule validated for walking (Stuart2014). If asked: the search chose it on the data; all four rules tied within resolution.
The EDA decomposition claim 'convex optimisation recovers both without a filter split' (Greco2016) is correct; the thesis's NeuroKit default was selected over it in the search.

BenedekDeconv2010 timing: an older sentence said SCR 'peaks around two seconds'; the audit marked that WRONG (the under-2 s figure is the impulse duration). The current Chapter 2 wording ('impulse lasts under two seconds, measured response rises and decays over several more') is the corrected one.
HF power in a 60 s window holds only about 9 to 24 respiratory cycles; Castaldo supports HF at 1 min, but it is the weakest of the kept indices.

cards.key: Literature Review > Aligning Asynchronous Modalities
cards.gist: 'Alignment' means three things: syncing device clocks, lining sensors up with the delayed rating (**label lag**), and matching two sensors' dynamics (**representation**). For the last, four methods are compared: a fixed shared window (learns nothing), DTW (warps time), DCTW (learns features and a warp) and DCCA (learns correlated features, no warp).
steps: Clock sync: streams are joined on their recorded timestamps. The RCEA file's 'timestamp_utc_plus1' column is mislabelled (actually CET wall clock), so the loader parses 'timestamp_cet' instead (scripts/annotation/rcea_alignment.py:33-39). No cross-correlation clock alignment was run.

Label lag: window direction (trailing/forward) and delay 0 to 6 s searched inside training folds for pupil and HRV; EDA only trails; held-out visitor gets the training median delay. Selected: trailing, 0 s delay for pupil and HRV (keys P_vt30_c0_t0, H_m3_t0 contain t0). Rigid shift, never a warp, because a warp would need the held-out visitor's ratings.

Representation level (Exp 2, Methods 3.4.1): four arms on the three physiological pairs (pupil-EDA, pupil-HRV, EDA-HRV). DTW adds 9 columns (cost normalised by path length, mean signed lag, path excess over diagonal) from a 12 s trailing window on a 4 Hz grid (archive/classification_based/alignment_methods_scripts/dtw_features.py:83-97). DCCA and DCTW projections fitted per outer training fold and applied to the held-out visitor (scripts/alignment_comparison/alignment_ccc.py:164). Scored with ExtraTreesRegressor(300, max_depth=None) at one fixed configuration (scripts/exp1_v2/exp2_alignment.py:44).
Result: the four span 0.006 CCC (DTW +0.0177 to DCCA +0.0236), far inside 0.08; fixed windowing carried.

qa.q: What are the three meanings of alignment?
qa.a: First, clock sync: getting devices with their own clocks onto one timeline. Second, label lag: the rating comes seconds after the feeling, so which sensor window explains it. Third, representation: two sensors on the same clock may still respond at different speeds, and the question is whether matching their dynamics needs a learned method.

qa.q: How did you do clock synchronisation?
qa.a: All streams carry absolute timestamps and I join them on those. The one real clock problem I found was that the RCEA file's column labelled UTC+1 is actually CET wall clock, so I parse the correctly tagged CET column. I did not run a cross-correlation clock alignment between devices.

qa.q: Why a rigid shift for label lag and not DTW?
qa.a: A shift is one number, learned on training visitors and applied unchanged to the new visitor. A warp is fitted per recording, so warping the held-out visitor would need their ratings, which is leakage. A warp is also flexible enough to align almost any two series, so agreement after warping is weak evidence.

qa.q: Why fixed windows as the main method?
qa.a: A sensor and its annotation come from the same person on the same clock, so the only thing separating them is a delay, which the searched direction and delay absorb. Fixed windowing learns nothing from the data, which matters with 16 to 22 people. And in Exp 2 the learned methods did not beat it.

qa.q: What does DTW return in your pipeline?
qa.a: Not a warped signal. For each second and pair, I warp the two z-scored 12 s windows against each other and keep three numbers: the remaining distance divided by path length, the mean signed lag along the path in 0.25 s steps, and how far the path departs from the diagonal. These are added as columns.

qa.q: What is the difference between DCCA and DCTW?
qa.a: DCCA learns two neural projections so the two views are maximally correlated, but it needs paired observations, one row of each view matched to one row of the other. DCTW adds a warping step, alternating between DTW and updating the projections. DCCA is DCTW with the warp fixed to identity.

qa.q: Is anything in the DCCA/DCTW arms fitted on the test visitor?
qa.a: No. The projections are fitted inside each outer LOSO fold on the training participants only and then applied to the held-out visitor's rows.

qa.q: Why does the sampling-rate ratio matter?
qa.a: At 30 to 1, hundreds of gaze samples meet a handful of EDA samples in the same window. Pairing them naively weakens the relation, and how well fusion works depends on how that gap is handled (Kumar 2025). Summarising each sensor over its own window before joining is how I handle it.

traps: The DTW used has no slope constraint or band: dtaidistance dtw.warping_path_fast is called with no window argument (archive/classification_based/alignment_methods_scripts/dtw_features.py:93). Chapter 2 itself says Sakoe and Chiba found DTW discriminates best under a slope constraint. Honest answer: an unconstrained warp within a 12 s window; a band could change the DTW columns but the four arms span 0.006, so it is unlikely to change the conclusion. Not tested.

The DTW feature code lives under archive/ but is imported by the live Exp 2 code (scripts/alignment_comparison/alignment_ccc.py imports archive.classification_based...dtw_features). It is live, not dead code.

DCTW's original experiments evaluate on the same sequences they are fitted to (Chapter 2 says so). The thesis applies DCTW across people, fitted on training visitors and applied to the held-out one, which is outside its original design. Trigeorgis2016 was marked WEAK for an earlier wording (citation_audit.md:787).

Andrew2013 was once paraphrased as 'needs both signals at the same rate'; the audit corrected it to 'needs paired observations' (citation_audit.md:788). The DCCA arm here runs on the already windowed 1 Hz features, which is how the pairing is obtained.
The 30:1 ratio uses the nominal 120 Hz; the achieved eye rate is a median 23 Hz, so the real ratio is closer to 6:1.

The alignment library docstring (alignment_ccc.py header) says the fixed model is 'untuned XGBoost'; the thesis run (scripts/exp1_v2/exp2_alignment.py:44) uses ExtraTreesRegressor(300). The docstring is stale; the thesis figure comes from the Extra Trees run.
Methods says a sensor and annotation are 'on the same clock'. That is an assumption based on shared timestamps, not a measured synchronisation.

cards.key: Literature Review > Modelling and Fusion for Small Multimodal Data
cards.gist: Four questions for a small multimodal cohort: what a cohort this size can support, which model family suits it, how to combine sensors, and whether the link between sensors is itself a feature. The answers used here: handcrafted features, tree ensembles, a comparison of fusion types, and a coupling block tested against a surrogate.
steps: 2.5.1 -> motivates handcrafted features (Methods 3.3.2).

2.5.2 -> motivates the eight families and choosing the standard model among tree ensembles (Methods 3.3.4). Selected: ExtraTreesRegressor, 300 trees, max_depth grid {None, 8, 4}, seed 42 (scripts/exp1_v2/predictions.py:21).
2.5.3 -> the four combination mechanisms of Exp 2 (Methods 3.4.3).
2.5.4 -> the eight-column cross-sensor block with a rotation surrogate (Methods 3.4.2).

qa.q: What model did you end up using and why?
qa.a: Extremely randomised trees, 300 trees, depth tuned over None, 8 and 4 by nested grouped CV. Tree ensembles are the strongest family on small tabular data. All eight families tied within the 0.08 resolution, and the tie-break picks the family whose scores vary least across the twenty cells.

traps: The section frames four questions but the thesis only answers three of them experimentally: it trains no neural networks and no foundation or self-supervised models. Those are reviewed to justify not using them.

visuals.title: Four questions and what the thesis did about each
rows: handcrafted features; no pretrained or self-supervised model
early, early + block, late simple, late CCC-weighted
visuals.caption: Look at the last column: neural networks are reviewed only to justify not training one.

cards.key: Literature Review > Modelling and Fusion for Small Multimodal Data > Learning from Small Cohorts
cards.gist: Wearable emotion data from real settings are scarce and mostly lab-based. Across 19 datasets scored on held-out people, handcrafted features generalise better than deep networks trained from raw signal (FEEL 2025). Pretrained models (NormWear) and self-supervised learning (SigRep) exist, but the thesis uses handcrafted features.
steps: Handcrafted, windowed features per sensor, 114 columns in total (Methods 3.3.2).
No foundation model or self-supervised pretraining was used.

qa.q: Why not train a deep network on the raw signals?
qa.a: With 16 to 22 people, a network trained from scratch has too little to learn from, and FEEL 2025 shows across 19 datasets, scored on held-out people, that handcrafted features generalise better than such networks.

qa.q: Why not use a pretrained foundation model like NormWear?
qa.a: It is a fair alternative, since it brings knowledge from large external corpora. I did not test it. It is a natural future step, but it would not fix the core problem that the ratings are mostly person-specific.

traps: FEEL2025 was once cited for 'the within-to-cross-subject gap recurs across nineteen datasets'; audit: WRONG, FEEL is LOSO throughout and has no within-subject baseline (citation_audit.md:381). It now carries only 'handcrafted beats scratch deep nets on held-out people', which is correct.
FEEL's claim concerns networks trained from scratch; the text says so. It does not rule out pretrained models.

cards.key: Literature Review > Modelling and Fusion for Small Multimodal Data > Model Families
cards.gist: Deep networks win on raw sequences, but on tabular features at this size **tree ensembles** beat them (Grinsztajn 2022, 45 datasets). So the thesis uses tree ensembles, compared against gradient boosting and a regularised linear model.
steps: Eight families: Ridge, SVR (RBF), RandomForest, ExtraTrees, HistGradientBoosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost (Methods 3.3.4). Each has a 3-candidate grid.
Nested tuning inside each outer LOSO fold: ridge inner LeaveOneGroupOut, others inner GroupKFold(5), candidate chosen by mean inner CCC (scripts/exp1_v2/families.py:119-131).
Every model sits in Pipeline(SimpleImputer(median), StandardScaler, model), fitted on training participants only (families.py:122, 130).
Standard model: ExtraTreesRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_depth in {None, 8, 4}, random_state=42) (scripts/exp1_v2/predictions.py:21).
Families span 0.0124 CCC across the twenty cells, inside 0.08.

qa.q: Why tree ensembles for this data?
qa.a: The features are tabular, heterogeneous (pupil millimetres, EDA microsiemens, 88 acoustic parameters), with outliers and missing values, and the training set is about 12,000 rows at most. Grinsztajn et al. show tree ensembles beat deep networks in exactly that regime, below about 10,000 training samples per dataset.

qa.q: Why Extra Trees and not XGBoost?
qa.a: All eight families tied within the 0.08 resolution. The pre-set tie-break picks the tree family whose scores vary least across the twenty cells, and that was Extra Trees. So it is the standard model by rule, not because it was clearly better.

qa.q: Why do you scale features for tree models, which don't need it?
qa.a: So every family sees exactly the same inputs. Scaling does not change a tree's splits but is needed for ridge and SVR. Keeping one pipeline means a difference between families is only a difference between models.

qa.q: Why impute for boosted trees that handle NaN natively?
qa.a: Same reason: identical inputs for all eight families. The imputer uses the training-fold median and is applied unchanged to the held-out visitor.

qa.q: Why review CNNs and TCNs if you don't use them?
qa.a: To show what the alternative would be for raw signals and why it does not fit here. An earlier draft had network arms, and they were removed because the review itself argues trees suit this data size.

traps: predictions.py's docstring still says CatBoost is the standard model; that is stale. The grid and the thesis use ExtraTreesRegressor (BRIEF; scripts/exp1_v2/predictions.py:21).

Grinsztajn truncated datasets to 10,000 training samples; the rcea training set is about 12,000 rows, but those rows come from only 21 people and are strongly autocorrelated, so the effective sample size is much smaller. That makes the small-data argument stronger, not weaker.
The Lundberg2017 (SHAP) citation for 'trees expose importances through gain' was WRONG and removed (citation_audit.md:380). The thesis reports no feature importances.

visuals.title: All eight model families score about zero in both streams
visuals.caption: Look at the diamonds: each is a family's mean over 10 sensor-by-axis cells (grey dots), and all sit inside the 0.08 band. The spread is 0.016 for rcea and 0.032 for retro, so ExtraTrees (orange) was carried as the standard model.

visuals.title: Tuning happens inside each training fold
visuals.caption: Look at the inner split: LeaveOneGroupOut for ridge, GroupKFold(5) for the rest. The best grid point is refitted on all training visitors, with imputer and scaler inside the Pipeline.

cards.key: Literature Review > Modelling and Fusion for Small Multimodal Data > Combining Sensors
cards.gist: Sensors can be joined in three places (Poria 2017): **early fusion** puts all features into one model, **late fusion** trains one model per sensor and combines their predictions, and **model-level fusion** couples them inside the model. The thesis tests early and late fusion.
steps: Exp 2 runs four mechanisms on every subset of the five sensors (Methods 3.4.3): early fusion (114 columns), early fusion + 8-column cross-sensor block (122), late simple average, late CCC-weighted average (weights = each sensor's Exp 1 CCC for the slice, negatives floored at 0, renormalised) (scripts/exp1_v2/exp2_fusion.py:101-143).
Decision made on the full five-sensor set only. Carried: early fusion + block at +0.0271 mean CCC (fusion_summary.json by_size early_plus_block 5).
Model-level fusion was not tested.

numbers.what: Five-sensor mean CCC over 4 slices (early / early+block / late CCC / late simple)

qa.q: What is the difference between early and late fusion?
qa.a: Early fusion puts all sensors' features in one matrix and lets one model weigh them. Late fusion trains one model per sensor and averages their predictions. Early fusion can use interactions between sensors; late fusion is more robust when a sensor is missing.

qa.q: Why no model-level fusion or transformer?
qa.a: Model-level fusion needs a network that couples modalities internally, which needs far more data than 16 to 22 people. I kept every arm on the standard tree model so a difference is only due to the combination rule.

qa.q: Did fusion help?
qa.a: No. The best combination equals the best single sensor, +0.0822, and the carried arm reaches +0.0271 on average. Everything is inside the 0.08 resolution.

qa.q: How does late fusion deal with a missing sensor?
qa.a: If a sensor produces no prediction for a row, the averaging renormalises the weights over the sensors that did, so every arm is scored on the same rows.

traps: Poria2017 is a review of multimodal sentiment analysis (text, audio, video), not physiology. It is cited for the taxonomy of fusion levels, which is general.

Earlier drafts cited Younis2022 for a stacking meta-learner (WRONG) and Singh2026 for sensor weighting (WEAK: entropy-based, not validation-score-based) (citation_audit.md:829-830). The CCC-weighted average still cites Singh2026 in Methods; if asked, the principle of reliability-weighted decision fusion is theirs, the exact weighting by Exp 1 CCC is mine.

cards.key: Literature Review > Modelling and Fusion for Small Multimodal Data > Measuring the Relationship Between Sensors
cards.gist: You can also measure **whether two sensors move together** and feed that in as a feature. Such measures depend on window length and find coupling even in unrelated series, so the fair reference is a **surrogate** (a time-shifted copy), not zero. Pupil and EDA are known to co-vary during affective picture viewing (Bradley 2008).
steps: Eight columns (Methods 3.4.2): Pearson correlation for pupil-EDA, pupil-HRV, EDA-HRV; lag-searched max correlation (up to 5 s either way) for the same three pairs; count and rate of SCR onsets within 3 s after a pupil dilation (scripts/exp1_v2/exp2_crosssensor.py:153 pair_columns, :179 event_columns).
Signals: baseline-corrected pupil, phasic EDA, instantaneous heart rate, on a shared 4 Hz grid (to_grid :123).
Window swept 5, 10, 15 s (not the 3/6/9 s of Multiverse2025).
Surrogate: one signal of each pair rotated by a random offset ('data sliding', Moulder2018), repeated (scripts/exp1_v2/exp2_block_surrogate.py; block_for rotate argument :196).
Result: the block beats its surrogate in 1 of 12 cells where chance gives 0.6 (Results 4.3.2).

qa.q: What does a cross-sensor feature add that the sensors alone don't?
qa.a: It says whether the pupil and the skin moved together in that window, not what each did. If arousal drives both, coupling could be a cleaner signal than either alone. In this data it was not: it beat its own surrogate in one cell of twelve.

qa.q: Why a surrogate baseline instead of comparing to zero?
qa.a: A maximum correlation over many lags is high even for unrelated signals. Rotating one signal in time keeps each signal's own rhythm and distribution but breaks the timing between them, so the surrogate shows what the column gives by chance. A column must beat that, not zero.

qa.q: Is your block the same as CorrNet?
qa.a: No. CorrNet learns a projection that maximises correlation between two modalities. My block measures correlation and hands the number to the model. The learned version is what the DCCA arm does in the alignment comparison.

qa.q: Why sweep the window?
qa.a: Window length changes the magnitude and even the direction of synchrony estimates (Multiverse 2025). So I tried 5, 10 and 15 s, about one, two and three coupled pupil-EDA episodes, and carried the best.

qa.q: Why is the lag bound 5 s?
qa.a: A pupil response peaks by about 3 s after a trigger; an EDA response starts 1 to 3 s after and can peak as late as 6 s. The widest plausible separation is about 3 s, and 5 s leaves margin for slower responses.

qa.q: Why include an EDA-HRV pair if Wass found EDA co-varies with nothing at the tonic level?
qa.a: The block covers all three physiological pairs for completeness, and every column faces the surrogate test. Wass is infants, so I treat it as a caution, not as a reason to exclude. The pupil-EDA pair has the most direct support (Bradley 2008) and is the only pair with event columns.

traps: Wass2015 studied 37 twelve-month-old infants. The audit first marked it CONTRADICTS, because it had been cited to support EDA-heart co-variation, which it disproves (citation_audit.md:816). It is now used correctly as a caution. If asked why cite infants at all: it is the only concurrent five-index co-variation study I found, and the text says it transfers as a caution, not a parameter.

Multiverse2025 is a PsyArXiv preprint on interpersonal cardiac synchrony between two people, sweeping 3, 6 and 9 s windows (citation_audit.md:831). The thesis sweeps 5, 10, 15 s within one person. The text scopes it correctly; only the lesson 'window length matters' transfers.
Moulder2018's demonstrations are between-person motion and video data. What transfers is the need for a surrogate, not a specific scheme (the text says so).

Bradley2008 (Psychophysiology 45:602) is measured across pictures in a seated dim room, so it supports that pupil and EDA respond to the same material, not second-by-second tracking in a walking visitor. Its verification status for this use is not recorded in citation_audit.md (an older Bradley2008 entry, the IAPS chapter, was removed from a different claim).
GroupSynchrony2023 measures synchrony between people; the text keeps it apart from within-person coupling.
The 'following-response' event window is one-directional (SCR after dilation); the audit noted a symmetric earlier design was wrong and it was changed (citation_audit.md:840s).

cards.key: Literature Review > The HERE Dataset and What Its Analysis Showed
cards.gist: Van der Kaaden collected this dataset (22 live RCEA, 23 retrospective RetroSketch) and classified seven k-means classes of valence and arousal. Within a person balanced accuracy was about **0.84**; for a new person it fell to **0.20 to 0.24** (chance 0.14), and visitors did not agree on the same painting (ICC at most 0.064). This thesis starts from his configuration and asks whether that collapse survives a continuous target and every tested remedy.
steps: His data: 12,706 RCEA samples from 22 people and 9,427 RetroSketch samples from 23 (Bas txt:2213).
His RCEA reduction: 4 Hz to 1 Hz by the modal value per second (Bas txt:1659). This thesis: median (features.py:57).

His delay: four methods did not converge; fixed 1 s arousal, 2 s valence; robustness check showed no difference in correlations (Bas txt:2160-2194). This thesis: no fixed label delay, window delay searched per fold.

His labels: k=7 k-means on raw (valence, arousal) per method; k=6 shared space for cross-method (Bas txt:2300, 2551-2565). This thesis: continuous 0 to 10 rating (Exp 1 to 2) and equal-width ordered levels (Exp 3 to 5).

His evaluation: within-participant CV and LOSO; balanced accuracy. Table 4.10: Extra Trees CV 0.84 / LOSO 0.24 (rcea), 0.84 / 0.20 (retro); RF 0.23 / 0.20; SVM 0.16 / 0.14; LogReg 0.17 / 0.10 (Bas txt:2525-2533).
His cross-method (6 classes): 0.17 to 0.18 best balanced accuracy, n_train/n_test 2424/1222 (Bas txt:2541-2565).
His correlations: speech/text |r| <= 0.11, physiology |r| <= 0.07 (Bas txt:2466).
His painting ICC: highest 0.064 (retro arousal, 5 s window, mean aggregation) (Bas txt:2275, 3417).

This thesis's starting configuration equals his published values (30 deg/s, no gaze correction, trailing 0 s, IBI multiplier 4, NeuroKit + 5-MAD, 12 s EDA window) (Methods 3.3.3), and the eight families include his four.

This thesis's usable cohort: 22 rcea, 16 retro. The raw drop holds 20 retro annotation files, and four (M33, M36, M38, M47) have entirely empty valence/arousal columns (checked in raw_data_from_sensors/RETRO annotation in 1hz), leaving 16 (scripts/exp1_v2/selection.py:53).

numbers.what: LOSO balanced accuracy (Extra Trees rcea / retro)

qa.q: What did van der Kaaden do and find, in short?
qa.a: He built the VR museum, collected eye, EDA, PPG and speech from 45 visitors with two annotation methods, and classified seven k-means regions of the valence-arousal plane. Within people he got about 0.84 balanced accuracy, but on a new person it fell to 0.20 to 0.24, near the 0.14 chance level. His conclusion: the patterns are individual, not shared.
qa.src: Thesis - Final - Bas van der Kaaden.txt:2551-2565, 2984-2986

qa.q: How exactly does your thesis differ from his?
qa.a: Four ways. Target: he predicted seven k-means classes; I predict the continuous 0 to 10 rating scored by CCC, then equal-width ordered levels scored by QWK. Protocol: I report only subject-independent LOSO, with every tuning and configuration choice made inside the training fold. Pipeline: I rebuilt the processing and searched five open parameters instead of fixing them, and removed his fixed label delay in favour of a searched window delay. New questions: fusion, scoping to the painting, variance decomposition and personalisation, none of which he ran.

qa.q: Why move away from k-means classes?
qa.a: K-means regions are fitted to the data, so their meaning depends on the cohort and, unless fitted inside each fold, leak information. They also mix valence and arousal into one label and ignore order. A continuous per-axis target with CCC keeps the full information; equal-width levels are fixed by design and ordered, so QWK can reward near misses.

qa.q: Is your result consistent with his?
qa.a: Yes, in a stricter form. His LOSO collapse to near chance reappears as CCC at the floor for every sensor, family, fusion, target and scoping I tried. And my variance decomposition explains why: 36 to 65% of a rating is the person and at most 1.5% the painting.

qa.q: His LOSO is 0.20 to 0.24, which is above 1/7 = 0.14. Isn't that some signal?
qa.a: It is a little above chance, but with standard deviations of 0.12 to 0.20 across folds, and balanced accuracy on k-means classes can pick up the person's typical region. My CCC asks whether the second-by-second movement is tracked, which is harder. His simplest model on retro was 0.10, below chance.
qa.src: Thesis - Final - Bas van der Kaaden.txt:2530-2533

qa.q: What was his within-person 0.84 measuring?
qa.a: Training and test data came from the same people, so the model could learn each person's typical feature levels and rating region. That is why it collapses on a new person. It is not evidence the features track affect.
qa.src: Thesis - Final - Bas van der Kaaden.txt:2551-2560

qa.q: How did he handle the RCEA delay, and why didn't you copy it?
qa.a: He tried four estimation methods, none converged, and he applied a fixed 1 s for arousal and 2 s for valence from the general trend and benchmark figures. His own robustness check found no difference in correlations. I instead search the window direction and delay inside each training fold, because lag varies by annotator and dimension.
qa.src: Thesis - Final - Bas van der Kaaden.txt:2160-2194; final_thesis_body.tex:334

qa.q: Why do you have 16 retro participants when he had 23?
qa.a: The raw drop I received has 20 retro annotation files, and four of them (M33, M36, M38, M47) have completely empty valence and arousal columns. That leaves 16 with usable labels.

qa.q: Your ICC is 0.000 to 0.002 and his best was 0.064. Why different?
qa.a: Different computations. He computed ICC(2) on short painting windows of 5 to 15 s with several aggregations and reported the best of many configurations. Mine is from a crossed variance model on one mean rating per visitor per painting. Both say visitors do not agree on a painting.
qa.src: Thesis - Final - Bas van der Kaaden.txt:3407-3417; scripts/exp1_v2/exp4_variance.py:156

qa.q: Did he fuse modalities or do variance decomposition?
qa.a: No variance decomposition and no painting-level modelling. His features were aligned into one table, and there is one feature-concatenation comparison in an appendix, but no decision-level fusion study.

traps: The thesis says he modelled 'roughly 2,500 real-time and 1,200 retrospective rows'. The only place those counts appear in his thesis is the cross-method table (n = 2,424 and 1,222, Bas txt:2541). His aligned dataset has 12,706 and 9,427 samples (Bas txt:2213). I could not find in his text how the within-method rows were reduced. If asked, say the figure comes from his reported train/test sizes and the reduction is not described.
'Close to chance' for 0.20 to 0.24: chance for seven balanced classes is 0.143, so it is modestly above chance. The honest phrase is 'a large drop from 0.84 to near chance'.

His 'CV' is described as within-participant cross-validation (Bas txt:2552). CLAUDE.md notes it was 5-fold not grouped by participant. His delay appendix used GroupKFold(5) (Bas txt:3277). Do not claim more detail than that.
The thesis says 'forty-five visitors' here, and Limitations says 'the 38 collected'. 45 were collected; 38 (22 + 16) are usable in this thesis. If pressed, that is the reconciliation.
The raw EDA cohort in Results 4.1.2 has 47 recordings, more than 45 visitors, because signal-quality figures are measured on the full raw cohort including files outside the two analysed subsets.

His RCEA reducer was the mode; this thesis uses the median. The loader default is still 'modal' (scripts/annotation/rcea_alignment.py:67), but the thesis code passes reducer='median' (features.py:57).

CLAUDE.md, CODEMAP and parts of DATA_FACTS still describe k=7 KMeans labels and a RandomForest model. Those are his (and this project's early replication) choices, not the submitted thesis. utils.py still carries CLUSTER_K = {rcea: 7, retro: 7, combined: 6}; it is not used by scripts/exp1_v2.

cards.key: Literature Review > Shared versus Person-Specific Response Across People
cards.gist: Predicting one person's feelings is a different question from whether people react alike. Mixed models split rating variance into a part the stimulus drives and a part the person drives, and the person part is reliable, not noise (Finn 2020). Responses to art are only partly shared, which motivates the Exp 4 variance split.
steps: Exp 4 variance decomposition (Methods 3.6.6): crossed random-intercept model y = mu + u_person + u_painting + e, fitted by REML on attended rows (scripts/exp1_v2/exp4_variance.py:102 stage_ratings, crossed_varcomp_with_fallback).
Checks: participant-cluster bootstrap CI, painting jackknife, one-way eta-squared, binned (3-level) target, and one mean per visitor-painting read as ICC (stage_icc :156).
Extended to every sensor feature (stage_sensors :185; 244 fits, 35 hit the boundary and excluded).
Significance elsewhere: Wilcoxon signed-rank over participants with BH-FDR (Aarts2014 unit-of-analysis logic, Benjamini1995).

qa.q: What is the difference between ICC and a variance decomposition?
qa.a: ICC asks how much raters agree on the same targets. A variance decomposition splits the total variance of all ratings into a person share, a painting share and a residual. At one mean per visitor-painting, the painting share is the ICC, but the decomposition also tells you how big the person share is, which is the key number for a subject-independent model.

qa.q: Why does a big person share matter for your prediction task?
qa.a: A large stable person offset is exactly what a LOSO model cannot know for a new visitor. So up to two thirds of a rating is out of reach before any sensor is considered. And the painting share, which a shared model could exploit, is at most 1.5%.

qa.q: Why does Finn 2020 matter?
qa.a: It shows the person-specific part of a naturalistic response is reliable, not noise. So a big person share is real structure, which is why personalisation in Exp 5 is the logical next test.

qa.q: Why test at the participant level?
qa.a: Seconds from one person are not independent. Treating them as independent inflates significance. So each test uses one score per participant, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with false-discovery control over the family (Aarts 2014, Benjamini and Hochberg 1995).

traps: The decomposition uses only attended rows, so it covers 20 rcea and 15 retro visitors, not the full 22 and 16.
The painting-share bootstrap CI is wide (up to 0.1 to 17.3%) because there are only five paintings. The honest claim is 'small', not 'precisely 0.1%'.

Stuldreher2020/2023 show EDA and heart rate can synchronise across people given the same content, partly through shared attention. That is a between-person synchrony result, not evidence the sensors track self-reported affect.
Bradley2008 was removed from the art-agreement claim here because that entry was the IAPS chapter (photographs, not art); Specker2020 carries it alone (citation_audit.md:577).

visuals.title: Who is looking explains far more than which painting
visuals.caption: Look at the thin orange slice: the painting explains 0.1 to 1.5% of a rating, the visitor 36 to 64%, in both streams. Only visitors with attended rows count (20 rcea, 15 retro).

cards.key: Literature Review > Personalising Affect Models to the Individual
cards.gist: If response is personal, adapt the model to the person. Methods differ in what they need from the new visitor: only unlabelled signal (subtract a resting baseline, align distributions), a few labels (few-shot tuning), or their own ratings to set level boundaries. Most successes are lab EEG with strong stimuli, and a gain on one axis need not carry to the other.
steps: Exp 5 tests three levers (Methods 3.7; scripts/exp1_v2/exp5_personalisation.py):

Baseline-window calibration: per visitor, median of each feature over the seconds before the first painting view, subtracted from all that visitor's rows; applied to training and held-out visitors alike; no labels (centre_by_baseline :105-117).
Labelled warm-up: the held-out visitor's first 30, 60, 120 or 180 s of rated rows appended unweighted to training, refit per duration and fold; warm-up rows never scored (run_arm :166-181).
Person-relative target: each visitor's 3-level boundaries at equal-frequency quantiles of their own ratings; held-out visitor's from the opening 180 s only (person_levels :123-134).
All levers scored on one common row set per visitor (after baseline window and longest warm-up). Paired Wilcoxon on per-participant QWK (and CCC where predictions differ), BH-FDR within each lever.
Not implemented: CORAL, fine-tuning, contrastive subject-invariant features, retrieval.

numbers.what: Best warm-up gain (pooled QWK, retro arousal, 180 s)

qa.q: Which personalisation methods from the review did you actually test?
qa.a: Three: removing each visitor's resting baseline, which needs no labels; a labelled warm-up of 30 to 180 s folded into training; and person-relative level boundaries. I did not test CORAL, fine-tuning or contrastive methods.

qa.q: Why not CORAL, since it needs no labels?
qa.a: It is a good candidate and I did not run it. Baseline subtraction is its simplest special case, a mean shift, and it did not help: it lowered CCC on three of four slices. With 16 to 22 people I could not have resolved a small gain from CORAL either.

qa.q: Is the labelled warm-up fine-tuning?
qa.a: Not in the neural-network sense. The held-out visitor's first N seconds are added to the other visitors' training rows and the tree model is refitted. It shows what a little of the visitor's own labelled data is worth.

qa.q: Why does the baseline lever use the median over the pre-painting window?
qa.a: The pre-painting stretch is the closest thing to rest in a free visit, and its boundary was already defined by Exp 4's attention labels, so I did not choose it again. The median resists one artefact in a short window.

qa.q: Why are lab EEG personalisation results a poor guide?
qa.a: The emotion there is deliberately provoked, the contrast between states is strong, and the signal is from the brain, not a wrist. A calm museum with wrist and eye sensors gives much weaker, noisier signal, so a 93% EEG figure says little about what is possible here.

qa.q: Did personalisation work?
qa.a: Not established. Figures rise in 21 of 24 cells, but none of 48 paired tests survives correction. The warm-up improves with more annotation, up to +0.30 pooled QWK on retro arousal at 180 s, but a museum cannot ask visitors for their ratings. The only no-label lever lowers CCC on three slices while raising QWK.

traps: Chapter 2 describes 'per-person standardisation' of the target; the Exp 5 implementation uses equal-frequency quantiles of each visitor's own ratings, not z-scoring (exp5_personalisation.py:134). Both make levels person-relative; say quantiles if asked.

The person-relative target leaves the regressor untouched, so its CCC equals the reference by construction; 4 of the 48 tests compare identical quantities, so 44 are informative (Results 4.6 Verdict).
Abinaya2026 is a single driver-cognitive-state paper; the audit softened the original 'most often reported' to 'has been reported' (citation_audit.md:383).
Lu2023DFFNet's 93.4% and 82.3% are categorical EEG accuracies; the text says so. Its exact figures are on the audit's to-verify list (citation_audit.md:86).

The baseline window is the seconds before the first painting view; for some visitors it is short, and HRV features (60 s windows) often have no valid value there, so they keep raw values (Methods 3.7.1).
The warm-up puts the held-out visitor's labels into training. That is deliberate and stated, but it means Exp 5 warm-up results are not subject-independent in the Exp 1 sense.

cards.key: DATA > The 60-second version
cards.gist: **38 visitors** of a VR museum in two groups that are never pooled: **22 rcea (rated live with a joystick)** and **16 retro (rated afterwards from a replay)**. **One row = one second of one visitor**, labelled with valence and arousal from 0 to 10: **12,660 rcea rows** and **7,022 retro rows**. Pupil, EDA, HRV and speech give **114 feature columns**, **122** with the eight cross-sensor columns.
steps: **Where it comes from.** Van der Kaaden ran a free-roaming VR version of the exhibition "HERE: Black in Rembrandt's Time". Visitors walked a room with **five paintings** (B1, B2, B3, C5, C6) and could talk to a guide agent by push-to-talk.

**Sensors.** An **HTC Vive Pro Eye** headset gave pupil diameter and gaze. An **Empatica EmbracePlus** wristband gave skin conductance (EDA), pulse (BVP, used for heart-rate variability), acceleration and skin temperature. The headset microphone gave speech. The VR engine logged where the visitor stood and which painting they faced.

**Labels.** Two groups, never mixed. **rcea**: the visitor moves a joystick during the visit, logged at 4 Hz; I take the **per-second median**. **retro**: the visitor re-watches their session afterwards and sketches a curve, delivered at 1 Hz. Both are **0 to 10** on valence and arousal.
**Cohort.** 48 raw participant folders. **22 usable rcea visitors**. For retro, 20 files exist, 4 contain only empty ratings, so **16 usable**. 38 people in total, never pooled.

**What a row is.** One UTC second of a visitor's analysed window. Each sensor is summarised over its own window that **ends at that second**: pupil over the previous **8 s**, EDA over **3 s**, heart-rate variability over **60 s**, speech over the **utterance** that covers the second.
**Size.** rcea **12,660 rows** (median 466 per visitor), retro **7,022 rows** (median 393.5).

**Columns.** pupil 7, EDA 10, HRV 8, speech acoustics 88 (eGeMAPS), speech content 1 (VADER) = **114**. Experiment 2 adds **8 cross-sensor columns** = **122**, the matrix carried into Experiments 3 to 5.

**What the model sees.** A float matrix X (rows by columns), with missing values filled by the **training-fold median** and every column **z-scored** by a scaler fitted on the training visitors only. Tested by **leave-one-visitor-out**: train on 21 (or 15), test on the one left out.
**The one-line honest caveat.** A lot is missing by design: EDA failed for 4 of 22 rcea and 9 of 16 retro visitors, and speech is only present inside utterance spans (about 71% of rows).
