qa.q: How did the timezone bug happen?
qa.a: The raw rcea file has two timestamp columns. The one called timestamp_utc_plus1 is tagged as UTC but its values are Dutch local time. Parsed as UTC it is one hour off, and the ratings did not overlap the sensors at all. The other column, timestamp_cet, is tagged correctly, so I parse that one.

qa.q: Did the accelerometer bug affect your results?
qa.a: Not the submitted ones. It was found and fixed on 8 September; the submitted features were built on 10 and 11 September. Before the fix the motion mask was essentially random because a timestamp column leaked into the magnitude and overflowed.

qa.q: Is there anything still wrong that you know of?
qa.a: One small thing. The rcea timestamp parser drops samples that fall on exact whole seconds, so the per-second median is usually of three samples, and for six visitors of one. I measured the effect: no second is lost, and labels change by 0.003 to 0.12 points on average on a 0 to 10 scale. It would not change any conclusion, but it should be fixed with format ISO8601.

qa.q: What happened with M19?
qa.a: Whisper transcribed silence as the word "you" 24 times. The segments are so short that none covers a whole second, so M19 simply has no speech rows. Its other sensors are fine and it stays in the other cells.

qa.q: What is the M07 clock problem?
qa.a: M07's VR-engine log and its eye file run on clocks that do not overlap, so I cannot place M07's painting views on its sensor timeline. It affects only the teleport mask for M07 and Experiment 4, where M07 has no attended second.

qa.q: How do you know the speech timeline bug is not in your results?
qa.a: The submitted acoustics come from a different function: openSMILE on each segment's own audio slice, mapped with the transcript's real-time start and end. The buggy timeline was only in the older frame-level extractor, which the thesis pipeline does not call.

traps: **Do not claim the pipeline is bug-free.** The RCEA parse issue is live in the submitted labels. Lead with the measured size: small, no second lost, conclusions unchanged in direction (not re-run, so say "I expect" rather than "I verified" for downstream numbers).

**The old EDA/BVP fix** ("rows lacking fractional seconds broke format inference") was solved with `errors="coerce"`, which works there because such rows are extremely rare in EDA/BVP (0 lost in checks). In RCEA, one row in four sits on a whole second, so the same approach loses data.

**Motion-mask calibration history**: `MOTION_MAD_MULTIPLIER = 5.0` was originally calibrated against the broken mask. In the submitted run k is searched (2, 3, 5) on the fixed mask, and 5 won. So the old calibration no longer matters, but the comment in `eda_processing.py` still describes it.

visuals.title: The submitted parse drops 39% of rcea samples and none of retro
visuals.caption: Look at the orange bars: pandas with errors='coerce' drops 25% or 75% of each rcea visitor's 4 Hz samples (**38.6%** overall), while retro's whole-second timestamps parse cleanly. No labelled second is lost; the per-second median just uses fewer samples.

cards.key: Methodology > Experiment 1: Unimodal Prediction
cards.gist: Experiment 1 tests each sensor on its own: can it predict valence or arousal for a visitor the model never saw? Five sensors x two axes x two streams (rcea, retro) give **20 cells**, each scored by leave-one-subject-out **CCC**. It also fixes the preprocessing settings and the model family that every later experiment inherits.
steps: Build a 1 Hz label grid per participant and stream (`features.py` `labels_v2`, `analysed_index`). rcea: 4 Hz joystick reduced by the **per-second median**, no fixed delay shift. retro: native 1 Hz.

For every candidate configuration, compute each sensor's features on that grid and cache them as `results/exp1_v2/features/{pid}_{stream}/{key}.parquet` (`features.py` `get`). Keys look like `P_vt30_c0_t0`, `E_nk_k5_w3`, `H_m3_t0`, `S_egemaps`, `S_vader`.
Pick the configuration inside every outer LOSO fold by a rank vote of the training participants, scored with Ridge(alpha=1) (`selection.py`).

With the selected configuration, compare **8 model families** per cell under outer LOSO with nested tuning (`families.py`), then carry **ExtraTrees** as the standard model and save its out-of-fold predictions (`predictions.py`).

Separately, describe each feature's relation to each axis by **within-participant Spearman**, Wilcoxon across participants, BH-FDR over all 436 tests (`relations.py`, `relations_literature.py`). This decides nothing downstream.
Speech is split into two sensors: acoustics (88 eGeMAPS functionals) and content (1 VADER compound score). Same recording, different information.
Feature counts per sensor: pupil 7, EDA 10, HRV 8, acoustics 88, content 1 = **114 columns**. A single-sensor model only ever sees its own sensor's columns.

qa.q: What is one row in your data?
qa.a: One second of one participant's visit, on a 1 Hz grid set by the ratings. Each row has that second's valence and arousal and the sensor features computed over a window around it. rcea has 12,660 such rows from 22 visitors, retro 7,022 from 16.

qa.q: Why treat speech as two sensors?
qa.a: The acoustics describe how something is said and the transcript describes what is said. They come from one recording but carry different information and different feature types, 88 acoustic numbers against one sentiment score. So I score them separately.

qa.q: Why not pool rcea and retro?
qa.a: They are different instruments with different label distributions, collected in different sessions. rcea is a live joystick, retro is drawn afterwards. Every selection and every model is run separately per stream.

qa.q: What is the order of the whole pipeline?
qa.a: Features for every candidate first, then the configuration vote inside each fold, then the family comparison on the selected configuration, then the standard model's predictions. The correlation analysis runs on the side and feeds nothing.

traps: The code folder is `scripts/exp1_v2/`, not `scripts/thesis_v2` as stale notes (CODEMAP.md, CLAUDE.md) say. Some docstrings are also stale: `predictions.py` says CatBoost, but its grid is ExtraTrees.

rcea labels have **no fixed delay correction**. The old code default (`rcea_alignment.py` VALENCE_DELAY_S = 2) is overridden with 0 in `labels_v2`. If asked about the 2 s delay from the origin study: the searched direction and delay (0 to 6 s) were meant to absorb it.

visuals.title: Each sensor gets its own window; 114 columns in all
visuals.caption: Look at the last column: 7 + 10 + 8 + 88 + 1 = **114**, and each cell uses one row only. The same keys won in every fold of both streams (22 rcea, 16 retro folds; `selection/winners_*.json`), so the table holds for rcea and retro alike.

cards.key: Methodology > Experiment 1: Unimodal Prediction > Signal Preparation
cards.gist: Each raw signal is cleaned before any feature is computed. Pupil: invalid samples dropped, eyes averaged, short blinks bridged, fast gaze marked as saccades, teleports masked. EDA: recordings without skin contact gated out, wrist motion masked, then a slow (tonic) and fast (phasic) part with SCR peaks; HRV: impossible or jumpy beat intervals replaced; speech: cut per utterance, then openSMILE and VADER.
steps: **Pupil 1, validity.** Samples with `valid_left==0` or `valid_right==0` set to NaN for that eye (`pupil_processing.py:141-144`).
**Pupil 2, range.** Diameters outside **1.5 to 9.0 mm** set to NaN (`pupil_processing.py:23-24, 146-148`).
**Pupil 3, eye averaging.** `pupil_mean = mean(left, right)` with NaN skipped, so if one eye is invalid the other eye alone is used (`pupil_processing.py:150-151`).

**Pupil 4, optional gaze-angle correction** (candidate c1 only): per participant, least squares of diameter on [1, x, y, x^2, y^2, xy] of gaze direction, keep residual plus the participant's mean; skipped if < 30 valid samples (`pupil_processing.py:101-122`). Runs before interpolation and baseline.
**Pupil 5, blinks.** `blink_flag = 1` when **both** eyes' validity flags are 0 (`pupil_processing.py:159-160`). Blinks are counted from this flag, not from gaps.

**Pupil 6, gap interpolation.** NaN runs whose wall-clock span (from the last valid sample before to the first valid after) is **<= 0.5 s** are linearly interpolated in time; longer gaps stay NaN (`pupil_processing.py:25, 76-98, 170`).
**Pupil 7, drift.** `pupil_mean_bc = pupil_mean - rolling 30 s time-window mean` (pandas `rolling('30s')`, which is **trailing**, min_periods=1) (`pupil_processing.py:26, 171-172`).
**Gaze 1, smoothing.** gaze_dir_x/y/z each smoothed with a **5-sample centred rolling median** (`pupil_processing.py:178-180`).
**Gaze 2, velocity.** Angle between consecutive unit vectors divided by dt; pairs with **dt > 0.1 s** get NaN velocity (`pupil_processing.py:53-73`, line 68).

**Gaze 3, classification.** Saccade = velocity above the rule's threshold (30, 240 or the adaptive value) or dispersion > 1 deg for I-DT (`features.py:117-191`). The 15 deg/s constant in `pupil_processing.py:33` is **not used** by exp1_v2.

**Teleports.** From `neo_data/observings.csv` positions: **jump** = records < 0.5 s apart with speed > **3 m/s**; **gap** = records >= 0.5 s apart with endpoint speed > **1.5 m/s**. Each event padded **+-0.5 s**; eye samples in it get saccade = NaN, which also breaks fixation and saccade runs (`teleport_detection.py:29-74`, `features.py:170-176, 190`). The diameter itself is **not** masked.
**EDA 1, gate.** Recording removed (all features NaN) if **>= 50% samples negative** or **P95 - P5 < 0.02 uS** (`eda_processing.py:43-55`). 20 of 47 recordings fail (18 negative, 2 flat).

**EDA 2, motion mask.** |acc| = sqrt(x^2+y^2+z^2) at 64 Hz; trailing 1 s rolling **RMS**; flag samples with RMS > **median + k x MAD** (raw MAD, no 1.4826), k in {2, 3, 5} (`eda_processing.py:101-114`). EDA samples (4 Hz) take the nearest ACC flag within 1 s, flagged samples set NaN and time-interpolated (`eda_processing.py:117-124`).

**EDA 3, decomposition.** NeuroKit: `nk.eda_process(method='neurokit')`, which is a **0.05 Hz Butterworth split** (low-pass = tonic, high-pass = phasic); at 4 Hz NeuroKit skips its cleaning filter. cvxEDA: `eda_clean` then `eda_phasic(method='cvxeda')` then the same `eda_peaks` (`eda_processing.py:127-168`).

**EDA 4, SCR peaks.** NeuroKit peak finder with `amplitude_min=0.1`: a peak is kept if its **prominence >= 0.1 x the largest peak prominence in the whole recording's phasic signal** (neurokit2 0.2.13 `signal_findpeaks(relative_height_min=0.1, relative_max=True)`).

**HRV 1, peaks.** BVP at 64 Hz, `nk.ppg_clean` then `nk.ppg_peaks(method='elgendi')` (dual moving average) (`hrv_processing.py:44-55`). IBI = peak-to-peak difference in ms, stamped at the later peak (`hrv_processing.py:58-63`).
**HRV 2, range.** IBIs outside **333.3 to 1500 ms (40 to 180 bpm)** set NaN (`hrv_processing.py:16-19, 81-82`).

**HRV 3, successive-difference filter.** dRR = diff of IBIs; flag an interval if |dRR - rolling median(dRR)| > **k x rolling MAD** of dRR, both over a **centred 45-beat window**, min 10 beats; k in {3, 4, 5} (`hrv_processing.py:83-87`).
**HRV 4, interpolation.** Flagged intervals set NaN and filled by time interpolation, so the beat count is kept and a `removed` flag remembers which were repaired (`hrv_processing.py:88-90`).

**Speech.** Transcript segments give `trimmed_start_sec`/`trimmed_end_sec` into the silence-removed audio and `dt_start`/`dt_end` in UTC. Clips < 0.1 s skipped. openSMILE eGeMAPSv02 Functionals per clip; VADER compound per segment text (`speech_sweep.py:38-92`, `text_features.py:63-100`).

numbers.value: median 23 Hz per session (18 at paintings, 47 elsewhere), nominal 120
EDA 4 Hz, ACC 64 Hz, BVP 64 Hz

qa.q: Is the gaze-angle correction a geometric model?
qa.a: No. It is a per-participant regression: I regress that person's diameter on their own gaze direction, with linear, squared and cross terms, and keep the residual plus their mean. It uses no labels and never crosses participants. It is only used in the c1 candidate, and c1 was not carried.

qa.q: Why subtract a baseline rather than divide?
qa.a: Subtractive baseline correction is the recommended standard for pupil data. Division distorts the signal when the baseline is small or noisy. With no trials in a free visit, I use a rolling 30 second window as the baseline.

qa.q: Is the rolling baseline centred or trailing?
qa.a: Trailing. pandas `rolling('30s')` on a time index uses the past 30 seconds up to the current sample. So the baseline never uses future samples.

qa.q: The tracker is 120 Hz. Does a 5-sample median mean 40 ms?
qa.a: Not in practice. The logger writes one sample per rendered frame, so the real rate is a median 23 Hz, and 18 Hz at the paintings. Five samples then span roughly 100 to 250 ms. The filter is defined in samples, not in time.

qa.q: What exactly does the 100 ms rule do?
qa.a: If two consecutive samples are more than 100 ms apart, the velocity for that pair is set to missing. So I never compute a velocity across a pause. Those missing velocities also break fixation and saccade runs.

qa.q: What is the adaptive threshold exactly?
qa.a: Per recording, median plus 3 times 1.4826 times the MAD of all finite smoothed velocities. It is one pass, not iterative. If fewer than 100 velocities exist it falls back to 240 deg/s. For M22 it came out at 31.6 deg/s.

qa.q: How is a teleport detected?
qa.a: From the engine's position log. Two records less than half a second apart with a speed above 3 m/s is a jump. A gap of half a second or more whose endpoints imply more than 1.5 m/s must contain a teleport, and the whole gap is masked. Each event is padded by half a second on each side.

qa.q: Is the SCR threshold absolute?
qa.a: No. NeuroKit's amplitude_min of 0.1 is relative: a candidate peak is kept only if its prominence is at least a tenth of the largest peak prominence in that recording's phasic signal. So each recording has its own bar. The absolute 0.01 to 0.05 uS figure only motivates the flat-recording gate.

qa.q: What is the NeuroKit decomposition?
qa.a: With method='neurokit', NeuroKit splits the signal with a 0.05 Hz Butterworth filter: below is tonic, above is phasic. cvxEDA instead solves a convex optimisation model. Because EDA is only 4 Hz, NeuroKit skips its 3 Hz cleaning low-pass.

qa.q: Is motion removed from HRV?
qa.a: No. There is no motion mask on the pulse channel. Instead every HRV window carries the share of its intervals that were repaired and the share of accelerometer samples flagged as motion, so the model can see bad stretches.

qa.q: What happens to a gated EDA recording?
qa.a: All ten EDA features become missing for that participant, never zero. In a single-sensor EDA cell those rows are dropped because no EDA feature is finite, so that visitor has no EDA fold.

traps: **Adaptive threshold wording.** The thesis says the adaptive threshold 'is estimated iteratively from the velocity samples below the current threshold' and then that median-based statistics are used 'instead'. The code is a **single pass**: median + 3 x 1.4826 x MAD of all finite velocities, with a 240 deg/s fallback (`features.py:117-123`). Honest answer: I used the robust median-based version in the spirit of Nystrom and Holmqvist and Voloh; it is not iterative.

**I-DT is an approximation.** The dispersion rule uses a centred 0.25 s window per sample and measures dispersion as 2 x the largest angle from the window's mean vector (`features.py:126-157`). It is not the classic I-DT with a minimum fixation duration. No rule has a minimum fixation duration.

**Teleport mask affects only classification.** The thesis gives luminance change after a teleport as one reason to exclude samples, but only saccade/fixation labels are masked. Pupil diameter samples near a teleport are kept. Also teleports happen between paintings where the position log has no records (records exist only while a painting is viewed), so only the gap rule catches them. M07's clock does not overlap and M26 has no records, so those get no mask.
**Real eye rate is 23 Hz, not 120.** The 5-sample median and the 100 ms rule behave very differently at 18 to 47 Hz. Pauses > 100 ms cover a median 57% of a session, so many velocities are NaN.
**One eye can stand in for both.** `mean(axis=1)` skips NaN, so seconds where one eye is invalid use a single eye. Eyes agree at median r = 0.92, M38 is the outlier at 0.12 and was kept.

**IBI filter formula.** The thesis says an interval whose 'difference from its predecessor exceeds a multiple of the rolling spread'. The code tests |dRR - rolling median(dRR)| > k x rolling MAD (raw MAD, no 1.4826). Close in spirit; state it precisely if asked.

**HRV magnitudes are implausible.** Across participants the median window SDNN is about 237 ms and RMSSD about 249 ms (normal short-term values are tens of ms), and k=3 still repairs a median 23% of intervals. The 'HRV' indices on walking wrist PPG largely measure beat-detection noise. The thesis flags that the Elgendi validation is at rest on fingertips and that this is pulse-rate variability, but it does not report these magnitudes. Answer honestly: the cardiac features are dominated by noise, which is consistent with the null result.

**Motion-mask threshold uses the recording's own median and MAD over the whole session**, the SCR threshold uses the whole recording's maximum, and the gaze correction is fitted on the whole session. These are label-free but not causal, so a real-time system would need running versions.
RUNBOOK.md's 'OPEN' note calls amplitude_min '0.1 uS'. That note is stale: the code comment and NeuroKit's source confirm it is relative, and the thesis text now says relative.
EDA wording 'smoothed over one second' is a trailing 1 s rolling **RMS** of the magnitude, with the window length in samples taken from the first sample gap.

**The SCR threshold sweep is not part of the submitted pipeline.** The Methods say the SCR amplitude threshold 'is swept from 0.02 to 0.2 so that the detected response counts are read against the choice'. That sweep was run in the earlier calibration phase (`scripts/pipeline_rebuild/calibration/calibrate_eda.py`, against van der Kaaden's output), and the code comment records that it 'had no effect in the 0.02-0.2 range tested' (`eda_processing.py:30-33`). The Exp 1 pipeline itself uses a fixed 0.1 (relative to the recording's largest phasic peak). **If asked:** 'The sweep was done during pipeline calibration, before the experiments; the detected counts did not change across that range, so the experiments use the inherited 0.1.'

visuals.title: Short blinks are bridged, longer gaps stay empty; fast gaze counts as a saccade
visuals.caption: Top row, look at the yellow dots: gaps of 0.5 s or less are bridged (147 samples for M01, 106 for M34), while longer gaps (red) and stretches with no tracker rows (grey) stay empty. Bottom row: a gaze sample faster than **30 deg/s** is a **saccade** sample (orange: 27% for M01, 43% for M34), and crosses are teleport samples, which get no label.

visuals.title: Motion samples are masked, then the signal splits into a slow and a fast part
visuals.caption: Look at the orange dots: samples taken during wrist motion are masked and interpolated (28 in each 90 s stretch). The y scales differ because M34's skin conductance is about 10 times M01's; the green **phasic** part carries the SCR peaks (11 and 10).

visuals.title: Bad heartbeat intervals are replaced by interpolation, not dropped
visuals.caption: Look at the crosses and diamonds: intervals outside 333 to 1,500 ms, or jumping too far from their neighbours, are replaced by the green interpolated line, so the beat count is kept. Over the whole visit that is **33%** of M01's intervals (230 of 699) and **29%** of M34's (100 of 346); crosses above 2,400 ms are drawn at 2,400.

cards.key: Methodology > Experiment 1: Unimodal Prediction > Feature Extraction
cards.gist: Each sensor is summarised over a window tied to every rated second, which puts all sensors on the 1 Hz label grid: pupil 8 s, EDA 3 s (searched), HRV 60 s, all ending at the rated second, and speech the whole utterance covering it. A window may shift by a searched delay but is never warped. The section also defines the correlation analysis, which only describes the data.
steps: **Window semantics** (`features.py:93-99`): trailing = [t - d - w, t - d), forward = [t + d, t + d + w). t is the start of the rated second (label second = floor to 1 s). Pupil and HRV use `searchsorted`, so the window includes lo and excludes hi. EDA uses `.loc[t-w : t]`, inclusive both ends.
**Pupil (8 s window, carried t0: [t-8, t))** (`features.py:194-239`). rec_s = number of distinct whole seconds in the window that contain a finite diameter.
`pupil_mean`: mean of the interpolated diameter in **mm**, NOT baseline-corrected (needs >= 3 finite samples).
`pupil_std`: population SD (ddof=0) of the same uncorrected diameter, mm.
`pupil_slope`: `np.polyfit(time, pupil_mean_bc, 1)` slope on the **baseline-corrected** series, mm per second (needs > 3 samples).
`blink_rate`: number of blink onsets (starts of runs of both-eyes-invalid samples) in the window **divided by rec_s**, i.e. blinks per recorded second.
`saccade_freq`: number of saccade-run onsets in the window **divided by rec_s**. Runs are broken by NaN (teleport mask, >100 ms pauses).

`fixation_duration`: the **longest overlap** in seconds between any fixation run (run of sub-threshold samples) and the window; 0 if none. A run's end is its last sample, so a 1-sample run has length 0.
`sample_count`: `i1 - i0`, number of tracker rows in the window, valid or not. Always numeric (0 if no rows).
**EDA (trailing w in {3,6,8,12,20} s, carried 3 s: [t-3, t])** (`eda_features.py:22-72`). EDA is 4 Hz, so 3 s is about 13 samples.
`eda_scl_mean`, `eda_scl_std` (ddof=0): tonic component, uS. `eda_scl_slope_per_sample`: polyfit slope of tonic against sample index, **uS per sample** (per 0.25 s).
`eda_scr_count`: number of SCR peak samples in the window.
`eda_scr_amp_mean/median/std`: phasic value (uS) **at the peak samples**; 0 when no peak; std 0 with one peak.
`eda_scr_risetime_mean_s/median_s`: per peak, seconds from the lowest phasic value in the preceding 5 s to the peak; NaN when no peak.
`eda_motion_fraction`: mean of the motion flag over the window's EDA samples.
**HRV (60 s window, carried t0: [t-60, t))** (`features.py:258-301`), on the cleaned NN series in ms.
`hrv_n`: number of NN intervals (beats) whose time stamp is in the window, including repaired ones. Always numeric.
`hrv_motion_frac`: ACC motion mask (fixed k=5) resampled to per-second mean, averaged over the window.

Needs >= 10 intervals for the rest: `hrv_repaired_frac` = share of intervals in the window flagged and interpolated; `hrv_meanNN` mean (ms); `hrv_SDNN` SD ddof=1 (ms); `hrv_RMSSD` sqrt(mean(diff^2)) (ms).
`hrv_SD2`: SD1^2 = 0.5 x var(diff, ddof=1); SD2 = sqrt(2 x var(NN, ddof=1) - SD1^2) (Brennan formula) (ms).

`hrv_HF`: `_frequency_domain`: NN resampled to a 4 Hz uniform grid, mean removed, Welch PSD (nperseg = min(n, 256)), power summed over **0.15 to 0.4 Hz** times bin width, **ms^2**; needs >= 8 intervals and >= 16 grid points (`hrv_features.py:39-83`).

**Speech acoustics (88)**: eGeMAPSv02 Functionals per utterance, copied onto every 1 Hz second from `dt_start` to `dt_end` (`speech_sweep.py:53-92`). Groups: F0 semitone (10), loudness (10), spectral flux (2), MFCC 1-4 (8), jitter (2), shimmer (2), HNR (2), H1-H2 (2), H1-A3 (2), formants F1-F3 frequency, bandwidth, amplitude (18), voiced-segment alpha ratio, Hammarberg, two spectral slopes, spectral flux (10), voiced MFCC 1-4 (8), five unvoiced means (5), six rhythm measures (loudness peaks per s, voiced segments per s, mean and SD of voiced and unvoiced segment length) (6), equivalent sound level (1). Sum 88.
**Speech content (1)**: `vader_compound` in [-1, 1] per transcript segment, copied onto every second from `dt_start` to `dt_end` (`text_features.py:63-100`).

**Correlation analysis** (defined here, run in `relations.py`): Spearman within each participant (>= 30 paired seconds), median and quartiles across participants, Wilcoxon signed-rank on the coefficients (>= 8 participants), BH-FDR over all tests.

numbers.value: HF 0.15 to 0.4 Hz, ms^2, 4 Hz resampling
about 71% of rows, although voiced speech is a median 6.9% of a visit
pupil_mean 3.8 mm, sample_count 191 per 8 s, blink_rate 0.27 /s, saccade_freq 3.9 /s

qa.q: How many columns go into each model?
qa.a: Only the sensor's own columns: 7 for pupil, 10 for EDA, 8 for HRV, 88 for speech acoustics and 1 for speech content. For example the HRV valence model on rcea sees a matrix of 12,152 rows by 8 columns, and each fold trains on that minus the held-out visitor's rows.

qa.q: Why is the pupil window fixed at 8 seconds?
qa.a: A cognitive pupil response starts about half a second after its trigger and unfolds over two to three seconds, so a full episode is three to four seconds. Triggers are not controlled here, so 8 seconds holds a full episode even if it starts a few seconds off the rated second. Only direction and delay are searched.

qa.q: Why 60 seconds for HRV?
qa.a: It is the shortest length at which the indices I use stay valid according to Castaldo. RMSSD is valid even at 10 seconds. I dropped LF and VLF because their bands need two and five minutes.

qa.q: What is the denominator for blink rate and saccade frequency?
qa.a: The number of seconds in the window that contain at least one recorded pupil sample. So they are events per recorded second, not per 8 seconds. That stops tracking gaps from looking like low rates.

qa.q: Is pupil_mean drift-corrected?
qa.a: No. pupil_mean and pupil_std use the interpolated diameter in millimetres. Only pupil_slope is computed on the baseline-corrected series. The mean of a baseline-corrected series would sit near zero and lose the level.

qa.q: How is fixation duration defined?
qa.a: The longest time any single fixation run overlaps the window, in seconds. A fixation run is a stretch of consecutive samples below the velocity threshold, broken by saccades or missing samples. There is no minimum duration.

qa.q: How is SD2 computed?
qa.a: From the NN intervals in the window. SD1 squared is half the variance of the successive differences. SD2 is the square root of twice the NN variance minus SD1 squared. That is the standard Poincare identity.

qa.q: How is HF power computed?
qa.a: I resample the window's NN intervals onto a 4 Hz grid, remove the mean, run a Welch periodogram and sum power between 0.15 and 0.4 Hz. The unit is ms squared.

qa.q: Why is speech present on 71% of rows if people spoke 7% of the time?
qa.a: Each utterance's features are copied onto every second of its transcript segment, from dt_start to dt_end. Whisper segments include pauses, often 5 to 20 seconds and sometimes over 100. So the utterance span is much longer than the voiced audio.

qa.q: What are the 88 eGeMAPS features?
qa.a: The extended Geneva Minimalistic Acoustic Parameter Set from openSMILE, at the functionals level. It covers pitch, loudness, voice quality (jitter, shimmer, HNR), spectral shape (MFCCs, slopes, alpha ratio, Hammarberg), formants, and rhythm such as voiced segments per second. Mostly each descriptor's mean and normalised SD over the utterance.

qa.q: Why a fixed window and not DTW?
qa.a: The sensor and the rating come from the same person on the same clock. All that separates them is a lag, and a searched shift can absorb a lag. A warp would need the held-out visitor's own ratings, and it can align almost anything.

traps: **pupil_mean is not drift-corrected.** The thesis says a rolling 30 s mean is subtracted from the diameter, then lists 'diameter mean, standard deviation and dilation slope'. In code only the slope uses the corrected series; mean and SD use the absolute diameter in mm (`features.py:199-229`). So pupil_mean carries between-person level differences and slow drift. Say this plainly if asked.
**Denominator of rates was cut from the Methods text.** Blink rate and saccade frequency are per recorded second (RUNBOOK notes the half-sentence was removed). Examiners may assume per window.

**Trailing window excludes the rated second.** With delay 0 the pupil window is [t-8, t) and the HRV window [t-60, t), ending at the start of the rated second, whose label is the median of [t, t+1). EDA's `.loc` window includes the sample at t.

**sample_count and hrv_n are always numeric.** A second with no eye data still has sample_count = 0, so the row stays in the pupil cell with every other feature imputed. M28 (retro) has zero eye data in the window yet counts as a pupil fold (see Per-Fold card).

**3 s EDA window makes columns near duplicates.** About 13 samples per window, SCR count is mostly 0 or 1, so amp_mean equals amp_median in about 93% of windows, amp_std is almost always 0, and rise-time mean equals median. Effectively about 6 distinct EDA features.

**SCR amplitude is the phasic value at the peak**, not peak minus onset as in the SPR convention; rise time is peak minus the minimum in the preceding 5 s, not NeuroKit's own onset. The thesis says SCRs are 'reported according to' the SPR standard; that is loose.

**Fixation durations are very short.** Median of the per-window longest fixation is about 0.27 s across participants, because runs are broken by the frequent >100 ms frame pauses. The feature partly measures frame rate.

**Speech broadcast gap.** 'Speech features exist only for the seconds an utterance covers' is literally true (the segment span) but voiced audio is far shorter. Also, acoustics overwrite with the later segment when segments overlap, VADER takes the first matching segment.

Some HRV and EDA units: eda_scl_slope is per sample (0.25 s), not per second; HF is ms^2; everything is z-scored inside the model anyway, so units only matter for the correlation analysis signs, which are rank-based.

visuals.caption: Look at the black line: the pupil, EDA and HRV windows all end where the rated second starts. The speech bar is the whole transcript segment covering that second: **73 s** for M01 ("I will go to this one as well."), 9 s for M34 ("Can you tell me more about this thing he is holding?").

visuals.caption: Look at hrv_RMSSD: **334** and **271 ms**, far above normal resting values (tens of ms), which is beat-detection noise (see the HRV weak point). Read from `results/exp1_v2/features/M01_rcea/` and `M34_retro/` (`*.parquet`, `labels.parquet`).

cards.key: Methodology > Experiment 1: Unimodal Prediction > Selection of Configuration Parameters
cards.gist: Five preprocessing settings have no single accepted value, so their candidates compete on this data, inside every outer fold. Each training visitor scores every candidate, candidates are ranked within each visitor, and the best mean rank wins, unless a simpler candidate is within 0.08 CCC. In practice that tie rule decided every step in every fold, so the first-listed candidate always won.
steps: **Five parameters and candidates** (declared order = simplicity order): fixation rule vt30, vt240, idt, adaptive; gaze correction c0 (off), c1 (on); window direction and delay t0..t6, f0..f6 (pupil and HRV), plus per-participant estimated delay; interbeat multiplier 3, 4, 5; EDA decomposition x mask nk_k5, nk_k3, nk_k2, cvx_k5, cvx_k3, cvx_k2 (at 12 s), then EDA window 3, 6, 8, 12, 20 (`selection.py:152-179`).
**Starting values** (`features.py:50` DEFAULTS): P_vt30_c0_t0, E_nk_k5_w12, H_m4_t0. Used before any vote.
**Per outer fold o** (22 rcea, 16 retro): train_pids = everyone except o (`selection.py:247`).

**Scoring** (`score_candidates`, `selection.py:82-108`): for each candidate c and each training participant q, fit **Ridge(alpha=1)** after median imputation and StandardScaler on the other training participants (training minus q), predict q, CCC per axis, **average of valence and arousal**. All candidates use identical rows (label finite on both axes and at least one finite feature under every candidate). q is skipped if < 5 rows or training < 50.

**Vote** (`vote`, `selection.py:111-125`): rank candidates within each participant (1 = best), take mean rank; rank winner = lowest mean rank. Then walk the candidates **in declared order** and pick the first whose **mean CCC >= rank winner's mean CCC - 0.08**. That is the winner.

**Sequence**: pupil rule (4) -> correction (2) -> direction/delay (14 + estimated); HRV multiplier (3) -> direction/delay (14 + estimated); EDA joint decomposition x mask (6) -> window (5). 48 scored candidates per fold instead of 4 x 2 x 14 = **112** pupil combinations alone.

**Estimated delay** (`dirdelay_step`, `selection.py:128-149`): each training participant's estimate = the direction/delay cell with their highest score (argmax over the 14). An 'estimated' column (each participant's max) competes against the fixed winner in a 2-candidate vote with fixed listed first, so estimated wins only if its mean CCC beats fixed by more than 0.08.

**What the held-out visitor would get** if estimated won: the majority direction among training estimates and the **median delay** among participants with that direction (`heldout_dirdelay`). Estimated never won, so every visitor got the same fixed key.

**Outputs**: `results/exp1_v2/selection/winners_{stream}.json` (per fold: every step's mean rank, mean CCC, rank winner, winner). `candidate_stats_{stream}.csv` holds the full-cohort descriptive version (every participant scored by LOSO over all participants) used for the appendix table.
**Fit count**: about 48 candidates x ~15 to 21 training participants x 2 axes per fold, over 38 folds, roughly **61,000 ridge fits**.

numbers.what: Folds where the winner differed from the first-listed candidate

qa.q: Walk me through the vote in one fold.
qa.a: Take rcea and hold out M01. The other 21 are the training participants. For each candidate, I leave out one of them, fit ridge on the other 20, and score that person by CCC on valence and arousal, averaged. That gives a 21 by candidates table. I rank candidates within each person, average the ranks, and then apply the tie rule on mean CCC.

qa.q: Why ranks and not mean CCC?
qa.a: So that one participant with an extreme score cannot swing the result. Each participant gets one ordering. Mean CCC is still used for the tie check against the 0.08 resolution.

qa.q: What does 'simpler' mean?
qa.a: It is the declared list order, fixed before the run: 30 before 240 before dispersion before adaptive, no correction before correction, trailing before forward, smaller delay first, fixed before estimated, NeuroKit before cvxEDA, larger mask multiplier first, shorter window first, multiplier 3 first.

qa.q: Did the winner change across folds?
qa.a: No. In all 22 rcea folds and all 16 retro folds the winner was the same: vt30, uncorrected, trailing 0 s, multiplier 3, NeuroKit with a 5 MAD mask, 3 second EDA window. The rank winner did vary, for example the adaptive rule had the best mean rank in 18 of 22 rcea folds, but it was always within 0.08 of the first-listed candidate.

qa.q: Why ridge for the vote and not the final model?
qa.a: Ridge is cheap enough to fit every candidate for every participant in every fold, and using the reference family stops the configuration being tuned to the family that later wins. The cost is that a setting that only helps trees would be missed, and I say so.

qa.q: Why decide one parameter at a time?
qa.a: All pupil settings together would be 112 combinations. Picking the best of 112 on 21 people mostly picks noise. The pupil steps act on different parts of the signal, so little is lost. EDA decomposition and mask are decided jointly because both shape the SCRs.

qa.q: How is a participant's own delay estimated, and is that not leakage?
qa.a: Only training participants get one: the delay with their best inner score in the 14-cell sweep. The held-out visitor never gets their own; they would get the median of the training estimates. In the end the estimated option never beat the fixed one by 0.08, so it was never used.

qa.q: Is the held-out visitor used anywhere in selection?
qa.a: No. train_pids excludes the held-out visitor, and the vote only scores training participants against each other.

qa.q: Why do rcea and retro decide separately?
qa.a: They are different instruments and cohorts. It turned out not to matter, because both streams chose the identical configuration.

traps: **The tie rule made the search a formality.** Because every candidate's mean CCC sat within 0.08 of the rank winner, the first-listed candidate won every step in every fold. So the carried configuration is the declared-simplest one, not a measured best. The thesis says this ('decided by the tie rule'), but be ready to say it bluntly.

**Multiplier 3 replaced the default 4 partly because 3 is listed first.** On rcea 3 was also the rank winner in 21 of 22 folds, but on retro only in 8 of 16 (4 won 7), and full-cohort mean CCC is highest for 5 on rcea and 4 on retro. Calling 3 'simpler' is a declared convention; it is also the most aggressive filter (median 23% of intervals repaired vs 18% at 4). Similarly the 3 s EDA window replaced the default 12 s because shorter was declared simpler, even though 20 s had the best mean rank in 21 of 22 rcea folds and 14 of 16 retro folds.

**'The HRV annotation delay is estimated per participant'** in the text reads as if only HRV had this. In code the same fixed-versus-estimated comparison runs for both pupil and HRV, and the estimated option lost in every fold for both.

**Held-out delay rule.** The text says the held-out visitor gets the median of training estimates. The code first takes the majority direction, then the median delay among those. Never used in practice.
**Estimated delay is optimistically biased** (each participant's max of 14 noisy scores), and it still did not clear 0.08. That strengthens the 'no lag signal' reading.
**Retro EDA was voted on 6 or 7 people** (only 7 retro visitors pass the EDA gate). The tie rule made that moot.

**Appendix numbers are not the fold votes.** candidate_stats_*.csv is a full-cohort LOSO pass over all participants (I reproduced the rcea fixation-rule row exactly: vt30 0.0184, SD 0.0589). The generating script is not in `scripts/`; only a notebook reads the file. The per-fold decisions are in winners_*.json.
RUNBOOK.md still flags the Hayes and Petrov geometric correction as a Methods fix; the current thesis text already describes the regression, so that note is stale.

**The window-direction votes leaned forward.** In the rcea fold votes the forward f0 pupil window had the best mean rank in all 22 folds, and forward f1 won the HRV rank vote in 12 of 22. The trailing t0 window was carried only through the tie rule (all differences inside 0.08, trailing listed first as simpler). So on the full-cohort mean CCC the direction sweep is flat (on rcea pupil, forward is even slightly higher at every delay), and the rank vote leans forward. **If asked:** 'Rank and mean CCC disagreed, every difference was inside the resolution, so the declared tie rule picked trailing.'

visuals.caption: Look along each row: the candidate means (blue) sit within 0.036 of each other in both streams, inside the yellow tie band, so the first-listed candidate (orange) is carried. The grey bar, one SD across visitors, is much wider (full-cohort numbers from `candidate_stats_*.csv`).

visuals.title: The rank vote and the tie rule
visuals.caption: Lines 114-117 rank the candidates within each training visitor; the lowest mean rank is the rank winner. Lines 119-122 then take the first candidate, in declared order, whose mean CCC is within 0.08 of the rank winner's.

cards.key: Methodology > Experiment 1: Unimodal Prediction > Prediction Models
cards.gist: Eight model families are compared on every cell with nested tuning, so no tuning choice sees the held-out visitor. The standard model is picked among the tree ensembles only, by highest mean CCC over the 20 cells, with ties within 0.08 going to the family whose cell scores vary least. Ridge and SVR are references.
steps: **Grids** (`families.py:48-79`), all seed 42 where applicable: Ridge alpha {0.1, 1, 10}; SVR(rbf, gamma='scale') C {0.1, 1, 10}; RandomForest 300 trees max_depth {None, 8, 4}; ExtraTrees 300 trees max_depth {None, 8, 4}; HistGradientBoosting 300 iter lr {0.03, 0.1, 0.3}; XGBoost 300 lr {0.03, 0.1, 0.3}; LightGBM 300 lr {0.03, 0.1, 0.3}; CatBoost 300 iterations lr {0.03, 0.1, 0.3}.
**Every model is a Pipeline**: SimpleImputer(median) -> StandardScaler -> model, fitted on training rows only (`families.py:124-133`).
**Rows per cell** (`run_cell`, `families.py:147`): keep rows with a finite label and at least one finite feature of that sensor. Skip the fold if held-out < 5 rows or training < 50.

**Nested tuning** (`nested_fold`, `families.py:111-134`): inner split on the training participants only. Ridge: LeaveOneGroupOut (about 20 inner folds on rcea). Others: GroupKFold(5). Each grid candidate scored by mean inner CCC; best (first on ties) refitted on the whole training fold; score the held-out visitor's CCC.
**Per-cell score** = mean over held-out visitors of per-visitor CCC.
**Standard model rule**: among RF, ET, HGB, XGB, LGBM, CatBoost, highest mean over the 20 cell means; within 0.08, prefer lowest SD across cells.

**Standard model predictions**: `predictions.py` re-runs ExtraTrees with the same nested procedure and saves every held-out row's y and yhat per cell (`results/exp1_v2/predictions/*.parquet`); they match the families ExtraTrees scores exactly.

**Fit count**: 346 scored fold-cells. Ridge about 3 x (n-1) + 1 fits each (18,346 total), the other seven 16 fits each (38,752), so about **57,000 fits** in the family comparison, plus about 5,500 for the saved predictions.

numbers.value: ridge 0.5 s, ET 246 s, RF 570 s, LightGBM 3 s

qa.q: Is the data normalised?
qa.a: Yes, the features are z-scored per column by a StandardScaler inside the pipeline, fitted on the training participants only and then applied to the held-out visitor. Missing values are filled with the training median first. The labels are not normalised; they stay on the raw 0 to 10 scale.

qa.q: Is anything fitted on the held-out visitor?
qa.a: No model, imputer, scaler, hyperparameter or configuration choice sees the held-out visitor. The only thing computed from that visitor's own data is label-free preprocessing of their own signal, like the 30 second pupil baseline, the motion threshold or the SCR relative threshold. None of that uses their ratings.

qa.q: Why inner LOSO for ridge and GroupKFold for the rest?
qa.a: Ridge fits in under a second, so leave-one-subject-out is affordable. The tree and boosting models take minutes per fit on 12,000 rows, so I use five folds grouped by participant. Both keep participants separate between inner train and test.

qa.q: Why only three candidates per grid?
qa.a: The cohort is small, and every extra candidate adds a chance to fit noise in the inner split. Three values spanning the main capacity knob, depth or learning rate or regularisation, is enough to show whether tuning matters. It did not change the picture.

qa.q: Why four boosting libraries?
qa.a: They are one method under four implementations. Including all four means a library choice cannot decide the result, and the origin study used several of them.

qa.q: Why is the standard model chosen only among tree ensembles?
qa.a: The literature I reviewed supports tree ensembles for tabular features at this sample size. Ridge and SVR are there as references to read the trees against, not as candidates.

qa.q: What does SimpleImputer do with a column that is all missing in training?
qa.a: sklearn drops it, because keep_empty_features is False by default. That only matters for sparse cells such as retro EDA, and it happens inside the fold.

traps: `predictions.py` docstring still says 'CatBoost'; the grid in the same file is ExtraTrees. Stale docstring only.

Scaling is irrelevant to the tree models (splits are scale-invariant) but matters for ridge and SVR. The scaler is global across training participants, not per participant: there is no per-person normalisation in Experiments 1 and 2.
Grid choices (which knob, which three values) are declared in RUNBOOK.md as an implementation call, not taken from a source.
SVR uses sklearn defaults besides C (gamma='scale', epsilon=0.1). Ties in inner score go to the first grid candidate (Python max keeps the first).

visuals.title: Imputer, scaler and model are all fitted inside the fold
visuals.caption: Only training visitors (`g != o`) enter tuning and fitting; the median imputer and StandardScaler are fitted on their rows (lines 124-126, 131-133). The held-out visitor is touched once, at line 134.

visuals.title: No family stands out in either stream
visuals.caption: Look at the black bars: in both streams every family's mean sits inside the yellow band around 0. Over all 20 cells CatBoost (+0.0062) and ExtraTrees (+0.0055, orange) tie, and ExtraTrees is carried because its cells vary less (SD 0.034 vs 0.043).

cards.key: Results > Experiment 1: Unimodal Prediction (RQ1)
cards.gist: No sensor predicts an unseen visitor's valence or arousal: all 20 cells sit between -0.072 and +0.084 CCC, where 0 means no information. Neither the settings nor the model family change this. The section opens with the selection resolution, **0.08 CCC**: two scores closer than that cannot be told apart.
steps: **Resolution** (`selection.py` `measure_resolution`, lines 182-220): cell rcea / H_m4_t0 (default HRV) / arousal. 20 repeats; each repeat is a full LOSO pass where each fold's training participants are **bootstrap resampled** and the model is a **RandomForest(300 trees, seed 42 + repeat)** with median imputation and scaling. Resolution = p95 - p5 of the 20 repeat means, rounded **up** to two decimals.
Repeat means range -0.031 to +0.074; 4 negative, 16 positive; p5 -0.0250, p95 +0.0533, gap 0.078 -> **0.08**.
QWK resolution: same cell, 20 repeats, pooled QWK on 5 levels: p5 -0.211, p95 -0.007, gap 0.204 -> **0.21** (`resolution_qwk.json`). The 3-level and 10-level variants give 0.22 and 0.24.
Then: parameter sweep (4.2.1), correlations (4.2.2), family comparison and standard model scores (4.2.3), findings (4.2.4).

qa.q: Why is CCC near zero even though the model is not random?
qa.a: CCC here is computed within each held-out visitor and then averaged. The model mostly learns differences between people and predicts roughly the population level with little movement: prediction SD is around 0.5 against a rating SD of 1.4 to 1.9 within a visitor. Within the visit, predictions do not move with the ratings, and the gap between the predicted and true mean is also penalised. So a model that is systematic but does not track within-visit change scores near zero.

qa.q: What does a negative CCC mean?
qa.a: Within that visitor, predictions move against the ratings: the covariance is negative. For example retro HRV arousal averages -0.072, negative in 13 of 15 folds. That pattern suggests a relation learned across people that runs the other way within a person.

qa.q: Why measure the resolution before comparing anything?
qa.a: So the threshold could not be tuned to make a preferred difference count. It was fixed on one reference cell with the starting configuration and a model that was not a candidate for selection.

qa.q: What exactly varies between the 20 repeats?
qa.a: Two things: the random forest seed, and a bootstrap resample of each fold's training participants. The data and features are identical. The answer still swings from -0.03 to +0.07.

qa.q: Why p95 minus p5 and rounded up?
qa.a: It is a robust range of what the same pipeline gives by chance, ignoring the single most extreme repeat on each side. Rounding up makes the rule conservative.

traps: The resolution was measured with a RandomForest and bootstrap resampling on one HRV cell. It is then applied to CCC differences from ridge (config vote) and from ExtraTrees and others (families). Whether 0.08 describes other cells or models was assumed; Experiment 2 later checked it for fusion arms and found it fails for the averaging rules.

The draw is with replacement, but rows are selected with np.isin, so a participant drawn twice is used once: each repeat trains on about 64% of the unique participants. That makes the margin wider (more conservative), not narrower. The resolution is deliberately a conservative 'same pipeline, different luck' band.
The Results intro says 'chance-corrected floor'. For CCC that floor is 0; the chance-corrected floor concept is used properly from Experiment 3 on QWK.

visuals.title: One rerun cell spreads over 0.078, so gaps under 0.08 are noise
visuals.caption: Look at the yellow band: one rcea cell (default HRV, arousal), rerun 20 times with new seeds and resampled training visitors, spans p5 **-0.025** to p95 **+0.053**, and the 0.078 gap rounds up to **0.08**. It exists for rcea only by design: the thesis fixes one reference cell so a single noise floor serves both streams.

visuals.title: Visitors scatter widely; every cell mean sits near 0
visuals.caption: Look at the black bars: visitors range from about -0.35 to +0.35, but every cell mean stays between **-0.072** and **+0.084** (both retro HRV). Retro EDA has only 7 visitors because 9 retro recordings fail the EDA gate.

cards.key: Results > Experiment 1: Unimodal Prediction (RQ1) > Parameter Sweep
cards.gist: The five searched settings made no measurable difference. The biggest gap between candidates was 0.036 CCC (trailing vs forward HRV windows on retro), far inside the 0.08 resolution, and people varied at least twice as much as candidates. So every choice fell to the tie rule, which carries the first-listed candidate.
steps: Sweep spans (max minus min of candidate mean CCC, `candidate_stats_*.csv`), rcea / retro: fixation rule 0.006 / 0.010; gaze correction 0.002 / 0.001; pupil direction/delay 0.008 / 0.009; interbeat multiplier 0.003 / 0.003; HRV direction/delay 0.018 / **0.036**; EDA decomposition x mask 0.010 / 0.009; EDA window 0.003 / 0.016.
The 0.036 is retro H_m3_t1 (+0.0249) minus H_m3_f6 (-0.0113). Trailing beats forward at every delay for HRV in both streams.
Between-participant SD in the same sweeps: 0.017 to 0.067 on rcea, 0.035 to 0.115 on retro, at least about twice each span.

**What 'decided by the tie rule' means, with real numbers.** rcea fixation rule: adaptive has the best mean CCC (+0.0194) and the best mean rank in 18 of 22 folds; vt30 has +0.0184. Gap 0.001 < 0.08, so vt30 (listed first) wins. rcea EDA window: 20 s is the rank winner in 21 of 22 folds, 3 s wins because it is listed first and is within 0.08. retro EDA mask: cvx_k2 rank winner in 11 of 16 folds, nk_k5 (+0.012 vs +0.021) carried.
Carried: P_vt30_c0_t0, H_m3_t0, E_nk_k5_w3, S_egemaps, S_vader, in every fold of both streams.

Check of whether the search changed the model's result (`default_check.py`): ExtraTrees on the default EDA (12 s) and HRV (k=4) configs: rcea EDA valence -0.004 (vs +0.032 selected), retro HRV valence +0.029 (vs +0.084 selected), all differences within 0.08. Not reported in the thesis.

numbers.what: Largest span of any other parameter
Folds with an identical carried configuration

qa.q: What does 'decided by the tie rule rather than by its score' mean?
qa.a: Every candidate's mean CCC was within 0.08 of the best one, so the scores could not separate them. The rule then takes the first candidate in the declared order. For example on rcea the adaptive fixation rule had the best average rank, but it beat the 30 degree rule by only 0.001, so the 30 degree rule was carried.

qa.q: So are your chosen settings the best ones?
qa.a: No, and I do not claim that. The sweep shows the candidates are indistinguishable on this cohort. The carried ones are the simplest by a rule fixed in advance.

qa.q: Did the winner vary between folds?
qa.a: Not once. All 38 outer folds carried the same keys. The rank winner varied, but never by enough to beat the simpler candidate by 0.08.

qa.q: Why did HRV trailing beat forward?
qa.a: A trailing 60 second window uses heartbeats before the rated second; a forward one uses the next minute. Trailing was higher at every delay in both streams, but the gap, 0.036 at most, is inside the resolution, so I do not read it as real.

qa.q: Why does this sweep rule out an explanation?
qa.a: If the null result came from a bad preprocessing choice, some candidate should have scored clearly better. None did, so the near-zero scores are not caused by these five settings.

traps: 'No other parameter moved it by more than 0.016' is true only if HRV direction/delay counts as one parameter: on rcea the same HRV direction sweep spans 0.018. Answer: the 0.036 and 0.018 are the same parameter on two streams.

The sweep is scored with ridge, but under ExtraTrees the carried choice mattered more: retro HRV valence is +0.084 with k=3 but +0.029 with the default k=4 (`families/default_retro_hrv.csv`), and rcea EDA valence +0.032 (3 s) vs -0.004 (12 s). Both inside 0.08, but the best cell of Experiment 1 partly depends on a tie-rule choice. Not in the thesis.
Mean rank and mean CCC can disagree: the vote ranks by mean rank but the tie check uses mean CCC. Here it did not matter.
Appendix table numbers are full-cohort LOSO scores, not the per-fold vote scores (see Selection card).

**'Visitor variation was at least twice the variation between candidates'** holds only if candidate variation is the SD of candidate means. Against the spread of candidate means, rcea EDA decomposition x mask is 1.9x. **If asked:** 'Visitor spread is about twice the candidate spread or more in every sweep; the claim that matters, that no candidate separates, holds.'

visuals.title: Every sweep is flat against the 0.08 band, in both streams
visuals.caption: Look for the widest row: retro HRV direction/delay, **0.036** (trailing above forward); every other span is at most 0.018. The grey bar, one SD across visitors, is several times wider than any span.

visuals.title: The fold votes often preferred another candidate, but the tie rule carried the first-listed one
visuals.caption: Counted from `winners_{rcea,retro}.json` (most frequent rank winner per step). Where the rank winner differs from the carried candidate, its mean CCC was within 0.08, so the tie rule decided.

cards.key: Results > Experiment 1: Unimodal Prediction (RQ1) > Sensor--Annotation Correlation
cards.gist: Before any model, this checks whether single features move with the ratings inside each visitor. They do not: of 436 tests none survives FDR correction and 14 are nominally significant, about what chance gives. The strongest, saccade frequency with retro arousal, really tracks how many tracker rows arrive, and where the literature predicts a sign the data agree only 12 of 28 times.
steps: Features: the carried configuration (`relations.py` SELECTED: P_vt30_c0_t0, E_nk_k5_w3, H_m3_t0, S_egemaps, S_vader).
For each stream x axis x feature: per participant with **>= 30 paired seconds**, Spearman r between feature and rating; constant series give NaN and are skipped (`relations.py:60-80`).
A test needs **>= 8 participants** with a coefficient. Wilcoxon signed-rank (scipy, two-sided) on those coefficients against 0.
BH-FDR over **all 436 tests at once** (`relations.py:84-91`).
**436 arithmetic**: 114 features x 2 axes x 2 streams = 456; retro EDA has only 7 visitors, so 10 x 2 = 20 tests drop; 456 - 20 = **436** (rcea 228, retro 208).

Per-sensor counts: rcea pupil 14 (n 22), EDA 20 (n 14 to 18), HRV 16 (n 21), acoustics 176 (n 20 to 21), content 2 (n 21); retro pupil 14 (n 14), HRV 16 (n 14), acoustics 176 (n 14 to 15), content 2 (n 14).
Retro pupil n = 14 of 16 because M45's retro ratings are constant (Spearman undefined) and M28 has no eye data (sample_count always 0).
Results: 0 survive, min q = 0.665, 14 with p < 0.05 (4 rcea acoustics, 5 retro pupil, 5 retro acoustics). 14 / 436 = 3.2%, below the 5% chance expectation.
**Collinearity** (`relations.py:96-114`): within-participant Spearman of saccade_freq vs sample_count: median 0.90 rcea, 0.92 retro, min 0.80. Diameter vs count median -0.20.

**Literature directions** (`relations_literature.py`): 18 features listed; saccade frequency and blink rate carry no sign ('contested'/'low'), leaving **16 directional features**: EDA 4, HRV 4, pupil 2, acoustics 5, content 1. Each tested on its predicted axis in both streams = 32 cells, minus 4 retro EDA = **28**.
12 agree, 16 opposite. Two-sided binomial test of 12 of 28 at 0.5: **p = 0.572**. High confidence 5 of 16 agree, medium 5 of 10, low (HNR) 2 of 2.

qa.q: Why correlate within each participant instead of pooling?
qa.a: If I pool, differences between people can look like a relation. For example someone with bigger pupils who also rates higher would create a pooled correlation even if nothing moves together within anyone's visit. Within-person correlation asks the question the model faces: does the feature move with the rating inside a visit.

qa.q: How do you get from coefficients to a p value?
qa.a: Each participant gives one Spearman coefficient. I test whether those coefficients are centred on zero with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Then I correct all 436 p values together with Benjamini-Hochberg.

qa.q: Where does 436 come from?
qa.a: 114 features times 2 axes times 2 streams is 456. Retro EDA has only 7 usable visitors, below my minimum of 8, so its 20 tests are not run. 456 minus 20 is 436.

qa.q: Why at least 30 seconds and 8 visitors?
qa.a: Below about 30 paired seconds a single Spearman coefficient is too noisy. Eight is half the smaller cohort, so every summary rests on at least half the people in that stream.

qa.q: 14 tests are significant before correction. Is that something?
qa.a: No. 14 of 436 is 3.2%, less than the 5% you would expect from noise alone. After correction the lowest q is 0.67.

qa.q: Why is saccade frequency not a real finding?
qa.a: The tracker writes one sample per rendered frame and slows down at paintings, 18 against 47 samples per second. Fewer samples means fewer detectable saccades. Saccade frequency correlates 0.90 with the window's sample count within visitors, so its link to arousal is really a link to where the visitor is standing.

qa.q: But saccade frequency is already divided by recorded seconds. Why does it still track sample count?
qa.a: The denominator only removes seconds with no samples at all. Within a recorded second, fewer frames still mean fewer velocity samples and more pauses over 100 ms, so fewer saccade runs are detected.

qa.q: How did you get 28 directional cells and p = 0.57?
qa.a: 16 features have a predicted sign in my literature table. Each is tested on its predicted axis in both streams, 32 cells, minus the 4 retro EDA cells that could not be tested. 12 agree in sign, 16 do not. A two-sided binomial test of 12 out of 28 against one half gives 0.57.

qa.q: Which predictions held?
qa.a: Pupil diameter rose with arousal on both streams, +0.31 on retro, and HNR, jitter and shimmer went the predicted way on both. Mean interbeat interval, fixation duration, pitch and loudness went the opposite way on both. None survive correction.

qa.q: Does this analysis select features?
qa.a: No. It is purely descriptive. Every model gets all of its sensor's columns regardless of these results.

traps: **Retro coefficients look larger because n is smaller** (14 vs 21 to 22 visitors); the median of fewer noisy coefficients drifts further from 0. The thesis says this.
**Pupil diameter +0.31 is on uncorrected diameter.** pupil_mean is absolute mm (not drift-corrected), so its within-visit movement includes slow drift and luminance. And luminance is uncontrolled.
**HNR's expected sign is 'inferred', low confidence**, source 'voice-quality literature, inferred'. It supplies 2 of the 12 agreements. Without it: 10 of 26.
**Only central-tendency acoustic parameters get a sign** (5 of 88), because the literature commits on pitch, loudness, jitter, shimmer, HNR and not their spread.
**M45 (retro) has perfectly constant ratings** (valence 2.08, arousal 8.72 for all 641 seconds), so M45 gives no coefficient anywhere. M28 retro has no eye data. Hence retro pupil n = 14.

**Choice of correction family matters for retro pupil.** BH is pooled over all 436 tests (the thesis says so). If instead each stream x sensor were corrected on its own, 3 retro pupil arousal tests would pass q < 0.05: sample_count, saccade_freq and pupil_mean (I recomputed this). Two of the three are the sample-density artefact, and the pooled family was declared in the Methods before the run. Know this if an examiner asks why you pooled.
The eight-visitor rule is an in-house choice ('half the smaller cohort'), not from a source.
**Line 251 says 'across 436 features'; it is 436 tests** (218 feature columns, 114 rcea + 104 retro, each tested on two axes). **If asked:** 'That should read 436 tests; the count itself is right.'

qa.q: How exactly was the family table computed?
qa.a: For each family and each of the 20 cells I average the held-out visitors' CCC. That gives 20 numbers per family. The table shows their mean, median, SD, min and max, the average rank of the family within each cell, and how many cells it won.

qa.q: Why ExtraTrees and not CatBoost, which has the higher mean?
qa.a: CatBoost is ahead by 0.0007, a hundredth of the resolution, so they are tied. My pre-set tie rule picks the family whose cell scores vary least, and ExtraTrees has SD 0.034 against 0.043. I say openly that the choice is arbitrary on this cohort.

qa.q: Ridge has an even lower SD. Why not ridge?
qa.a: Ridge was a reference, not a candidate. The candidate pool was fixed to the tree ensembles before the comparison.

qa.q: What is X's shape for HRV valence on rcea?
qa.a: 12,152 rows by 8 columns: all rcea seconds except M18's, who has no pulse recording. In each fold the training part is that minus the held-out visitor's rows, for example 11,287 when M01 is held out.

qa.q: Why is the retro HRV cell both the best and the worst?
qa.a: Valence +0.084 and arousal -0.072 come from 15 visitors with large spread, SD 0.16 and 0.08. With so few people, one cell can land at either extreme by chance. Both are inside the resolution of zero.

qa.q: How many models did you fit in Experiment 1?
qa.a: Roughly 125,000. About 61,000 ridge fits for the configuration vote, about 57,000 for the family comparison with nested tuning, about 5,500 for the saved ExtraTrees predictions, plus a few thousand for the default check and the resolution.

qa.q: What were the tuned hyperparameters?
qa.a: They were tuned per fold and not stored, so I cannot list the chosen depth per fold. Only the grids and the procedure are fixed.

traps: **M45 retro scores exactly 0 in every retro cell.** Its retro ratings are constant (valence 2.0763, arousal 8.7178 for all 641 seconds), so CCC has zero covariance. This pulls every retro cell mean toward zero by 1/16 of the difference. Honest answer: it is a retro drawing with no variation, kept because it passed the inclusion rules.

**M28 retro pupil fold has no eye data**: only sample_count = 0 is present, so all its rows have identical features after imputation, predictions are constant, CCC = 0. The caption's '16 retro visitors' for pupil includes it.
'The single highest cell of the experiment, +0.119, belongs to the random forest' is higher than the +0.084 'ceiling' used later. The ceiling refers to the standard model.
Per-fold hyperparameters were not saved, so 'which depth did ET pick' cannot be answered from results.
The mean-rank column and cells-won column both favour CatBoost; the tie rule uses SD. That is a declared rule, not a claim that ET is better.

qa.q: What would change your conclusion?
qa.a: A cell clearly above 0.08 that holds across folds, or a feature whose within-person correlation survives correction. Neither happened. A bigger cohort, cleaner cardiac signal or a label that varies more within visits could change it.

qa.q: Could this just be a bad model?
qa.a: Eight families including linear, kernel, bagging and four boosting libraries all land within 0.0124 of each other, and the features show no within-person relation before any model. So the limit is in the data, not the model.

qa.q: Is the explanation really between-person differences?
qa.a: That is the reading the rest of the thesis tests. Experiment 4's variance decomposition later shows a large share of rating variance sits between people, and Experiment 5 tries to use it.

cards.key: Methodology > Experiment 2: Multimodal Fusion
cards.gist: Experiment 2 tests whether combining sensors beats the best single sensor. It has three steps: choose how to align the signals, build 8 **cross-sensor** columns, and compare four ways of **combining** sensors. Every arm uses the same rows and one fixed **ExtraTrees** model, with no tuning.
steps: Data: the same 1 Hz feature matrix as Exp 1, loaded by `exp2_alignment.load()`: per stream, labels plus the 5 selected sensor blocks (pupil 7, EDA 10, HRV 8, speech acoustics 88, speech content 1 = **114 columns**). Rows with a missing valence **or** arousal are dropped (`dropna(subset=AXES)`). rcea 12,660 rows / 22 visitors, retro 7,022 rows / 16 visitors.

Model everywhere: `ExtraTreesRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_depth=None, random_state=42)` inside `SimpleImputer(median) -> StandardScaler -> model` (`make_pipeline` in `scripts/modeling/evaluation.py`), fitted on the training visitors only, LOSO over visitors. No inner grid search: max_depth is fixed at None.
Unlike Exp 1, there is **no per-sensor row filter**: every arm is scored on every labelled second, and a missing sensor is median-imputed inside the fold.

Step 1, alignment: fixed windowing vs DTW vs DCCA vs DCTW on the full 114-column matrix (`exp2_alignment.py`). Step 2, cross-sensor block: 8 columns at 5/10/15 s, scored alone and against a rotated surrogate (`exp2_crosssensor.py`). Step 3, combination: early, early + block, late simple, late CCC-weighted over all 31 sensor subsets (`exp2_fusion.py`, `exp2_block_arms.py --all`).
Score per cell = mean over held-out visitors of per-visitor CCC. Selection quantity = mean over the 4 slices (rcea/retro x valence/arousal). Resolution 0.08.

qa.q: Which model did you use in Experiment 2, and was it tuned?
qa.a: Extremely randomised trees, 300 trees, seed 42, with max_depth fixed at None. I did not tune it inside Experiment 2. I held it fixed so that differences between arms come from the alignment or combination rule, not from how hard each arm was searched.

qa.q: Is the data normalised?
qa.a: Yes. Every fit is a pipeline of median imputation, then z-scoring, then the trees. Both the imputer and the scaler are fitted on the training visitors only and then applied to the held-out visitor. The labels stay on the raw 0 to 10 scale.

qa.q: Why does alignment only matter for early fusion?
qa.a: Only early fusion puts features from different sensors into one model row. Late fusion trains one model per sensor and averages predictions that already sit on the same 1 Hz label grid. So there is nothing left to reconcile, beyond the fixed windowing each sensor already had in Experiment 1.

qa.q: Which rows go into Experiment 2?
qa.a: Every second with a valid valence and arousal label in the analysed window. That is 12,660 rcea rows and 7,022 retro rows. I do not drop a row because a sensor is missing. The imputer fills it inside the fold, so all arms and all subsets are scored on exactly the same rows.

qa.q: Why no nested tuning here, when Experiment 1 had it?
qa.a: Each mechanism is either fitting-free or a single fit of the standard model. A nested search would multiply the cost by the grid size for every one of the 31 subsets and every arm. It would also add tuning noise that is not about the combination rule itself.

traps: **Single-sensor numbers differ from Exp 1.** Exp 2 scores all labelled rows with a fixed max_depth=None. Exp 1 dropped rows where the sensor had no value and nested-tuned max_depth. Example: retro EDA valence is +0.045 over 7 folds in Exp 1 but +0.017 over 16 folds in Exp 2. For the 9 retro visitors with gated EDA the model gets only imputed medians, so its prediction is constant and CCC is 0 for them. Retro HRV valence is +0.0841 in Exp 1 (the +0.084 ceiling) and +0.0822 in Exp 2. If asked: the protocol is deliberately different (shared row universe), so the numbers are close but not identical.

The docstring of `scripts/alignment_comparison/alignment_ccc.py` still says 'untuned XGBoost'. That function (`_fixed_model`) is **not used** by Exp 2. `exp2_alignment.py` passes its own ExtraTrees `standard_model()` and imports only the helpers.

cards.key: Methodology > Experiment 2: Multimodal Fusion > Alignment Method Comparison
cards.gist: Four alignment arms are compared on the same 114 columns and the same rows. Fixed windowing adds nothing, DTW adds 9 warping columns from the raw signals, and DCCA and DCTW each add 12 learned columns, fitted inside each fold.
steps: **Fixed windowing** = the 114 Exp 1 columns only. This arm is literally identical to 'early fusion, five sensors' later (same numbers).

**DTW** (`build_dtw_block`, `archive/classification_based/alignment_methods_scripts/dtw_features.py`): for each label second t and each visitor, take the trailing window [t-12 s, t] of three cleaned native-rate signals: pupil `pupil_mean_bc` (baseline-corrected diameter, 30 s rolling mean subtracted), EDA `eda_phasic`, and the HRV **NN-interval series** (`process_hrv()[0]`, in ms).

Each window needs at least 6 samples (`MIN_SAMPLES=6`), is linearly interpolated onto a uniform grid of round(span x 4) points (about 4 Hz, `GRID_HZ=4`) and z-scored within the window (flat windows are dropped).

For each pair (pe, ph, eh) `dtaidistance.dtw.warping_path_fast(a, b)` gives the path and distance. **No Sakoe-Chiba band or window constraint is passed**, so the warp is unconstrained within the 12 s.

3 columns per pair, 9 total: `dtw_cost_<pair>` = DTW distance / path length; `dtw_lag_<pair>` = mean of (j - i) along the path, in grid samples of 0.25 s (>0 means the second signal lags); `dtw_warp_<pair>` = path length minus the longer input length (0 = pure diagonal).
The DTW block uses no labels, so it is computed once per stream outside the LOSO loop and appended to the base: X_dtw = 114 + 9 = 123 columns.

**DCCA** (`_dcca_or_dctw_features`, method 'dcca'): for each pair, view 1 = all of sensor A's windowed columns (pupil 7, EDA 10, HRV 8), view 2 = sensor B's. Training rows need **every** column of both views finite. Views are z-scored with training means/SDs.

Network (`deep_alignment._Encoder`): one MLP per view, Linear(in, 16) -> LayerNorm(16) -> ReLU -> Dropout(0.3) -> Linear(16, 2). Loss = minus the sum of the top 2 canonical correlations (ridge 1e-3 on covariances). Adam lr 1e-2, weight decay 1e-4, **150 full-batch epochs**, seed 42 + fold index.

Output: 2 dims per view, so 4 columns per pair, **12 columns** over 3 pairs (named like `dcca_pupil-eda_1_0`). Projected for every row where both views are fully finite, NaN elsewhere (then median-imputed). X = 114 + 12 = 126 columns.

**DCTW** (method 'dctw'): same encoders and loss. Training sequences are per training visitor, sorted by time, fully finite rows only, subsampled evenly to at most 150 rows (`MAX_ROWS_PER_PARTICIPANT_DTW`), visitors with < 20 rows skipped. `fit_dctw` alternates 3 outer iterations: project, run a classic unconstrained O(nm) DTW per visitor, pair rows along the path, then 60 CCA epochs on the paired rows. Output again 2 dims per view = 12 columns.

Both deep methods are refitted for each held-out visitor on the other visitors' rows only, then applied to all rows, including the held-out one (`_deep_fold`). Then the ExtraTrees pipeline is fitted on the training rows of the augmented matrix.
All four arms are scored by the same fixed ExtraTrees, LOSO, on identical rows. Arm selected on mean CCC over the 4 slices.

numbers.value: 150; 3 outer x 60 inner, max 150 rows per visitor

qa.q: What exactly are the three DTW columns?
qa.a: For each pair I warp two z-scored 12-second windows against each other. The first column is the DTW distance divided by the path length: how different the shapes still are after the best warp. The second is the mean signed offset along the path, in 0.25 s grid steps: which signal leads. The third is how many extra steps the path took beyond the longer window: how much stretching was needed.

qa.q: Did you use a Sakoe-Chiba band?
qa.a: No. I call dtaidistance's warping_path_fast with no window argument, so the warp is unconstrained inside the 12-second window. The window itself limits how far a path can go, since the grid holds about 48 points.

qa.q: Why twelve seconds and 4 Hz?
qa.a: 4 Hz is the native EDA rate, so I resample the faster pupil and the irregular heartbeat series down to it rather than inventing detail for EDA. Twelve seconds is long enough to hold a full pupil and electrodermal response and enough heartbeats for a warp. It is a design choice; I did not sweep it.

qa.q: What goes into DCCA: raw signals or features?
qa.a: The windowed Experiment 1 features. For the pupil-EDA pair, one view is the 7 pupil columns and the other the 10 EDA columns of the same second. DCCA needs synchronised input at one rate, and the 1 Hz features give exactly that.

qa.q: How big are the DCCA and DCTW networks?
qa.a: Deliberately tiny. One encoder per view: a linear layer to 16 units, LayerNorm, ReLU, 30% dropout, then a linear layer to 2 outputs. DCCA trains 150 full-batch epochs with Adam at learning rate 0.01. DCTW alternates DTW alignment and 60 epochs of training three times, on at most 150 rows per visitor.

qa.q: How many columns does each learned arm add?
qa.a: Two projected components per view, two views per pair, three pairs. That is 12 columns on top of the 114, so 126 in total.

qa.q: Is anything fitted on the held-out visitor?
qa.a: No. For every held-out visitor I refit the DCCA or DCTW encoders from scratch on the other visitors' rows, standardise with their means, and only then project all rows. The imputer, scaler and trees are fitted on the training rows too. DTW uses no labels and no cross-row statistics, since each window is z-scored within itself, so it is safe to compute once.

qa.q: Why not include speech in the alignment pairs?
qa.a: Speech features only exist per utterance, broadcast over the seconds the utterance covers. There is no continuous native-rate speech signal to warp, so only the three physiological pairs are aligned.

qa.q: Why score every arm with one fixed model setting?
qa.a: If each arm were tuned, a difference could come from the tuning rather than the alignment. With the model held fixed, the only thing that differs between arms is the added columns.

traps: **DCTW's warping is used only in training.** At inference `project()` maps each second's features through the encoders with no warping. So the DCTW columns are unwarped per-second projections from encoders that were trained on DTW-paired rows. The thesis wording 'adds a warping step to those projections' is true of the fitting, not the output.

**DCCA needs every column of both sensors finite.** EDA amplitude and rise-time columns are NaN in windows with no SCR, so the EDA pairs get projections on only about 42% of rcea rows and 7% of retro rows (pupil-HRV about 95% / 84%). Elsewhere the projection is NaN and gets median-imputed. This thins the learned arms a lot. The thesis does not say it.

In DTW the 'HRV' signal is the **NN-interval series** (ms), not heart rate in bpm. The cross-sensor block converts to bpm (60000/NN); DTW does not. Since each window is z-scored this only flips the sign of the relation, but be precise if asked.

The DTW grid length is round(span x 4) per signal, so two windows can have slightly different lengths when one signal has gaps. DTW handles unequal lengths; the `warp` column subtracts the longer length.

The thesis says 'a common twelve-second trailing window, placed on a shared 4 Hz grid'. In code each signal is resampled over **its own** span inside the window (t minus its first sample), not onto one shared clock. Close enough in practice, but not literally one shared grid.
No Sakoe-Chiba band. If asked 'did you constrain the warp?': no, only the 12 s window limits it.
