cards.key: Methodology > Experiment 2: Multimodal Fusion > Constructing Cross-Sensor Features
cards.gist: Eight hand-built columns measure whether pupil, phasic EDA and heart rate move together just before each rated second. Six are correlations in a short sliding window (plain, and lag-searched up to 5 s); two count skin-conductance responses that start within 3 s after a pupil dilation. Each version is tested against a copy where EDA and heart rate are shifted in time.
steps: Signals per visitor (`load_signals`): pupil `pupil_mean_bc` (mm, 30 s rolling mean subtracted), EDA `eda_phasic` from `process_eda` (NeuroKit, default 5-MAD motion mask; EDA-QC-gated visitors give all-NaN), and heart rate = 60000 / NN interval (bpm) from `process_hrv`.
Each is linearly interpolated onto one shared 4 Hz grid per visitor (`to_grid`), NaN outside its own span. Gaps inside the span are bridged by the interpolation.
**Exact 8 column names**: `r_pe`, `r_ph`, `r_eh` (plain correlation), `rl_pe`, `rl_ph`, `rl_eh` (lag-searched), `scr_after_n`, `scr_after_rate`. pe = pupil-EDA, ph = pupil-HR, eh = EDA-HR.
**Correlation = Pearson**: each window is z-scored within itself (population SD) and r = mean of the products (`_zwin`, `pair_columns`). A window with any NaN or zero variance gives NaN.
Window w = 5, 10, 15 s = **20, 40, 60 samples**. Each window ends at the grid point of the label second.

**Lag search**: shifts from -20 to +20 grid steps (+-5 s in 0.25 s steps, 41 shifts). The value kept is the correlation with the **largest absolute value, sign kept**. The shift compares window i of the first signal with window i+lag of the second.
**Dilation** = `scipy.signal.find_peaks(pupil_mean_bc, prominence=0.05)` on the native-rate series (0.05 mm prominence).
**SCR onset** = the minimum of the phasic signal in the 6 s before each NeuroKit SCR peak (`_onsets_from_peaks`; samples back = round(6 x estimated EDA rate)).

**Following**: an onset counts once, against the most recent dilation, if it starts 0 to 3 s after it (`event_columns`). Counts are binned at the onset's grid point and summed over the trailing window: `scr_after_n` = count, `scr_after_rate` = count / window length in seconds (per second).

**Surrogate**: for each rotation r, a generator seeded 42 + r rotates the EDA and the HR grid series with `np.roll`, each by its own random integer offset drawn from [20, n - 20) samples. That is at least 5 s away from zero and from a full wrap. Pupil is never rotated. 20 rotations per window.

Scoring the block alone: 8 columns into the same fixed ExtraTrees pipeline, LOSO, per stream and axis. Observed vs the 20 surrogate means: 'beats' = observed > the 0.95 quantile (pandas, linear interpolation) of the 20 surrogate mean-CCCs for that cell.

qa.q: Pearson or Spearman?
qa.a: Pearson. Within each window I z-score both signals and take the mean of their products, which is the Pearson coefficient.

qa.q: Why compute these from the running signals and not the Exp 1 features?
qa.a: Correlating two per-second summaries would tell me how the summaries co-vary, not how the signals do. So I put the three signals themselves on a 4 Hz grid. One second is too coarse for a 5 s lag search and for responses that take 2 to 3 s.

qa.q: What does the lag-searched column keep?
qa.a: I try every shift from minus to plus 5 seconds in quarter-second steps, 41 in all, and keep the correlation with the largest absolute value, with its sign. That is why it can look large even for unrelated signals, and why I need the surrogate.

qa.q: How do you define a pupil dilation and an SCR onset?
qa.a: A dilation is a peak in the baseline-corrected diameter with prominence of at least 0.05 mm. That is below the 0.1 to 0.5 mm of a task-evoked response, so small ones count too. An SCR onset is the lowest phasic value in the 6 seconds before the peak NeuroKit detects, because the claim is about when a response begins.

qa.q: Why only count SCRs after a dilation, not before?
qa.a: EDA is the slower system. It starts 1 to 3 s after a trigger, while the pupil starts after about half a second. An SCR that begins before the dilation cannot be a response to it. I count an onset once, against the most recent dilation, if it begins 0 to 3 s after it.

qa.q: How does the surrogate work?
qa.a: I rotate the EDA series and the heart-rate series in time, each by its own random offset of at least 5 s, and wrap the end round to the start. Each signal keeps its own rhythm and distribution; only the timing between signals breaks. I rebuild the block and score it, 20 times per window.

qa.q: What does 'exceeds the 95th percentile' mean exactly?
qa.a: For each cell I have 20 surrogate scores. Each is the LOSO mean CCC of the block rebuilt from one rotation. I take their 95th percentile with linear interpolation, which with 20 values sits between the second-largest and the largest. The observed block beats the surrogate if its score is strictly above that.

qa.q: Where does the 0.6 expected by chance come from?
qa.a: Twelve cells, three windows times four slices, each tested at the 95th percentile. If nothing were real, each cell has about a 5% chance of passing, so 12 times 0.05 gives 0.6 cells expected. One observed is in line with chance.

qa.q: Why sweep the window but fix the lag bound?
qa.a: The lag bound comes from physiology: a pupil response peaks by about 3 s and an EDA response by about 6 s, so 5 s covers the widest plausible separation. How long a window a correlation needs is not set by physiology in the same way, and estimates like these depend more on window length. So I tried roughly one, two and three coupled episodes.

traps: **The surrogate does not rotate the two event columns.** `event_columns` uses the dilation and onset timestamps directly, and `rotate` only rolls the EDA and HR grid series. So `scr_after_n` and `scr_after_rate` are identical in the observed and surrogate blocks, and only 6 of the 8 columns are 'broken'. The thesis says the block is computed on a surrogate with one signal of each pair rotated; for the event pair that is not true. Honest answer: the surrogate tests the timing information in the six correlation columns. The event columns are held constant, which also helps explain why the surrogate scores above zero.

**The lag search looks up to 5 s into the future.** For a positive shift, the second signal's window ends up to 5 s after the label second. This is not label leakage (no label is used), but the lag-searched columns are not strictly trailing, unlike every other feature. If asked: true, it is a symmetric search, and a real-time system would have to use negative lags only or accept a 5 s delay.
The pupil-HR and EDA-HR pairs use HR in bpm (60000/NN). DTW uses NN in ms. Different conventions in two scripts.

Rotation offsets use a generator re-seeded with 42 + r for every visitor, so the offset depends only on the visitor's grid length. Harmless, but it means rotations are not independent across visitors in the usual sense.

The EDA used here is `process_eda` at its defaults (NeuroKit, 5-MAD motion mask, `SCR_AMPLITUDE_MIN=0.1`). These match the selected configuration `E_nk_k5_w3`; the 3 s EDA window does not apply here because the block has its own windows.
`to_grid` interpolates linearly across gaps inside a signal's span (for example long pupil dropouts), so some windows correlate interpolated straight lines. There is no gap-length limit at this step.

**The 'SCR after a dilation' columns are really SCR counts.** A 0.05 mm pupil peak occurs about 2.5 times per second, so almost every SCR onset has a 'dilation' 0 to 3 s before it: 1,627 of 1,798 rcea onsets and 176 of 180 retro onsets. `scr_after_n` therefore behaves like a plain count of SCR onsets. **If asked:** 'The 0.05 mm prominence was set low to catch small responses; with a pupil this noisy it fires constantly, so those two columns carry little pupil information. It is one reason the block shows no coupling beyond its surrogate.'

cards.key: Methodology > Experiment 2: Multimodal Fusion > Combination Mechanisms
cards.gist: Four ways of combining sensors run on all 31 sensor subsets: early fusion (join the columns), early fusion plus the 8 block columns, a simple average of per-sensor predictions, and a CCC-weighted average. The full five-sensor set decides what is carried: highest mean CCC over the four slices.
steps: **Early fusion** (`early_score`): concatenate the subset's columns (full set = 114) and fit one ExtraTrees pipeline per LOSO fold. Missing sensor values are median-imputed with training-fold medians.

**Early + block**: same, plus the 8 cross-sensor columns at the 5 s window (full set = 122). `exp2_fusion.py` runs this for the full set; `exp2_block_arms.py --all` adds the block to **all 31 subsets**, including ones without P, E or H.
**Late fusion**: `oof_per_sensor` fits one ExtraTrees pipeline per sensor per LOSO fold on all rows (5 sensors x folds) and stores out-of-fold predictions. Averaging then costs no new fits.
**Simple**: equal weights across the subset's sensors.

**CCC-weighted** (`late_fuse`, weighted=True): for held-out visitor p, sensor j's weight = max(0, CCC) computed **pooled over all training visitors' rows** between their labels and sensor j's out-of-fold predictions. Negative CCC is floored at 0. If all weights are 0, it falls back to equal weights.
Row-wise combination: the weighted average is renormalised over sensors whose prediction is finite on that row. In practice every sensor predicts every row (imputation), so this never triggers.
Single-sensor subsets: weighted is skipped (undefined); simple = the sensor's own prediction, identical to early fusion on that sensor.
Score = mean per-visitor CCC; decision on the 5-sensor row, highest mean over the 4 slices.

qa.q: Where do the weights in CCC-weighted averaging come from?
qa.a: They are recomputed for every held-out visitor. For each sensor I take the out-of-fold predictions on the other visitors' rows and compute one pooled CCC against their labels. A negative CCC is set to zero, and the weights are normalised to sum to one. I do not use the Experiment 1 table, because that score includes the held-out visitor's own rows.

qa.q: Why floor negative weights at zero?
qa.a: A negative weight would flip that sensor's prediction rather than discount it. Floored at zero, a sensor that does worse than nothing on the training visitors is simply ignored.

qa.q: What happens if every sensor gets zero weight?
qa.a: The code falls back to equal weights, so the weighted rule becomes simple averaging for that fold. On the retro slices that happens often: in 11 of the 26 multi-sensor subsets the weighted and simple scores are identical.

qa.q: How do you handle missing sensors in early vs late fusion?
qa.a: In early fusion a missing sensor's columns are filled with training-fold medians, then z-scored. In late fusion each sensor model also sees median-imputed features, so it still produces a prediction on every row. The code can renormalise weights over sensors that did predict a row, but because of the imputation every sensor always predicts, so that path is never used.

qa.q: How many models did the 31-subset sweep fit?
qa.a: Across the four slices there are 76 held-out folds (22 + 22 + 16 + 16). exp2_fusion.py fitted 5 per-sensor models, 31 early-fusion models and one full-set block model per fold: 37 x 76 = 2,812 ExtraTrees fits. Late fusion needs no extra fits because it reuses the 380 per-sensor fits. Adding the block to all 31 subsets (exp2_block_arms --all) is another 2,356.

qa.q: Why decide on the full set only?
qa.a: The question is whether combining beats the best single sensor. Picking the best of 31 subsets would answer a different question and inflate the result through multiple comparisons. The subset table is read as description only.

qa.q: Why is late fusion not tuned or stacked?
qa.a: Averaging rules have no parameters to fit beyond the weights. A learned stacker would need its own nested fit, on 16 to 22 visitors, which is fragile. I kept every mechanism to at most one fit of the standard model.

traps: **The Conclusion (line 1373) says 'no combination scores above the best single sensor on either stream'. Literally false for two slices:** rcea arousal best combination +0.0599 vs best single +0.0439 (+0.016), retro arousal +0.0493 vs +0.028 (+0.021). Results line 885 reports these correctly as inside the 0.08 resolution. **If asked:** 'That sentence is too absolute. What holds is that no combination beats the best single sensor by more than the resolution, and the overall best score, +0.0822, is shared by a single sensor and combinations.'

**Methods vs code on the weights.** The Methods say each sensor is weighted 'by its own Experiment 1 CCC for that slice'. The code does not read Exp 1 at all: it recomputes a **pooled** CCC from Exp 2's own out-of-fold predictions on the training visitors, per held-out visitor. The Results section ('recompute their weights inside every fold') matches the code. If asked, say the code recomputes inside the fold, and the Methods sentence is a simplification.

**Second-order leakage in the weights (small).** Training visitor q's out-of-fold prediction came from a model trained on everyone except q, which includes the held-out visitor p. So p's labels influenced the predictions used to set p's weights. It is at most 5 scalars per fold, but a sharp examiner could spot it. Honest answer: a nested per-sensor refit would remove it; the effect on 1 to 5 weights is likely negligible, and it is not tested.
**Fallback to equal weights** when all weights floor to 0 is not mentioned in the thesis. It makes weighted = simple in 30 of 104 weighted cells (4 + 4 on rcea, 11 + 11 on retro).

The row-wise renormalisation never triggers, because imputation gives every sensor a prediction on every row. A visitor with gated EDA still gets an EDA prediction (constant, from imputed medians) averaged in at full weight.
The Methods call the four 'combination mechanisms' but the subset table has three mechanisms + a block column; the block is an arm of early fusion.

**Choices were made on the same LOSO scores that are reported, not nested.** Most were settled by the tie rule (fixed windowing over DCCA, 5 s over 15 s), but early + block was carried on its score (+0.0271), which is therefore slightly optimistic: in the repeats it averages +0.0212 vs +0.0235 for plain early fusion. Exp 3 to 5 compare arms within one pipeline on the same rows, so they are unaffected.

cards.key: Results > Experiment 2: Multimodal Fusion (RQ1)
cards.gist: Combining sensors does not beat the best single sensor. The four alignment methods tie, the cross-sensor block does not beat its shifted copies, and the four combination methods tie. Early fusion plus the block is carried into Experiment 3 because it has the highest mean (+0.0271).
steps: Alignment: `results/exp1_v2/exp2/alignment.csv` (+ `alignment_summary.json`), per-visitor in `exp2_perfold_alignment.csv`.
Cross-sensor: `crosssensor.csv` (observed + 20 surrogates per window per slice), `crosssensor_summary.json`.
Combination: `fusion.csv` (early, late_simple, late_ccc over 31 subsets + full-set early_plus_block), `fusion_block_arms_all.csv` (block added to all 31 subsets), `fusion_perfold.csv`.

Repeats: `repeats_headline.csv`, `repeats_subsets.csv` (5 repeats, bootstrap of training visitors). `repeats_summary.json` was never written (the script crashed on a JSON key type at the end), so the spreads are recomputed from the CSVs.
Per-fold check: `exp2_perfold_check.json`, 28 cells, all within 1e-4 of the reported means.

qa.q: In one sentence, what did Experiment 2 find?
qa.a: Combining sensors did not recover more than the best single sensor. Every difference between alignment methods and between combination rules was far inside the 0.08 selection resolution.

qa.q: Were the per-visitor tables in the appendix checked against the chapter's means?
qa.a: Yes. The per-fold script recomputes every headline arm with the same functions and compares its means to the stored ones. All 28 cells agree to within 0.0001.

qa.q: What would change your conclusion?
qa.a: A fusion arm beating the best single sensor by more than the 0.08 resolution in most slices, and holding across repeats. Nothing here comes close. The largest per-slice gain of any combination is +0.021.

traps: The thesis says every difference is inside the resolution, which is true. But the carried arm is the **most complex** of four tied arms, while in the alignment and window steps a tie was resolved toward the **simplest**. See the Combination card for how to answer.

visuals.title: Every Exp 2 comparison ends in a tie, in both streams
visuals.caption: Look along each row: the gaps between arms are a few hundredths, far below the 0.08 resolution. Mean per-visitor CCC from alignment.csv, crosssensor.csv and fusion.csv.

cards.key: Results > Experiment 2: Multimodal Fusion (RQ1) > Alignment Method Comparison
cards.gist: All four alignment methods score between +0.0177 and +0.0236 (mean over the four slices), a spread of 0.006 against a 0.08 resolution. Fixed windowing is carried: the methods tie and it is the simplest.
steps: Per cell = mean over visitors of per-visitor CCC, fixed ExtraTrees, LOSO (22 rcea / 16 retro folds).
4-slice means: fixed +0.0199, DTW +0.0177, DCCA +0.0236, DCTW +0.0179 (`alignment_summary.json`, spread 0.0059).
Within-cell SD across visitors (appendix summary): 0.045 (DTW rcea arousal) to 0.110 (fixed retro valence), so 8 to 19 times the 0.006 gap.
DCCA is lowest on rcea valence (-0.0102) and highest on rcea arousal (+0.0314): the ordering flips across slices.
DTW block coverage (run.log): rcea 12,480 of 12,660 rows carry a value; retro **6,173 of 7,022** (849 missing = 12.1%, 'an eighth').

I recomputed the retro missingness per visitor (read-only check). **M28**: all 378 rows missing (no usable raw pupil stream, EDA gated, HRV only 56% of windows). **M31**: 255 missing (EDA gated, HRV usable in only 47% of windows). **M17**: 128. **M30**: 38. **M40**: 21. Others 0 to 8. M28 + M31 = 633 of the 849.

Why: a row gets DTW values only if at least one pair has both signals usable (at least 6 samples, not flat) in the 12 s window. **9 of 16 retro visitors have EDA gated** by the EDA quality check, so for them only the pupil-HRV pair can produce values. Any second where pupil or HRV is thin then has no DTW value at all.
The missing DTW values are median-imputed inside the fold, so the DTW and DCTW arms are 'thinned' (constant columns) on those rows.

qa.q: DCCA scored highest. Why did you carry fixed windowing?
qa.a: DCCA leads by 0.004, one twentieth of the 0.08 resolution, so the four arms are tied. Among tied arms I take the simplest, and fixed windowing learns nothing from the data and adds no columns. DCCA also flips from worst on rcea valence to best on rcea arousal, so its lead is not stable.

qa.q: Why is the warped block missing on an eighth of the retro rows?
qa.a: A DTW value needs two usable signals in the same 12-second window. Nine of the sixteen retro visitors failed the EDA quality check, so only the pupil-heart pair is available for them. When pupil or heartbeat data is thin, that row gets nothing. Two visitors, M28 and M31, account for about three quarters of the 849 missing rows.

qa.q: How is a missing DTW value handled in the model?
qa.a: Like any missing feature: it is filled with the training-fold median before scaling. So on those rows the DTW columns carry no information, which is why I say the arm is thinned.

qa.q: Is fixed windowing the same as early fusion later on?
qa.a: Yes, exactly. Both are the 114 columns with the same fixed model, so their per-slice numbers are identical: +0.0028, +0.0168, +0.0559, +0.0041.

qa.q: Could the alignment methods help with more data?
qa.a: Possibly. DCCA and DCTW learn from about 20 visitors, and their EDA pairs can only use rows where every EDA column is present. Here they add nothing detectable. With these 38 visitors I cannot separate them.

qa.q: What does 'eight to nineteen times the gap' mean?
qa.a: Within each cell the per-visitor CCCs have a standard deviation of 0.045 to 0.110. Divided by the 0.006 gap between the best and worst arm, that is about 8 to 19. The differences between visitors dwarf the differences between methods.

traps: **Tie-break inconsistency.** Here a tie goes to the simplest arm (fixed). In the combination step the tied arms are resolved by highest mean, and the most complex arm wins. Be ready to say why (see the Combination card).

The thesis says the missing DTW rows thin DTW and DCTW. DCTW does not use the DTW block at all: it uses windowed features. DCTW is thinned for a different reason: its EDA pairs need all 10 EDA columns finite (7% of retro rows). The sentence groups the two arms loosely.

The learned arms' EDA pairs are projected on only about 42% of rcea and 7% of retro rows. Nobody reading the thesis would know that. If DCCA is pressed: its pupil-HRV pair carries most of the learned signal.

visuals.title: The four alignment methods differ by at most 0.006 on average: a tie
visuals.caption: Look along each row: blue is valence, orange arousal. The rows look alike in both streams, and the order even flips: DCCA is last on rcea valence (**-0.010**) and first on rcea arousal (**+0.031**).

cards.key: Results > Experiment 2: Multimodal Fusion (RQ1) > Cross-Sensor Features
cards.gist: On its own, the 8-column block beats its shifted copies in only 1 of 12 cells (rcea arousal, 5 s), about what chance gives (0.6). The shifted copies mostly score above zero too, so beating zero proves nothing. The 5 s window is carried as the shortest of three tied windows.
steps: For each stream, window (5/10/15 s) and axis: one observed LOSO score and 20 surrogate LOSO scores (`crosssensor.csv`).
Summary per cell: surrogate mean and 0.95 quantile of the 20 surrogate scores; beats = observed > quantile (`crosssensor_summary.json`).
Only rcea arousal 5 s beats: +0.0211 vs p95 +0.0208.
Observed positive in **8 of 12** cells (4 negative: retro valence at all 3 windows, retro arousal 10 s).
Observed below its own surrogate mean in 6 of 12.
Surrogate mean averaged over the 4 slices: 5 s +0.0049, 10 s +0.0083, 15 s +0.0139 (the '+0.005 to +0.014', rising with window).

Observed 4-slice means: 5 s +0.0050, 10 s -0.0046, 15 s +0.0077; span 0.0122, tied. 5 s is carried as the shortest, and it is the only window whose observed mean (+0.0050) is not below its surrogate mean (+0.0049), by 0.0001.
Coverage: the block carries a value on 12,625 of 12,660 rcea rows at 5 s (12,606 at 10 s, 12,587 at 15 s); retro 6,421 of 7,022 at 5 s.

qa.q: What is '8 of 12' versus '1 of 12'?
qa.a: Against a zero reference, 8 of the 12 cells are positive and would look like signal. Against the rotated surrogate, only 1 of 12 is above its 95th percentile. That is about what chance gives, 0.6. The surrogate is the right reference, because the block scores above zero even when the timing between signals is destroyed.

qa.q: Why is the surrogate mean above zero?
qa.a: The surrogate only breaks the timing between signals; everything else stays. Each rotated correlation still reflects how smooth or variable each signal is in that window, and the model can use that. Also, in my code the two SCR-after-dilation columns are not rotated at all, so the surrogate keeps them intact. These are my explanations, not something I tested separately.

qa.q: Why does the surrogate score rise with window length?
qa.a: Longer windows give smoother, less noisy column values, so whatever non-timing information they hold, such as each signal's local variability and the unrotated event counts, becomes more usable by the trees. The observed block rises too, but not faster than its surrogate. That is why the longer windows score higher under rotation than on the real timing.

qa.q: Does failing the surrogate prove the sensors are uncoupled?
qa.a: No. The test is one-sided. Passing would show that a column depends on the timing between two signals. Failing settles nothing: with 20 to 60 samples per window and a weak label, a real coupling could be too small to detect.

qa.q: Why carry 5 seconds if 15 s scored highest on rcea valence?
qa.a: The three windows span 0.012 in mean CCC, inside the 0.08 resolution, so they are tied, and I keep the shortest. Read against the surrogates, 15 s is worse: +0.0376 is below its own surrogate's 95th percentile of +0.0390.

qa.q: How many models went into the surrogate test?
qa.a: Per window and slice, one observed plus 20 surrogate LOSO runs. Over 3 windows and 76 fold-slices that is 21 x 3 x 76 = 4,788 ExtraTrees fits.

qa.q: Is the 95th percentile of 20 values reliable?
qa.a: It is coarse. With 20 rotations the 95th percentile sits between the second-largest and the largest value. It is enough to show the block is not clearly above its null; it would not resolve a small effect.

traps: **Event columns not rotated** (see Methods card). Only 6 of 8 columns change under the surrogate. This makes the surrogate test a test of the correlation columns only, and partly explains the above-zero surrogate.
5 s 'not below its surrogate mean' is by **0.0001** (+0.0050 vs +0.0049). Do not oversell it.
The thesis gives coverage for rcea only (12,625 of 12,660). Retro is 6,421 of 7,022 (91%), mostly because of the EDA-gated visitors.
The surrogate 'beats' test is a strict > against a pandas linear-interpolated quantile, per cell, with no correction for 12 tests. The thesis handles that by comparing 1 to the 0.6 expected.

visuals.title: The real block beats its rotated copies in only 1 of 12 cells
visuals.caption: Look for a big dot above its black bar (the 95th percentile of 20 rotated copies): only one clears it, orange, rcea arousal at 5 s, **+0.0211 vs +0.0208**. In retro valence the real block scores below most of its copies.

visuals.caption: Look at the roll: EDA and heart rate each move by their own random offset (at least 5 s), seeded 42 + r. Pupil and the count columns stay put.

cards.key: Results > Experiment 2: Multimodal Fusion (RQ1) > Combination Mechanisms
cards.gist: No combination beats the best single sensor overall: the top score, +0.0822, is HRV alone on retro valence, and weighted averaging reproduces it because only HRV gets a positive weight. All four methods tie within 0.08. Early fusion plus the block is carried as the highest mean (+0.0271).
steps: Subset table (`tab:alt-fusion-sizes`) = for each subset and mechanism, mean of the 4 slice scores from `fusion.csv`; 'With block' from `fusion_block_arms_all.csv`. Group means = mean over the subsets of that size.

Best cell overall (3 mechanisms, 31 subsets): +0.08224, retro valence. Under **late_ccc** all 15 multi-sensor subsets that contain H score exactly +0.08224, the same as H alone. So on retro valence every other sensor floors to weight 0 in every fold, and the weighted average is just HRV's prediction.

Per slice, best combination vs best single sensor: rcea valence P+E simple +0.0294 vs E +0.0389 (-0.0095); rcea arousal P+E+H+Sc early +0.0599 vs H +0.0439 (+0.016); retro valence tie +0.0822; retro arousal P+Sa early +0.0493 vs P +0.0280 (+0.021).

**Spearman agreement**: for each slice, rank the 26 multi-sensor subsets under two mechanisms, compute Spearman rho, then **average the four per-slice rhos**. In the order rcea valence, rcea arousal, retro valence, retro arousal: early vs weighted 0.279, 0.345, 0.820, 0.698 -> 0.54; early vs simple 0.027, 0.580, 0.675, 0.815 -> 0.52; weighted vs simple 0.428, 0.655, 0.881, 0.706 -> 0.67. (I recomputed these from `fusion.csv`; no stored script computes them.)

Block gain (early + block minus early, 4-slice means): over 31 subsets +0.0042, better in 25. On the 27 subsets lacking at least one of P/E/H: +0.0047, better in 23. On the 4 with all three: +0.0010, better in 2.

**Repeats** (`exp2_repeats.py`, 5 repeats): seed 42 + 1000 + r, and in every fold the training visitors are bootstrapped (drawn with replacement). Spread = p95 minus p5 of the 5 repeat scores per slice. Early 0.012 to 0.062; early + block 0.016 to 0.062; weighted 0.078 to 0.251; simple 0.036 to 0.095.
Carry: full-set 4-slice means: early + block +0.0271, early +0.0199, weighted +0.0170, simple +0.0018. Highest mean is carried.

numbers.value: +0.0822 (retro valence; H under weighted = H alone)
0.54 / 0.52 / 0.67, means of per-slice rhos over 26 subsets

numbers.what: Block gain, all / without full PEH / with PEH

qa.q: Why is the best combination exactly equal to the best single sensor?
qa.a: They are the same prediction. On retro valence, the other sensors have a pooled training CCC of zero or below in every fold, so they are floored to zero weight. Weighted averaging then returns HRV's prediction unchanged. That is why every subset containing HRV scores exactly +0.0822 there.

qa.q: Why does simple averaging get worse as you add sensors?
qa.a: Equal weights mix the one sensor that works in a slice with four that do not, which pulls the prediction toward noise. Early fusion and weighted averaging can effectively ignore a useless sensor: the trees by not splitting on it, the weights by flooring it to zero.

qa.q: How were the Spearman agreements 0.54, 0.52 and 0.67 computed?
qa.a: For each of the four slices I ranked the 26 subsets of two or more sensors under each mechanism and took Spearman's rho between two mechanisms. Then I averaged the four rhos. They vary a lot by slice: early versus simple is 0.03 on rcea arousal and 0.82 on retro valence.

qa.q: Why do the two averaging rules agree more with each other?
qa.a: They average the same per-sensor predictions. Only the weights differ, and in 30 of 104 cells the weighted rule falls back to equal weights and is identical to simple averaging. Agreement between them is partly built in.

qa.q: Why does the block help most on subsets that lack pupil, EDA or heart?
qa.a: The block is computed from the pupil, EDA and heart signals whatever subset it is added to. On a speech-only subset, for example, it brings in information from sensors the subset does not otherwise have. Where all three sensors are already present it adds almost nothing, +0.0010.

qa.q: Why do the averaging arms vary so much between repeats?
qa.a: Weights are recomputed in each fold from noisy training scores near zero, so a small change in training visitors can switch a sensor's weight on or off. That adds noise on top of the model's own. Also, in the repeat script the late-fusion arms are scored as one pooled CCC over all rows, not the mean of per-visitor CCCs, which is a different and more volatile number.

qa.q: Why carry early fusion with the block when all four are within 0.08?
qa.a: The Methods fixed the highest four-slice mean as the criterion, and early plus block has it, +0.0271 against +0.0199. I say plainly that the ordering is not established. Early fusion also has the smallest run-to-run spread of the mechanisms, within the resolution, which the averaging rules do not.

qa.q: What does 'scored on identical rows' mean in practice?
qa.a: Every mechanism and every subset is scored on the same set: every second with a valid valence and arousal label, 12,660 rcea and 7,022 retro. A missing sensor is imputed, not dropped, so a subset never scores on a friendlier smaller set.

qa.q: Does 'best sensor' change by slice?
qa.a: Yes. EDA on rcea valence, HRV on rcea arousal, HRV on retro valence, pupil on retro arousal. HRV is best on retro valence at +0.082 and worst on retro arousal at -0.074, on the same visitors. The subset ordering repeats across mechanisms; the sensor carrying it does not.

traps: **The +0.0271 advantage of the block does not survive the repeats.** Over the 5 bootstrap repeats, early fusion averages +0.0235 and early + block +0.0212; the block is ahead in only 5 of 20 slice-repeats. Honest answer: the carried arm was chosen on a single run by a margin (0.007) well inside the resolution, and the repeats show the order can flip. It is carried because the rule said highest mean, not because it is better. The repeats also use bootstrapped training sets, so they are not identical to the main protocol.

**Tie-break inconsistency.** In the alignment and window steps a tie went to the simplest candidate. Here the most complex (122 columns) was carried. Possible defence: the Methods state the combination criterion as highest mean, and the block costs little. But an examiner could argue that plain early fusion (or fixed windowing, the same thing) should have been carried under the simplicity rule.

**Block inside fusion vs rotated block (not in thesis).** `exp2_block_surrogate.py` compared early + real block against early + 20 rotated blocks. The real block beats the rotated p95 on 2 of 4 slices (both retro); on rcea arousal adding the block slightly lowers the score. The rotated-block early fusion averages about +0.0222, so about a third of the +0.0072 gain appears even with the timing destroyed (and the event columns are not rotated in that test either).

**Repeats use pooled CCC for late fusion.** `exp2_repeats.py` scores late_ccc_full and late_simple_full as ccc(all rows) (pooled), but early arms as the mean of per-visitor CCCs. The pooled late-fusion scores run from -0.22 to +0.18. So the 0.078 to 0.251 spread for weighted averaging is partly a metric difference. The thesis attributes it only to weight noise.

The thesis says 'the highest score of any combination is +0.0822, reached by pupil with cardiac under weighted averaging'. P+H is just the first of 15 tied subsets (every H-containing subset gives the identical +0.08224). Do not claim P+H is special.

'Two combinations improve on the best single sensor, by +0.016 and +0.021': both are early fusion (P+E+H+Sc on rcea arousal, P+Sa on retro arousal), picked as the max of 26 x 3 = 78 cells per slice, so selection-inflated.
Rank agreement 'averaged over the four slices' means the average of four per-slice rhos, not the rho of the 4-slice means (which would be 0.42 / 0.42 / 0.29).

**Bootstrap repeats train on fewer visitors than they seem to.** `exp2_repeats.py:68` selects training rows with `np.isin(g, boot)`, which turns the bootstrap draw into a set: a visitor drawn twice is not counted twice. So each repeat trains on the distinct drawn visitors (about 63% of them). Honest answer: the repeats measure stability under a smaller training set, not a true bootstrap.

visuals.caption: Look at the coloured lines against the dashed best-single line: each line is the mean over all subsets of that size. Only retro valence rises clearly, and weighted averaging there ends exactly on HRV's **+0.082**.

cards.key: Results > Experiment 2: Multimodal Fusion (RQ1) > Findings
cards.gist: Fusion ties the best single sensor (+0.0822), the alignment methods span 0.006, and the cross-sensor block beats its shifted copies in 1 of 12 cells. Experiment 3 inherits early fusion plus the block (+0.0271) and the QWK resolution of 0.21.
steps: +0.0822 = HRV on retro valence, both alone and under weighted averaging (the same prediction).
1 of 12 = rcea arousal at 5 s; 0.6 = 12 x 0.05.
+0.0271 = mean over 4 slices of early fusion + 5 s block (+0.0067, +0.0165, +0.0646, +0.0207).
0.21 = pooled-QWK selection resolution (`resolution_qwk.json`, gap 0.204, rounded up), used from Exp 3 on.

qa.q: 'Both reach +0.0822': is that a coincidence?
qa.a: No. It is literally the same prediction. Weighted averaging on retro valence gives zero weight to every sensor except the cardiac one, so it returns the cardiac prediction.

qa.q: What does Experiment 3 inherit exactly?
qa.a: The 122-column early-fusion matrix: all five sensors' 114 columns plus the 8 cross-sensor columns at 5 s, with the same ExtraTrees family. And a new resolution of 0.21 for the ordinal QWK score.

traps: The fourth bullet says early + block is 'the highest of those four columns'. True for this run, but the 5 repeats put plain early fusion ahead (+0.0235 vs +0.0212). Keep 'highest in the single run' in mind.

Arm names map: fixed = Fixed windowing, warp = DTW, proj = DCCA ('Learned projections'), p+w = DCTW, xs5/xs10/xs15 = cross-sensor block, early, early+b, wgt, simple.

qa.q: Why are the Fixed windowing and Early fusion rows identical?
qa.a: They are the same model on the same 114 columns and rows. Fixed windowing is the alignment baseline, and early fusion of all five sensors is exactly that matrix.

qa.q: Why is weighted averaging so spread across visitors?
qa.a: Its weights switch sensors on and off between folds, so one visitor may be scored on HRV alone and another on an equal mix. Retro valence runs from -0.21 to +0.34 across visitors.

qa.q: How do you know the per-visitor tables match the chapter?
qa.a: The per-fold script recomputes them with the same code and compares every mean with the stored result. All 28 checked cells agree to four decimals.

traps: The appendix labels DTW as 'Warping' and DCCA/DCTW as 'Learned projections (with warping)', not DTW/DCCA/DCTW as in the chapter. Same arms.
Two appendix captions contain a literal '\\ac{CCC}' (double backslash) typo in the LaTeX source (`tab:alt-app-crosssensor`, `tab:alt-app-fusion-full`), which may render oddly. Cosmetic.

cards.key: Methodology > Experiment 3: Binning
cards.gist: From Experiment 3 on, the 0 to 10 rating becomes a few **ordered levels** (low, mid, high at 3 levels). Two ways to predict them are compared: a classifier **trained on the levels**, and **post-hoc** binning of the Exp 2 predictions. The winner and its level count go on to Experiments 4 and 5.
steps: Load the carried matrix per stream with `carried_matrix` (exp3_binning.py:60): the 114 per-sensor columns of the selected configuration (pupil 7, EDA 10, HRV 8, speech acoustics 88, speech content 1) plus the 8 cross-sensor columns built at the 5 s window (`BLOCK_WINDOW = 5`, line 49) = **122 columns**. The log confirms: rcea 12,660 rows, 22 visitors, 122 columns; retro 7,022 rows, 16 visitors, 122 columns (results/exp1_v2/exp3_oof.log).

Rows: every second with a non-missing valence and arousal (`load` in exp2_alignment.py:66 drops rows with a missing label). There is no per-sensor row filter here: missing sensor values are median-imputed inside the fold, so every labelled row is scored.

Stage `oof` (line 70): refit the Exp 2 carried model (ExtraTreesRegressor, 300 trees, max_depth=None, seed 42, via `standard_model` in exp2_alignment.py:42) in leave-one-participant-out folds and store the out-of-fold continuous prediction for every row in `oof_carried.csv` (39,364 rows = 2 x 12,660 + 2 x 7,022). The mean per-participant CCC of these predictions over the four slices is +0.0271, exactly the Exp 2 figure, so they are the Exp 2 predictions.
Stage `occupancy` (line 91): bin the labels at every B from 3 to 20 and record the emptiest level's share and whether 5.0 falls on an edge.
Stage `posthoc` (line 124): bin both the stored truth and the stored prediction with the same fixed edges and score. No model is fitted.
Stage `trained` (line 156): for each B, fit an ExtraTreesClassifier (300 trees, seed 42, sklearn defaults otherwise) on the training visitors' binned labels and predict the held-out visitor's level.
Stage `select` (line 190): pick the arm, then the count per slice, then run the jackknife.
Every model is a Pipeline of SimpleImputer(median) then StandardScaler then the model, fitted on the training visitors only (exp3_binning.py:148, modeling/evaluation.py:29).

qa.q: Why change the target at all after Experiments 1 and 2?
qa.a: I argued the 0 to 10 ratings are person-relative: one visitor's 6 is not another's 6. A few ordered levels keep the ordering and drop fine distinctions that are probably not comparable across people. Experiments 1 and 2 stayed continuous on purpose, because CCC separates pipelines more finely while I was still choosing sensors and settings.

qa.q: What exactly goes into the classifier?
qa.a: The same 122 columns Experiment 2 carried: all five sensors' 114 feature columns plus the 8 cross-sensor columns at the 5 second window. Valence and arousal are never inputs. They only define the label.

qa.q: What is the difference between the two arms?
qa.a: The trained-on-levels arm fits a classifier on the binned rating. The post-hoc arm fits nothing: it takes the continuous Exp 2 predictions and cuts them with the same edges as the truth. Same rows, same features, same folds. Only the treatment of the target differs.

qa.q: Did the post-hoc arm really reuse stored predictions?
qa.a: It reuses predictions from the same model and matrix. Stage oof regenerates them with the same ExtraTreesRegressor, seed and folds as Experiment 2 and stores them in oof_carried.csv. Their mean per-participant CCC is +0.0271, identical to the Exp 2 figure, so they are the same predictions.

qa.q: Is anything fitted on the held-out visitor?
qa.a: No. Imputer, scaler and classifier are fitted on the training visitors only. The bin edges are fixed at equal spacing on 0 to 10 and never learned from data, so there is nothing to leak.

qa.q: Why not a proper ordinal model, like ordinal logistic regression or CORAL?
qa.a: I did not fit one, and the thesis says so as a gap. The classifier treats levels as unordered; the post-hoc arm keeps order by construction. Given that neither arm got above chance, and the continuous predictions they rest on are near zero CCC, I do not expect an ordinal loss to fix a signal problem. But I cannot rule it out.

traps: **Corrected in the thesis text on 23 Sep; the submitted PDF still has the old wording.** The submitted Methods say the classifier's hyperparameters are 'tuned per fold as elsewhere'. The code uses a fixed ExtraTreesClassifier (300 trees, unrestricted depth, seed 42), refitted every fold with no inner tuning (`exp3_binning.py:147-151`); Exp 4 and 5 use the same fixed classifier. The corrected text now says exactly that. **If asked:** 'That sentence in the submitted version was wrong: the classifier used fixed settings. Every Exp 3 difference is far inside the 0.21 resolution, so tuning could not have changed which arm or level count was carried. I have corrected the text.'

**'Classifier counterpart' differs in one default.** In sklearn 1.9 ExtraTreesClassifier defaults to max_features='sqrt' while ExtraTreesRegressor defaults to 1.0 (all features). So the classifier looks at about 11 of 122 columns per split, the regressor at all 122. No class_weight is set either.

**Person-relative motivation vs absolute bins.** The target is discretised because ratings are person-relative, but the edges are fixed absolute cuts on 0 to 10, the same for everyone. Binning coarsens the scale; it does not remove a visitor's personal offset. Per-person edges would need the held-out visitor's ratings, which is exactly what Experiment 5's warm-up explores.
Methods say the post-hoc arm uses 'stored' predictions. They were regenerated in stage oof, not read from Exp 2 files, but they are numerically the same (mean per-participant CCC +0.0271).

cards.key: Methodology > Experiment 3: Binning > Discretising the Target
cards.gist: Each rating axis is cut into B **equal-width** levels on the fixed 0 to 10 scale; the edges come from `np.linspace(0, 10, B+1)`, never from the data. With an odd B, the rcea joystick rest value 5.0 falls inside the middle level; with an even B it sits on an edge and goes up.
steps: `to_levels(y, B)` (exp3_binning.py:55): `np.digitize(np.clip(y, 0, 10), np.linspace(0, 10, B+1)[1:-1])`. Only the B-1 interior edges are passed.
`np.digitize` default is right=False, so each level is **[lower edge, upper edge)**: closed on the left, open on the right. A value exactly on an interior edge goes to the **upper** level.

0 goes to level 0. 10 goes to the top level B-1 (the top level is effectively [edge, 10], because 10 is larger than every interior edge). Values outside 0 to 10 would be clipped first, but none exist.
B=3: edges 3.333 and 6.667. Levels are low [0, 3.33), mid [3.33, 6.67), high [6.67, 10]. 5.0 lands in the middle level.

B=4: edges 2.5, 5, 7.5. 5.0 sits on an edge and, by the right=False rule, goes to level 2 = [5, 7.5), the upper-middle level. So at even B all the rcea resting seconds are pushed into the level just above the midpoint.
Occupancy stage (line 91) records `midpoint_share` (share of ratings within 1e-6 of 5.0) and `midpoint_on_edge` (whether any edge equals 5.0, true for every even B).
Truth and post-hoc predictions are binned with the identical function and edges.

numbers.what: rcea arousal rows on an edge at B=4

qa.q: How are the bin edges computed?
qa.a: np.linspace(0, 10, B+1), so B equal slices of the 0 to 10 scale. I pass the inner B-1 edges to np.digitize. They are fixed by design and never fitted to anyone's data.

qa.q: What happens to a rating exactly on an edge, or exactly 10?
qa.a: np.digitize is closed on the left, so a value exactly on an edge goes to the level above. A 10 goes to the top level and a 0 to the bottom level.

qa.q: Where does the rcea resting value 5.0 go at 3 levels and at 4?
qa.a: At 3 levels the edges are 3.33 and 6.67, so 5.0 is safely inside the middle level. At 4 levels 5.0 is an edge, and it goes into the level [5, 7.5). So about one rcea second in five is pushed into the upper-middle level at every even count.

qa.q: Why equal-width and not quantile bins?
qa.a: Three reasons. Quantile edges are learned from data, so they would have to be fitted inside every fold and the meaning of a level would shift from fold to fold. One rcea second in five sits exactly at 5.0, so quantile cuts would tie and collapse. And equal-width levels mean the same thing to a museum: low is below 3.3 on the scale for everyone. The cost is unequal occupancy, which is why I added the 1% rule.

qa.q: Why discretise valence and arousal separately rather than as a 2D grid?
qa.a: Each axis is its own target, as in Experiments 1 and 2. A joint grid would multiply the cells (9 at B=3) and empty many of them, and the two axes barely correlate in rcea (0.07) so a joint cell would not add structure.

qa.q: Does parity matter for retro?
qa.a: No. Retro has no rating exactly at 5.0, so whether 5.0 is on an edge changes nothing there. It only matters for rcea.

traps: The edge rule is asymmetric: at even B the rcea resting value always goes **up** a level, never down. That is a numpy default (right=False), not a design choice. It does not affect the carried result because B=3 is odd.
Equal-width levels assume each step feels the same size to the rater; the thesis itself notes this may not hold on a subjective scale (final_thesis_body.tex:119).
The Methods sentence that the midpoint share is 'recorded alongside' is true in occupancy.csv, but the value is the same at every count (20.0% / 20.5% / 0%), because it does not depend on B.

visuals.title: Two fixed cuts make 3 levels; the rcea spike at 5 lands in 'mid'
visuals.caption: Look at the orange cuts (3.33, 6.67): same place for both streams. The rcea spike at exactly 5 (**20.0%** valence, **20.5%** arousal) falls in 'mid'; retro has no such spike. Boxes give seconds per level.

visuals.title: Binning is two lines: fixed edges, then np.digitize
visuals.caption: `np.linspace(0, 10, B+1)[1:-1]` gives the B-1 inner edges; `np.digitize` puts a value on an edge into the upper level.

visuals.title: Even B puts 5.0 on an edge, and it goes up
visuals.caption: At every even B, 5.0 is an edge and all rcea rest seconds go to the level just above the midpoint.

cards.key: Methodology > Experiment 3: Binning > Fitting and Scoring the Ordinal Target
cards.gist: The trained arm fits a fixed ExtraTreesClassifier in every fold for every level count; the post-hoc arm just bins the stored Exp 2 predictions. Both are scored by **pooled QWK** (all held-out rows in one table) and **balanced accuracy**, which must be read against its chance value 1/B.
steps: Trained arm `_fit_fold` (line 147): Pipeline(SimpleImputer(median), StandardScaler, ExtraTreesClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=42, n_jobs=1)). Fit on training visitors' 122 columns and binned labels, predict the held-out visitor's level. Leave-one-participant-out: 22 folds rcea, 16 retro. One fit per fold per count: 18 counts x 4 slices x folds.
Post-hoc arm (line 124): `to_levels(y)` and `to_levels(yhat)` on the stored out-of-fold rows, same edges.
`score_binned` (line 118): `cohen_kappa_score(t, p, weights='quadratic', labels=range(B))` and `balanced_accuracy_score(t, p)`, over all folds concatenated. That is the **pooled QWK**.
Passing `labels=range(B)` fixes the confusion matrix at B x B even when a level is never predicted.

Per-participant QWK: the same kappa inside each held-out visitor, only if the visitor has at least 5 rows (always true: the smallest has 257). Stored in `sweep_*_perfold.csv`, 1,368 scores per arm (18 counts x 76 visitor-slices). No NaNs.
Chance for balanced accuracy is stored as `chance = 1/B` per cell.

qa.q: How is pooled QWK computed?
qa.a: I concatenate every held-out visitor's true and predicted levels and call sklearn's cohen_kappa_score with weights='quadratic' once on all of them. So it is one confusion matrix over all rows, not an average of per-visitor kappas.

qa.q: What does QWK measure?
qa.a: Agreement between true and predicted levels, corrected for the agreement you would expect by chance from the two marginal distributions. Each disagreement is weighted by the squared distance between levels, so predicting high for low costs four times as much as predicting mid for low. 1 is perfect, 0 is chance, negative is worse than chance.

qa.q: Why is balanced accuracy read against 1/B?
qa.a: Balanced accuracy is the mean recall per level. A model that always predicts one level gets recall 1 on that level and 0 on the others, so exactly 1/B. Chance falls from 0.333 at 3 levels to 0.05 at 20, so I only compare an accuracy with the chance on its own row.

qa.q: Could a constant predictor get QWK 0 and balanced accuracy 1/B?
qa.a: Yes, exactly. I checked: predicting one level for every second at B=3 gives QWK 0.0000 and balanced accuracy 0.3333 on all four slices. That is why my results are read against 0 and 1/B.

qa.q: Was the classifier tuned per fold?
qa.a: No. It is ExtraTreesClassifier at fixed settings: 300 trees, unrestricted depth, seed 42, refitted in every fold. The submitted Methods wrongly said it was tuned per fold; I have corrected that. Tuning could not change the outcome, because every difference in this experiment is far inside the 0.21 resolution.

qa.q: Did you handle class imbalance?
qa.a: No class weights were used. At 3 levels the middle level holds 50 to 61% of seconds, so an untuned forest leans toward it. Balanced accuracy is exactly the metric that exposes that, and it sits at chance.

traps: **Corrected in the thesis text on 23 Sep; the submitted PDF still has the old wording.** The submitted Methods say the classifier's hyperparameters are 'tuned per fold as elsewhere'. The code uses a fixed ExtraTreesClassifier (300 trees, unrestricted depth, seed 42), refitted every fold with no inner tuning (`exp3_binning.py:147-151`); Exp 4 and 5 use the same fixed classifier. The corrected text now says exactly that. **If asked:** 'That sentence in the submitted version was wrong: the classifier used fixed settings. Every Exp 3 difference is far inside the 0.21 resolution, so tuning could not have changed which arm or level count was carried. I have corrected the text.'
The trained arm's predictions are **not stored**, only the pooled scores and per-participant QWK. So a confusion matrix or per-level recall for the trained arm cannot be shown without re-running.

Per-participant QWK is only computed for visitors with at least 5 rows, which never excludes anyone. The appendix caption about visitors dropped for a single level never actually triggers (n is always 22 or 16).

**The corrected line 449 says every difference falls 'far inside' 0.21.** Level-count spans reach 0.110 (trained) and 0.147 (post-hoc); inside, but 'far inside' overstates it. **If asked:** 'Inside the 0.21 resolution, the largest span being 0.147.'

visuals.title: The trained arm is a fixed classifier, not tuned
visuals.caption: 300 trees, seed 42, sklearn defaults otherwise, no inner search. The submitted text said 'tuned per fold'; it was corrected on 23 Sep to say fixed hyperparameters.

visuals.title: Scores are computed once on all held-out rows (pooled)
visuals.caption: Called once on all held-out rows joined (line 171), so this is pooled QWK. `labels=range(B)` keeps the table B x B even when a level is never predicted.

visuals.title: At 3 levels most predictions land in 'mid', whatever the true level
visuals.caption: Look at the middle column: **58% to 99%** of each true level is predicted 'mid', in both streams. Post-hoc arm only, because the trained arm's predictions were not stored.

cards.key: Methodology > Experiment 3: Binning > Level-Count Sweep and Selection
cards.gist: Only level counts where **every level holds at least 1% of rated seconds in every slice** can be chosen. The arm is picked once on mean pooled QWK; then each slice keeps the **coarsest** count within 0.21 of its best. A jackknife checks how stable the ranking is.
steps: Occupancy rule (line 108): `out.groupby('B').min_share.min() >= 0.01`. The minimum is over all four slices, so one sparse level anywhere disqualifies the count. Fixed before scores were seen (MIN_LEVEL_SHARE, line 50).

Arm (lines 205 to 217): mean pooled QWK over the selectable counts and the four slices (20 cells per arm). If the gap is below 0.21, keep trained. The code simply sets `carried = 'trained'` (line 214); it would not switch even if post-hoc won by more than 0.21.
Count (lines 224 to 227): per slice, take the best pooled QWK among selectable counts, call tied every count with QWK >= best - 0.21, and carry `min(tied)`, the coarsest.
The parity preference is written in the Methods but is not coded: `min(tied)` already returns 3, which is odd, so it never had to act.

Jackknife (lines 228 to 233): pivot the stored per-participant QWK (visitor x count). The winner is the count with the highest **mean per-participant QWK** (not pooled QWK). Drop each visitor in turn, recompute the means, and count how often the same winner comes first. No refitting.

numbers.value: 1% of rated seconds, every level, every slice

qa.q: Why sweep 3 to 20 instead of picking a few counts?
qa.a: There is no agreed granularity in the literature, so sweeping everything avoids the question of why I chose some counts and not others. It also shows the cost of finer levels, and every count has a neighbour of each parity.

qa.q: Why the 1% occupancy rule?
qa.a: A level that almost nobody occupies cannot be learned from the training visitors and cannot be scored on a held-out one. So I fixed, before seeing any score, that every level must hold at least 1% of rated seconds in every slice. It is a floor, not a tuned value.

qa.q: How was the arm chosen?
qa.a: The mean pooled QWK over the 5 selectable counts and 4 slices, 20 cells each. Trained -0.0387, post-hoc -0.0510, gap 0.0123, well under 0.21. Inside the margin I keep the trained arm because it optimises what it is scored on.

qa.q: How was the count chosen?
qa.a: Per slice, on pooled QWK only. Every count within 0.21 of the best is treated as tied, and I keep the coarsest. All five selectable counts tied in all four slices, so 3 was carried everywhere.

qa.q: What does the jackknife actually rank on?
qa.a: On the mean per-participant QWK, from the stored scores, not on pooled QWK. I drop one visitor at a time and check whether the same count still has the highest mean. It is a stability check on the ranking, not on the carried count.

qa.q: Why is the tie-break 'coarsest'?
qa.a: A coarser target is the more conservative claim: fewer levels, more rows per level, and less room to fit noise. When I cannot tell counts apart, I take the one that asks the least of the data.

qa.q: How was the 0.21 QWK resolution measured?
qa.a: resolution_qwk.py repeats one reference cell 20 times: HRV features (starting configuration H_m4_t0) against rcea arousal, binned at 5 levels, a RandomForestClassifier with 300 trees. Each repeat changes the seed and bootstraps each fold's training visitors. The score per repeat is pooled QWK. p95 minus p5 is 0.204, rounded up to 0.21.

qa.q: What are the b3 and b10 resolution files?
qa.a: A robustness check declared in advance: the same procedure at 3 and 10 levels. They give 0.22 and 0.24. Only the 5-level run defines the margin. Every Exp 3 gap is far below all three values, so the choice does not matter.

traps: **The jackknife winner is not the carried count.** It ranks on mean per-participant QWK and finds winners 5, 4, 7 and 5 (selection.csv `jackknife_winner`), while 3 is carried everywhere. So the 91/100/75/100% says the per-participant ranking is stable, not that 3 is stable. The Methods phrase 'the selected count's stability' is misleading; the Results phrase 'ranking the counts on the mean per-participant QWK' is the accurate one. The appendix table shows both columns side by side.

The jackknife uses a different metric (mean per-participant) from the selection (pooled). A sharp examiner may ask why. Honest answer: pooled QWK cannot be recomputed without a visitor from stored per-visitor kappas alone, since it needs the rows; the per-participant scores were what was stored.

`stage_select` docstring (line 193) says the arm is summarised by 'the mean of its best selectable pooled QWK'. The code (line 208) takes the mean over all selectable counts and slices, which matches the thesis. Stale docstring.
Arm choice is hardcoded `carried = 'trained'` (line 214). Harmless here, because post-hoc was lower anyway.
Tie rule in code is 'within 0.21 of the best count', not pairwise. Same outcome here.

**The QWK resolution was not measured on the Exp 3 setup.** It uses HRV-only features (8 columns, key H_m4_t0), a RandomForestClassifier (not ExtraTrees), at 5 levels, not the carried 3. At 3 levels the same procedure gives 0.22, at 10 levels 0.24 (resolution_qwk_b3.json, _b10.json). The thesis calls it 'the same twenty repeats', which is loose: it is the same procedure, rerun with a classifier. No conclusion changes, because the largest Exp 3 gap is 0.147.

In the resolution runs, 19 of 20 repeat pooled QWKs are negative (-0.27 to +0.003). Useful: it shows negative pooled QWK is normal on this cohort even for the reference cell, not something special to Exp 3.

visuals.title: The arm is set to 'trained' in code; the gap is only printed
visuals.caption: Mean pooled QWK over the 5 selectable counts x 4 slices (20 cells). Line 214 simply sets `carried = 'trained'`; the gap is only printed against 0.21.

visuals.title: The coarsest tied count wins; the jackknife ranks per visitor instead
visuals.caption: Tied = every count within 0.21 of the best; carried = `min(tied)`, the coarsest. The jackknife ranks counts on mean **per-participant** QWK, not pooled, so its winner can differ from the carried count.

cards.key: Results > Experiment 3: Binning (RQ2)
cards.gist: Ordered levels do not lift agreement above chance at any level count, and no count beats another. Pooled QWK is below zero in every slice except retro valence, and balanced accuracy sits at chance. The trained arm with 3 levels is carried into Experiment 4.
steps: Pooled QWK and balanced accuracy for 18 counts x 4 slices x 2 arms = 144 cells (sweep_trained.csv, sweep_posthoc.csv).
Occupancy rule leaves counts 3 to 7 selectable.
Arms: trained -0.0387, post-hoc -0.0510 mean pooled QWK over the 20 selectable cells; gap 0.0123 < 0.21.
Counts: all five tied in every slice; 3 carried as the coarsest.
Per-participant QWK is near zero and differs in sign from the pooled figure in several slices.

numbers.value: trained arm, 3 levels in all four slices

numbers.what: Best balanced accuracy excess over chance

qa.q: What is the headline of Experiment 3?
qa.a: Turning the rating into ordered levels does not help. Pooled QWK is negative on three slices and small positive on retro valence, balanced accuracy is at chance, and no level count separates from another inside the 0.21 margin.

qa.q: Why did Experiment 2 show positive CCC but Experiment 3 negative QWK? Can QWK fall while CCC rises?
qa.a: Mostly it is the aggregation, not the metric. The Exp 2 +0.0271 is a mean of per-visitor CCCs. Exp 3 reports pooled QWK over all rows. Pooling the same continuous predictions gives pooled CCC -0.071 rcea valence, -0.038 rcea arousal, -0.217 retro arousal and +0.088 retro valence, the same signs as pooled QWK. Binning also throws away within-level movement, which can lower agreement further.

qa.q: Does this answer RQ2?
qa.a: Yes, negatively on this cohort: no count lifts agreement above chance, and the cohort supports up to 7 levels by occupancy but gives no reason to prefer any of them.

traps: The CCC-to-QWK drop mixes two changes at once: the metric (CCC to QWK) and the aggregation (mean per-participant to pooled). Say this plainly if asked why the numbers 'got worse'.

visuals.title: Agreement stays near or below zero at every level count
visuals.caption: Look at the circles (the carried 3 levels) and the yellow band: every usable count ties with the best. Only retro valence is above zero; grey counts (8 to 20) are not usable.

cards.key: Results > Experiment 3: Binning (RQ2) > The Selectable Range
cards.gist: Of 18 level counts, only 3 to 7 pass the 1% rule. At 7 levels the emptiest level anywhere holds 1.72% (rcea arousal); at 8 it drops to 0.44% (retro arousal).
steps: Computed on all labelled rows (rcea 12,660, retro 7,022) with `to_levels`, per slice, per B (occupancy.csv).
B=7: emptiest is **rcea arousal level 5 of 0 to 6**, i.e. [7.14, 8.57), 218 seconds = 1.72%.
B=8: emptiest is **retro arousal top level** [8.75, 10], 31 seconds = 0.44%. (rcea arousal at B=8 is still 1.24%.)
B=20: emptiest is **retro arousal top level** [9.5, 10], 2 seconds = 0.03%.
So it is the high end of retro arousal that runs out first: very few retro seconds were drawn near the top of the arousal scale.

numbers.value: rcea val 7.87%, rcea aro 4.83%, retro val 16.98%, retro aro 21.39%

qa.q: Which level and which stream breaks the rule first?
qa.a: Retro arousal. At 8 levels its top level, 8.75 to 10, holds only 31 seconds, 0.44%. At 7 levels the emptiest level anywhere is rcea arousal between 7.14 and 8.57, at 1.72%, which still passes.

qa.q: Is the occupancy computed on the same rows as the models?
qa.a: Yes. It uses the same labelled rows the models are scored on, 12,660 rcea and 7,022 retro, with the same binning function.

qa.q: How many rows fall in each level at 3 levels?
Is the counts-above-7 exclusion based on scores?
qa.a: No. The rule only looks at how the true ratings fall across levels, and it was fixed before any score was computed.

traps: The thesis says 'in both streams'. The code takes the minimum over all four slices (both axes too), which is stricter and is what produced the numbers.
At B=3 rcea arousal's high level holds only 4.8% (612 s), and rcea valence's low level 7.9%. The carried target is quite unbalanced, which matters when reading balanced accuracy and QWK.

visuals.title: Above 7 levels some level holds under 1% of seconds, so only 3 to 7 are usable
visuals.caption: Look at the dashed 1% line: a count is usable only if all four lines stay above it. Retro arousal falls below first, at 8 levels (**0.44%**, 31 s). Log scale.

visuals.title: The emptiest level shrinks fast above 7 levels
visuals.caption: From occupancy.csv `min_share`. The rule takes the minimum over all four slices.

cards.key: Results > Experiment 3: Binning (RQ2) > The Two Arms
cards.gist: The two arms tie: mean pooled QWK -0.0387 (trained) vs -0.0510 (post-hoc), a gap of 0.0123 against a 0.21 margin. Positive QWK appears almost only on retro valence, and balanced accuracy stays at chance.
steps: Arm mean = mean of 20 cells (5 selectable counts x 4 slices) of pooled QWK (selection_summary.json `arm_means`).
Peak = count with the highest mean over slices: both at B=5, trained -0.0248, post-hoc -0.0431.
Positive cells over all 72: trained 17, all retro valence; post-hoc 19, 18 retro valence plus rcea arousal at B=4 (+0.0350). Within selectable counts: 5 of 20 and 6 of 20.

Balanced accuracy: 64 of 144 cells exceed chance (trained 30, post-hoc 34). Largest excess 0.041, post-hoc retro valence B=4 (0.291 vs 0.250). Trained arm's largest excess is 0.031 (retro arousal B=6).
Trained-arm mean BA over slices: 0.312 at B=3 vs chance 0.333; 0.137 at B=7 vs 0.143. At B=3 all four trained slices are below chance (0.325, 0.303, 0.319, 0.299).

qa.q: Why is pooled QWK negative, and is negative worse than chance?
qa.a: Zero is what chance agreement gives, so negative means slightly systematic disagreement. The cause is between visitors: the model's average prediction for a visitor runs against that visitor's average rating. For rcea valence and retro arousal the correlation between a visitor's mean rating and mean prediction is about -0.55 and -0.51. Pooling puts everyone in one confusion matrix, so that shows up as negative QWK. The values, -0.01 to -0.22, sit inside the 0.21 noise margin, and even the reference cell used to measure the margin gave negative pooled QWK in 19 of 20 repeats.

qa.q: Why keep the trained arm if the post-hoc arm has the higher peak in some slices?
qa.a: The arms are compared on one summary: the mean over all 20 selectable cells. The gap is 0.0123, far inside 0.21, so they are tied. Inside a tie the rule fixed in advance keeps the trained arm, because it optimises the thing it is scored on.

qa.q: Why is only retro valence positive?
qa.a: Retro valence is also the only slice where the continuous predictions have positive pooled CCC (+0.088) and a positive between-visitor relation (+0.21). I read it as the one slice with a small signal, not as a finding, because it is inside the margin.

qa.q: Is balanced accuracy below chance a problem?
qa.a: No, it is consistent with no information. At 3 levels the middle level holds more than half the seconds and an untuned forest drifts toward it, so recall on the small levels is poor. A value slightly below 1/B is as uninformative as one slightly above.

qa.q: Would a model that predicts the same level always do as well?
qa.a: Yes. A constant prediction gets exactly QWK 0 and balanced accuracy 1/B. My best excess over 1/B is 0.041 and QWK is mostly negative, so the sensors do not separate from that.

traps: The post-hoc arm is **very compressed**: continuous predictions have SD 0.6 to 0.8 against rating SD 2.0 to 2.5. At B=3 the post-hoc arm predicts the middle level for 69 to 97% of seconds (e.g. retro valence 6,805 of 7,022; rcea arousal never predicts high). This is why its QWK and BA sit near chance: it barely uses the outer levels.
The thesis says 'Both peak at five levels'. That is the peak of the mean over slices. Per slice, the trained arm's best counts are 5, 5, 7, 4.
'Balanced accuracy tracks its own chance value': true, and at B=3 the trained arm is below chance in all four slices. Do not claim it is 'slightly above'.

visuals.title: Balanced accuracy never beats chance by more than 0.041
visuals.caption: Look at the black zero line: that is chance (1/B). Every line stays close to it; **64 of 144** cells are above, the largest by **+0.041** (post-hoc, retro valence, 4 levels).

visuals.title: Both arms are negative in three slices and positive only on retro valence
visuals.caption: Mean pooled QWK over the five usable counts (3 to 7). Gap 0.0123 against the 0.21 margin (selection_summary.json). Positive cells over all 72: trained 17, post-hoc 19, all but one on retro valence.

cards.gist: All five usable counts tie in every slice, so the coarsest, **3 levels**, is carried everywhere. The jackknife says the per-visitor ranking of counts is stable (91, 100, 75, 100%), but the count it ranks first is never 3.
steps: Per-slice span over counts 3 to 7 (trained): rcea val 0.024, rcea aro 0.075, retro val 0.075, retro aro 0.110. Post-hoc max span 0.147 (retro arousal). All < 0.21.
Trained mean over slices across all 18 counts ranges from -0.0789 (B=18) to -0.0248 (B=5): 0.054.
Tied = counts 3,4,5,6,7 in all slices; carried = min = 3 (selection.csv).

Trained mean over slices, range over 18 counts

numbers.value: 91% / 100% / 75% / 100% (rcea val, rcea aro, retro val, retro aro)

qa.q: Why 3 levels?
qa.a: Because no count could be told apart from another: within each slice the five selectable counts span at most 0.110 pooled QWK against a 0.21 margin. With all tied, the rule fixed in advance keeps the coarsest, which is 3. It is also odd, so the rcea resting value 5.0 sits inside the middle level.

qa.q: What do 3 levels mean in practice for a museum guide?
qa.a: Low below 3.33, mid 3.33 to 6.67, high above 6.67 on the 0 to 10 scale, for each axis. For a guide that would be 'calm / neutral / excited' for arousal and 'unpleasant / neutral / pleasant' for valence. In practice most seconds are mid: 50 to 61% depending on the slice.

qa.q: What does the jackknife stability mean?
qa.a: I drop one visitor at a time and re-rank the counts by the mean per-participant QWK of the rest. In 91, 100, 75 and 100% of repeats the same count comes first. So the ordering is not driven by one visitor. It does not make the differences large: they are still inside the margin.

qa.q: Is the jackknife winner the count you carried?
qa.a: No. The jackknife ranks on mean per-participant QWK and its winners are 5, 4, 7 and 5. I carried 3 because selection is on pooled QWK and all counts tied. The jackknife tells you the per-participant ordering is consistent, not that 3 is best.

qa.q: Did the parity preference decide anything?
qa.a: No. The coarsest tied count was already 3, which is odd. The parity rule is not even coded, because it never had to act.

traps: **Biggest trap in this section:** 'returns the same best count in 91%...' refers to the per-participant winner (5, 4, 7, 5), not to 3. If an examiner reads it as '3 is stable', correct it straight away.
The comparison 'which is the pattern Experiment 2 reports for its sensor subsets' is an analogy; I did not verify the Exp 2 claim here.
Methods say 'where tied counts also differ in parity, the one placing the midpoint inside a level is preferred'. Not implemented, never needed.

visuals.title: 3 levels is carried in every slice, though it is never the top count
visuals.caption: Tied counts are 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 in every slice. The jackknife column is about the per-participant winner, never about 3.

cards.key: Results > Experiment 3: Binning (RQ2) > Pooled Against Per-Participant Agreement
cards.gist: Pooled QWK puts all visitors' rows into one table; per-visitor QWK scores each visitor alone and averages. The two can differ in sign. The negative pooled scores come mainly from differences **between** visitors: a visitor's mean prediction does not follow, and in two slices runs against, that visitor's mean rating.
steps: Pooled: `score_binned` over all folds concatenated (line 171). Per-participant: kappa within each visitor (lines 175 to 181), then averaged.
At B=5 trained: rcea arousal -0.0582 pooled vs +0.0130 per-participant mean; rcea valence -0.0486 vs +0.0047; retro arousal -0.0597 vs +0.0575; retro valence +0.0673 vs +0.0626 (no flip).
Post-hoc retro arousal B=5: pooled -0.1585; per-participant median +0.0019, mean -0.0051, 7 of 16 negative.
At the carried B=3 trained: rcea arousal -0.0837 vs +0.0129 (flip); rcea valence -0.0615 vs -0.0070 (no flip); retro arousal -0.0817 vs -0.0047 (no flip); retro valence +0.0182 vs +0.0147.

Mechanism check on the continuous Exp 2 predictions: correlation across visitors between mean rating and mean prediction is -0.55 rcea valence, -0.51 retro arousal, -0.03 rcea arousal, +0.21 retro valence. Pooled within-person correlation (both centred per visitor) is near zero: +0.06, -0.01, -0.02, +0.14. Visitors' mean ratings spread with SD 1.3 to 1.7, the predicted means with SD 0.3 to 0.7.

numbers.what: Between-visitor r (mean rating vs mean prediction)

qa.q: Why do pooled and per-participant QWK disagree?
qa.a: Pooled QWK computes the chance correction from the level distributions of all visitors together. Visitors differ a lot in their average rating, and the model gets those averages wrong, sometimes backwards. For rcea valence and retro arousal, visitors who rate higher on average get lower average predictions, r about -0.5. Inside one visitor that offset does not count, so the per-visitor kappas sit around zero, while pooled kappa goes negative.

qa.q: Is this Simpson's paradox?
qa.a: It is the same family: a between-person relation dominates the pooled number and has a different sign from the within-person relation. It is why the thesis computes within-participant correlations in the data characterisation.

qa.q: So is the model actually good within each visitor?
qa.a: No, it is near zero within each visitor too. The per-participant means at B=5 are +0.005 to +0.063, the medians around zero, and 6 to 11 visitors per slice are negative. The honest reading is: pooled is negative because of the between-visitor error; within visitors there is essentially no signal either.

qa.q: Why keep pooled QWK as the headline then?
qa.a: It was fixed in advance in the protocol, and changing the headline after seeing the results would be selective reporting. I report the per-participant figures beside it so the gap is visible.

traps: **The sign flip is shown at B=5, not at the carried B=3.** At B=3 only rcea arousal flips (-0.0837 vs +0.0129); rcea valence (-0.0615 vs -0.0070) and retro arousal (-0.0817 vs -0.0047) stay negative. 'On three of the four slices a different sign' is true at B=5 on the trained arm. Be ready to say that.

**'A prediction that tracks each visitor around their own centre' overstates it.** The pooled within-person correlation of the continuous predictions is about zero (-0.02 to +0.14), and per-participant QWK means are near zero. The between-person anti-correlation is real; strong within-person tracking is not.
The appendix caption says pooled and per-participant 'disagree in sign on three of the four slices'. That holds at B=5 (trained) but not at every selectable count.
