visuals.caption: Look at `np.unique`: when both tertiles are equal it keeps one edge. The held-out visitor's edges come from their first 180 ratings only.

cards.key: Results > Experiment 5: Personalisation (RQ5)
cards.gist: The levers push pooled QWK up in 21 of 24 cells, but **no paired test survives correction**. The warm-up is the only lever with an ordered response. Baseline calibration and the person-relative target raise QWK without better continuous prediction, so that QWK movement is mostly the **level mix shifting**.
steps: Table 4.x numbers come straight from `results/exp1_v2/exp5/levers.csv` (via `make_body_tables_exp45.py:107`). CCC = mean of per-visitor CCC; QWK and BA pooled over all held-out predictions.

Counts verified from levers.csv: pooled QWK rises in **21** of 24 cells (falls: baseline retro valence, warm-up 30 and 60 on rcea valence); BA rises in **20**; CCC rises in **15** (the 4 person-relative cells are equal, baseline rises only on retro arousal, warm-up 30/60 fall on retro valence).
Warm-up 180 pooled QWK rises: retro valence +0.1986 (thesis rounds to +0.1985), retro arousal +0.3019, rcea arousal +0.2268, rcea valence +0.1538.
Baseline CCC falls: rcea valence -0.0219, rcea arousal -0.0262, retro valence -0.0393; rises retro arousal +0.0146.
Person-relative pooled QWK rises: +0.0679, +0.1038, +0.0839, +0.1682.

numbers.what: Cells moving up (pooled QWK / BA / CCC)

qa.q: How can a lever raise QWK but lower CCC?
qa.a: They measure different things, from two different models. CCC is per visitor and continuous, from the regressor. Pooled QWK is on three levels, pooled over all visitors, from the classifier. If a lever shifts which level predictions land in, so the predicted level shares match the true shares better, chance-corrected agreement goes up even if no second is tracked better. Pooled QWK also rewards getting each visitor's overall level right, which is between-person, not within-visit.

qa.q: Can you show the pooled QWK gain is not a per-visitor gain?
qa.a: Yes. For baseline on retro arousal, pooled QWK rises from -0.122 to -0.039, but per-visitor QWK falls from -0.036 to -0.057 and only 2 of 12 visitors improve. For the 180 s warm-up on rcea arousal, pooled QWK rises by +0.227 but per-visitor QWK only by +0.054, p = 0.47.

qa.q: Why are pooled QWK values so negative in the reference?
qa.a: Pooled over visitors, the classifier's levels tend to be off in the wrong direction between people: it predicts the typical cohort level, and visitors differ a lot in their own level. A negative value means worse than chance on the pooled set. Per visitor the mean QWK is close to zero.

qa.q: Why does the warm-up at 180 s jump so much from 120 s?
qa.a: On pooled QWK most of the gain arrives at 180 s. With 180 rows the model sees more of this visitor's own level. But the 180 s CCC gain is carried mainly by two visitors, so I read the jump carefully.

qa.q: Are the 21 of 24 cells independent evidence?
qa.a: No. They share one reference per slice, the same visitors, and the four warm-up durations are nested. And 7 of the 21 are baseline and person-relative cells that I myself explain as marginal shifts. So I use 21 of 24 as a description, not as a test.

qa.q: Does BA above 0.333 mean above chance?
qa.a: The warm-up at 180 s gives 0.364 to 0.437, above the 0.333 chance value. But it is pooled and untested, and the per-visitor tests do not survive. So it is a lead, not a result.

traps: **The 21 of 24 'expected direction' count includes the baseline and person-relative cells that the same section explains as marginal shifts.** Do not use 21/24 as support for personalisation. Say: 'the pooled figures move, but part of that movement is a change in level shares, and none of it survives a paired test.'

**The rcea valence reference CCC (+0.0257) is mostly one visitor, M08 (+0.70).** Without M08 the reference is near zero. Baseline's CCC drop on rcea valence is also largely M08 going from +0.70 to +0.08 (appendix per-visitor table). If asked why baseline lowered rcea valence CCC: 'mostly one visitor.'
Headline QWK numbers (e.g. +0.3019) are **pooled** QWK; the paired tests use **per-visitor** QWK, which moves far less. Keep the two apart when answering.
Retro valence rise is +0.1986 in the data; the thesis prints +0.1985 (rounding of a difference of rounded values). Harmless.

visuals.caption: Look at the shaded baseline column: CCC falls on 3 slices (rcea -0.0219 and -0.0262, retro valence -0.0393) while pooled QWK rises on 3. Person-relative CCC is exactly 0 because its regressor is unchanged.

visuals.caption: Look at the 180 s points: pooled QWK is **+0.1538 to +0.3019** above the reference, largest on retro arousal.

cards.key: Results > Experiment 5: Personalisation (RQ5) > Verdict
cards.gist: **No lever earns a credited gain**: 0 of 48 tests survive, smallest q = 0.138. The best case, a 180 s warm-up on rcea arousal, improves 16 of 22 visitors (p = 0.0066, q = 0.138). The honest reading is a null at 12 to 22 visitors, not proof that personalisation fails.
steps: Wilcoxon signed-rank (`scipy.stats.wilcoxon`, default settings: zero differences dropped) on per-visitor scores, lever vs reference (`exp5_personalisation.py:274`).

BH per metric family of 24 (`exp4_localisation.py:263` `bh`). CCC family: p = 0.0066 (w180 rcea arousal) and p = 0.0115 (w60 rcea valence) both give **q = 0.138** (0.0115 x 24 / 2 = 0.138; the step-up makes the first one equal). QWK family: every q is 0.996 or 1.0.
The 4 identical-by-construction tests: person-relative CCC in 4 slices, p set to 1.0 (`np.allclose`, line 271). 44 informative.
n per test: 22 rcea, 16 retro; retro arousal QWK tests have n = 12 to 14 because per-visitor QWK is NaN when truth and prediction both sit in one level.

Robustness of the null to the family choice (my recomputation): per-lever warm-up CCC family (16) min q = 0.092; warm-up both metrics (32) 0.184; CCC without the 4 identical tests (20) 0.115; all 48 together 0.275. None below 0.05.

The rcea arousal w180 CCC gain is skewed: per-visitor deltas have mean +0.052 but **median +0.013**; two visitors carry it (M10 +0.52, M02 +0.42). Without them the mean gain is +0.010. The Wilcoxon still ranks it well because 16 of 22 deltas are positive.

**Power estimate (rough, labelled as an estimate).** From stored per-visitor deltas (`levers_perfold.csv`): rcea arousal w180 CCC has effect size dz = 0.37 (mean/SD of deltas). Paired-t approximation adjusted for Wilcoxon efficiency (0.955): about **59 visitors** for 80% power at uncorrected alpha 0.05, about **116** at alpha 0.05/24. A sign-test view (16/22 = 73% improve) gives about **35** (uncorrected) and **70** (0.05/24). So roughly 35 to 60 per stream uncorrected, 70 to 120 with correction. This is the best of 48 comparisons picked after the fact, so the true effect is probably smaller and these numbers are optimistic.

numbers.value: w180 rcea arousal CCC +0.0217 to +0.0739, 16/22 improved, p = 0.0066
w60 rcea valence CCC p = 0.0115, 16/22 improved
about 35 to 60 per stream uncorrected, 70 to 120 corrected

qa.q: p = 0.0066 is below 0.05. Why is it not significant?
qa.a: Because it is one of 24 CCC tests. With 24 tests, several small p-values appear by chance. After Benjamini-Hochberg it becomes q = 0.138, above 0.05. I fixed that rule before looking.

qa.q: Why do two different tests have the same q?
qa.a: BH is a step-up procedure. The second smallest p, 0.0115, gives 0.0115 times 24 over 2, which is 0.138. The smallest p would give 0.16 on its own, but BH never lets a smaller p get a larger q, so it is lowered to 0.138 too.

qa.q: How many participants would you have needed?
qa.a: This is a rough estimate from my own per-visitor differences, not a formal power analysis. For the strongest effect, the standardised effect is about 0.37. That suggests roughly 35 to 60 visitors per stream for an uncorrected test, and about 70 to 120 once I correct for 24 tests. It is the best of 48 comparisons, so the real effect is probably smaller and the real number higher.

qa.q: Is the 180 s gain real or two visitors?
qa.a: Mostly two visitors. The median visitor gains about 0.013 CCC; two visitors gain about 0.4 to 0.5. But 16 of 22 move up, which is why the rank test gives a small p. So it is a broad small shift plus two large ones, and it does not survive correction.

qa.q: Why say 'null' and not 'negative'?
qa.a: A negative result would show personalisation does not help. I cannot show that: the direction is mostly positive and the test is weak at 12 to 22 visitors. I can only say I could not establish a gain.

qa.q: Which tests are identical by construction, and why keep them?
qa.a: The person-relative target's CCC in four slices. That lever never touches the regressor, so CCC is exactly the reference. The script runs every lever through the same test loop and sets p to 1 for identical inputs. I report 48 and say 4 are uninformative.

qa.q: Why Wilcoxon and not a t-test?
qa.a: Per-visitor differences are skewed, as here where two visitors dominate. The Wilcoxon uses ranks, so one large visitor cannot drive it.

traps: If an examiner says 'you picked the family that makes it non-significant': under every grouping I recomputed (per lever, per metric, all 48, excluding the identical 4) the smallest q is between 0.092 and 0.275. The null does not depend on the family choice.

The mean CCC gain on the headline case is carried by two visitors (M10 +0.52, M02 +0.42; median +0.013). M10 has only 293 rows, so 180 warm-up rows are 61% of their session. Mention this before the examiner finds it in the appendix table.
The ordered-response argument ('favours the second reading') leans on pooled QWK, which the same chapter says moves with marginals. Safer phrasing: 'the ordering is suggestive, not evidence.'
Power numbers are my own post-hoc estimate, not in the thesis. Say 'rough estimate' every time.

cards.key: Results > Experiment 5: Personalisation (RQ5) > Findings
cards.gist: Three take-aways. Personalisation is not established at this size (21 of 24 cells move, 0 of 48 tests survive). The warm-up responds to how much annotation it gets (pooled QWK up to +0.3019), and the only label-free lever lowers CCC on three slices while raising QWK.
steps: Bullet 1: 21 of 24 pooled QWK cells up; 0 of 48 tests; from tests_summary.json.

Bullet 2: +0.3019 = retro arousal w180 pooled QWK minus reference (+0.1798 - (-0.1221)). 'On three of four slices each shorter warm-up raises it less' = pooled QWK monotone in duration on rcea arousal, retro valence, retro arousal.
Bullet 3: baseline CCC down on 3 of 4 slices, max drop 0.0393 (retro valence).

qa.q: What is the one-line answer to RQ5?
qa.a: Personalisation is not established at this cohort size. The pooled numbers move the expected way, but no paired test survives correction, and the lever that comes closest needs the visitor's own ratings.

qa.q: Why is the warm-up 'the one a museum cannot ask for'?
qa.a: It needs three minutes of moment-to-moment ratings from the visitor. That defeats the point of a guide that reads affect without asking.

traps: 'Raises pooled agreement by up to +0.3019' is pooled QWK. Per-visitor QWK for the same case rises +0.097 (p = 0.17). Know the difference if pressed.

cards.key: Results > Summary of Findings
cards.gist: One paragraph per research question. No sensor or combination beats the floor (RQ1), ordinal levels do not help (RQ2), scoping does not help (RQ3), ratings sit mostly with the visitor (RQ4), and personalisation is not established (RQ5).
steps: Every number restates an Exp findings box: Exp 1 (line 807), Exp 2 (996), Exp 3 (1091), Exp 4 (1200 to 1202), Exp 5 (1294).
RQ4 shares are REML crossed mixed-model point estimates on attended rows (Exp 4 variance table).

qa.q: Give me the thesis in one sentence per RQ.
qa.a: No sensor or combination predicts an unseen visitor's affect above the chance floor. Ordered levels do not help. Scoping to the attended painting does not help. The person explains 36 to 65% of a rating and the painting 0.1 to 1.5%. Personalisation moves the numbers but cannot be established with 12 to 22 people.

qa.q: 'It holds for any pipeline applied to these data' (RQ4). Does it?
qa.a: The split itself does, because it uses only the ratings, not any model. What it bounds is how much knowing the painting can explain. It does not by itself bound what a sensor model could learn about the within-visit part.

traps: **RQ4 sentence 'so it holds for any pipeline'** is true of the variance split (it is computed on ratings only) but should not be stretched into 'no pipeline could do better'. The painting share bounds what painting identity can contribute; the residual within-visit part (35 to 62%) is where sensors would have to find signal. Say that distinction aloud.

RQ1 'No combination scores above the best single sensor: both reach +0.0822': the single-sensor +0.0822 is the Exp 2 fixed-model HRV retro valence figure; the Exp 1 tuned HRV figure is +0.0841. Different runs, both fine.

cards.key: Results
cards.gist: The Results chapter runs data characterisation, then five experiments in a chain: each hands its chosen setting to the next. Every headline has the same shape: nothing beats the chance-corrected floor or the selection resolution, and the variance split explains why.
steps: **Data Characterisation (4.1):** 12,654 rcea and 6,880 retro analysed seconds (19,534); the feature matrices hold 12,660 and 7,022. Hands on: the row counts and per-sensor coverage every later percentage uses.

**Exp 1 Unimodal (4.2, RQ1):** all 20 sensor-by-slice CCC between -0.072 and +0.084; 8 model families span 0.0124; 0 of 436 feature-rating correlations survive. Hands on: the selected configuration, extremely randomised trees, selection resolution 0.08.

**Exp 2 Fusion (4.3, RQ1):** best combination +0.0822 = best single sensor; 4 alignment methods span 0.006; cross-sensor block beats its surrogate in 1 of 12 cells (0.6 expected). Hands on: early fusion of all five sensors plus the cross-sensor block (+0.0271 mean) and a QWK resolution of 0.21.

**Exp 3 Binning (4.4, RQ2):** pooled QWK negative on all slices but retro valence; BA at most 0.041 above chance; only 5 level counts selectable; the two arms differ by 0.0123 vs 0.21. Hands on: 3 levels, trained-on-levels classifier.

**Exp 4 Localisation (4.5, RQ3, RQ4):** 0 of 48 scoping tests survive; two CCC-only losses on painting B2 survive correction but are not credited (QWK does not confirm); painting share 0.1 to 1.5%, person 36.4 to 64.5%, cross-visitor agreement 0.000 to 0.002. Hands on: the whole-session pipeline.

**Exp 5 Personalisation (4.6, RQ5):** pooled QWK up in 21 of 24 cells; 0 of 48 tests survive, smallest q = 0.138; only the warm-up has an ordered response. Hands on: nothing (last experiment); the open question is label-free personalisation.
**Summary (4.7):** one line per RQ.

qa.q: Walk me through the chain of experiments.
qa.a: Exp 1 picks settings and a model per sensor. Exp 2 combines sensors and carries early fusion forward. Exp 3 turns the target into three ordered levels. Exp 4 asks whether scoping to the attended painting helps, and splits the rating variance. Exp 5 adapts the model to each visitor. Each passes its choice on, even when the choice is a tie, using the fixed tie rule.

qa.q: Why carry a winner forward when nothing is significant?
qa.a: Each later experiment needs one fixed pipeline. When options tie inside the resolution I pick by a pre-set rule, the highest mean or the simplest. The choice does not change the conclusion, because all options are tied.

qa.q: Is a null result just a failed project?
qa.a: No. The question was whether a guide can rely on these sensors for an unseen visitor, and the answer is a measured no, across a wide search. I also explain why: the rating is mostly the person, almost none the painting. That tells the next study where to spend effort. A failed project would be one that cannot say why it failed.

traps: Data Characterisation has no Findings box, unlike Exp 1 to 5. If asked for its headline, use the row counts and coverage.

visuals.title: Each experiment hands its setting to the next
visuals.caption: Read top to bottom: the right column is what the next section starts from. Row counts cover both streams.

cards.key: Limitations
cards.gist: The chapter opens by saying the labels set the ceiling. Then three blocks: a calm, natural setting where affect is weak and mixed up with walking and light; a small cohort (22 and 16) searched over fixed candidate sets; and sensors that measure correlates, not feelings, with no person-level covariates.
steps: '22 or 16 people ... never on the 38 collected': 22 rcea + 16 retro = 38 usable. Bas recruited 45 (22 + 23); 23 retro assigned, 20 in the aligned data, 16 with valid annotation.
'Configuration search compared candidate sets fixed in advance': 5 configuration parameters with literature-grounded candidates (Methodology 3.3.3).
'No demographic, questionnaire ... measure': confirmed by CLAUDE.md (no questionnaire data in the project).

qa.q: Would more participants fix it?
qa.a: More participants would make the person-specific share estimated more precisely, and would give the personalisation tests the power they lacked, roughly 35 to 120 per stream by my rough estimate. But they would not turn a person-specific response into a shared one. The painting share is small in the ratings themselves, so more of the same visitors viewing the same five paintings would not create shared signal.

qa.q: Why not pool the two streams to get 38?
qa.a: They are two different instruments: a live joystick and a retrospective sketch. Their distributions differ (for example 20% of rcea seconds sit at the rest value 5, none in retro) and prior work found they do not converge. Pooling would mix two definitions of the label.

qa.q: Is the ceiling really set by the labels?
qa.a: The labels set a ceiling on what the painting can explain: 0.1 to 1.5%. The sensors could still in principle track the within-visit part, and they did not in my data. So the fair statement is: the labels leave little shared signal, and the sensors did not find the rest.

qa.q: What limitation is missing from this chapter?
qa.a: A few I would add if asked: one fixed seed; the Exp 5 models are held at one setting rather than tuned; the rcea joystick rests at 5 for about a fifth of seconds; and the annotation delay is absorbed by a searched window, not measured.

qa.q: Why was luminance not controlled?
qa.a: The study was designed as a natural visit, so no covariate was controlled. Scene luminance was not logged, so I cannot regress it out of the pupil.

traps: **'Never on the 38 collected'.** 38 is the usable count; 45 were recruited (Lit Review says forty-five visitors, 22 + 23), and 46 have a usable behaviour log. Say 'the 38 usable participants'.

**Opening line: 'the ceiling reported here is set by the labels themselves'.** Too strong. The rating decomposition bounds what painting identity can add (0.1 to 1.5%); it does not bound what sensors could learn about the within-visit residual (35 to 62%). Safer: 'the labels leave little signal shared across people, which is what an unseen-visitor model needs.'

The chapter mentions 'intermittent affect' only via the Discussion's pointer; the Limitations text does not have a paragraph on it, though the Discussion cites Chapter 5 for it. If asked, it is covered under the naturalistic setting paragraph in spirit.

cards.key: Discussion
cards.gist: The Discussion explains the null. Ratings are mostly the visitor's own (36 to 65%) and barely the painting's (0.1 to 1.5%), so scoping and binning cannot create shared signal. Personalisation is the natural remedy but needs ratings a museum cannot ask for, and everything is about this collection, not VR museums in general.
steps: Section 6.1 backs its main claim with Exp 4's variance table; 6.2 with Exp 4 scoping tests; 6.3 with Exp 3 and the Exp 1 sensor table plus Exp 4 per-feature decomposition; 6.4 with Exp 2 combination (+0.0822) and Exp 5 verdict.

qa.q: Isn't a null result just a failed project?
qa.a: No. I asked whether an unseen visitor's affect can be read from these sensors in this setting. The answer is no, and it holds over a wide search: five configuration choices, eight model families, four alignment methods, 31 sensor subsets under three fusion rules, ordinal targets, scoping, and three personalisation levers. I also give the reason, from the ratings alone, and a method a next study can run before building any sensor pipeline.

qa.q: Why not deep learning or foundation models?
qa.a: With 22 and 16 people and a few thousand rows, tree ensembles are the stronger family on tabular features, and handcrafted features generalise to new people better than networks trained from scratch on raw signal. Foundation models and self-supervised learning are real options I reviewed but did not run. They do not change the variance split, which is computed on the ratings: if only about 1% of a rating is shared, a bigger model has little shared signal to find.

qa.q: What is the single most important sentence of the Discussion?
qa.a: The rating is mostly the person: 36 to 65% belongs to who is rating, 0.1 to 1.5% to which painting they look at. A model for an unseen visitor needs shared signal, and there is very little.

traps: The intro says 'None did so'. True for every credited comparison; some pooled Exp 5 figures sit above zero (warm-up 180 BA 0.44, QWK +0.27) but are not credited. If challenged: 'no model established a gain over the floor that survives the resolution or correction.'

visuals.title: Ratings are mostly the visitor's own, on both streams
visuals.caption: Look at the blue bars: the visitor holds 36.4 to 64.5% of a rating, the painting (orange) 0.1 to 1.5%. These are the same REML shares as Experiment 4.

cards.key: Discussion > Sources of the Near-Chance Ceiling
cards.gist: The main cause is in the ratings: only the painting part recurs across people, and it is 0.1 to 1.5%. Sensors also react to movement, load and light (literature signs agree 12 of 28, like chance), and affect comes and goes; lab studies score higher because they elicit strongly. With a selection resolution of 0.08 / 0.21, almost every difference is noise.
steps: Claim 'painting 0.1 to 1.5%, visitor 36.4 to 64.5%' <- Exp 4 variance table (REML crossed model on attended rows).
Claim 'computed on the ratings alone' <- methodology: intercept-only crossed model, no features.
Claim '12 of 28 signs agree' <- Results Exp 1 line 696 (16 features with a literature direction, 28 cells).
Claim 'resolution 0.08 / 0.21 fixed before comparison' <- resolution.json (20 repeats, p95 minus p5).

qa.q: How do you know the ceiling is in the data and not your pipeline?
qa.a: Three lines of evidence. First, the variance split uses only the ratings, no pipeline at all, and finds the painting explains 0.1 to 1.5%, and two visitors on the same painting agree at 0.000 to 0.002. Second, van der Kaaden's independent pipeline, with different preprocessing and a classification target, also fell to near chance for new people. Third, my own search spans preprocessing, eight model families, alignment, fusion, targets, scoping and personalisation, and nothing separates. I cannot prove no pipeline could do better, and the thesis says approaches outside this set remain open.

qa.q: You say a model trained on others can only use the painting part. Isn't that too strong?
qa.a: It is the strict reading for a model that knows only which painting is on view. A sensor model could in principle predict a new person's level, or the within-visit movement, if the sensors carried it. My Exp 1 correlations (0 of 436 survive) and the LOSO scores show they did not here. So the fair version is: little is shared across people, and the sensors did not find the rest.

qa.q: Would more visitors help?
qa.a: They would estimate the person share more precisely and give tests more power. They would not make the person share shared. What would change it is different stimuli that provoke different responses.

qa.q: Why do lab studies score higher?
qa.a: They elicit strong, well separated states with short stimuli and seated people. That creates a large stimulus-driven share. Here the stimulus share is almost absent. The variance split can be computed on their data too; the method transfers, not my numbers.

qa.q: What is the selection resolution?
qa.a: How much two runs of the same model on the same data differ by chance: 0.08 CCC and 0.21 QWK, measured from 20 repeats before I compared anything. A difference smaller than that is not a difference I can trust.

qa.q: Is 12 of 28 really 'indistinguishable from chance'?
qa.a: Yes. Under chance you expect 14 of 28. Twelve is below that, and a binomial test is far from significant.

traps: **Biggest logical trap: 'A model trained on other people can only use the painting part, because only that part recurs across people.'** The variance split bounds what **painting identity** can explain. It does not bound a **sensor** model: a sensor could track the within-visit residual (35 to 62%) or predict a new person's level from their physiology. Safer to say: 'The painting share bounds what knowing the stimulus can add. Sensors would have to find the within-visit part, and in these data they did not (0 of 436 correlations survive, all LOSO scores near zero).'
**'No preprocessing, model, or fusion choice can recover shared signal the ratings do not carry.'** True of stimulus-shared signal only. Same fix as above.

**'Three independent reimplementations of Bas's LOSO collapse'** is NOT in the thesis, and the stored results for it (`results/baseline_replication/`, `results/pipeline_rebuild/RESULT.md`) are not in the current results folder (only the aligned CSVs remain in `results/pipeline_rebuild/`). If you mention it, say it is earlier project work, not a reported result. What the thesis does report is Bas's own LOSO collapse (about 0.20 to 0.24 balanced accuracy on 7 classes, Lit Review 2.6).
'Differences between sensors are small beside differences between visitors': backed by Exp 2 alignment spread (per-visitor SD 0.045 to 0.110 vs arm gaps 0.006) and Exp 1 sensor table SDs. Fine.

visuals.title: Only the painting part is the same for every visitor
visuals.caption: Look at the orange slivers: 0.1 to 1.5%. This limits what painting identity can carry, not what sensors can: the visitor part (36 to 65%) and the leftover (35 to 62%) stay open to a sensor model in principle.

cards.key: Discussion > Effects of Scoping to the Attended Painting
cards.gist: Scoping to attended seconds was the most direct test for painting-driven signal and found none: the painting share is small, attended training lowered pooled QWK on every slice, and 0 of 48 tests survive. Its value is that the attended moment is the only point where two free-roaming visitors are comparable. On retro the sensors follow the painting more than the ratings do, most simply a light or content confound.
steps: 'Lowered the ordinal score on every slice' <- Exp 4 table: attended-trained pooled QWK below whole-on-attended in all 4 slices (-0.1292 vs -0.1100, -0.1447 vs -0.1151, -0.0983 vs +0.0130, -0.1506 vs -0.0986); BA also lower in all 4.
'0 of 48' <- Exp 4 scoping test family.
'Painting's part ... at or below 3.3%' <- the maximum of the eta-squared column (3.33, retro arousal).

'On retro every sensor category's painting share exceeds the ratings' 0.1%' <- Exp 4 per-feature decomposition (EDA by a factor of 38). The EDA factor is an lbfgs early stop: refitted with the best optimiser, retro EDA is 0.23% on 3 features, not 3.85% on 4 (see the Exp 4 Results variance card). The EDA factor is an lbfgs early stop: refitted with the best optimiser, retro EDA is 0.23% on 3 features, not 3.85% on 4 (see the Exp 4 Results variance card).

qa.q: Is 'at or below 3.3%' consistent with the 0.1 to 1.5% table?
qa.a: The 3.3% is the largest value from a different estimator, the one-way eta-squared check, 0.80 to 3.33%. The main mixed-model estimate is 0.1 to 1.5%. So 3.3% is a generous upper summary of the point estimates, not the headline figure. It is not the upper edge of the uncertainty: at three levels one slice reads 3.7%, and the bootstrap interval reaches 17.3% on retro arousal.

qa.q: Why did training on attended rows hurt?
qa.a: It has fewer rows, about 60% of the stream, and it removes three visitors with no attended second. There was no extra stimulus signal to make up for the smaller training set.

qa.q: If sensors track the painting more than ratings do, why not use that?
qa.a: Because tracking the painting is not tracking affect. The most likely reason EDA or pupil varies by painting is the painting's light and content. That is a confound I cannot remove here, since luminance was not logged.

qa.q: What did scoping give you, then?
qa.a: A place where visitors are comparable: the same painting at the same moment. Only there could I split the rating into person, painting and residual with the stimulus known.

traps: **'At or below 3.3%' is not a fair restatement of the uncertainty.** 3.3% is the eta-squared maximum (3.33). The REML point estimates are 0.1 to 1.5; the at-3-levels share reaches 3.7; the jackknife on retro arousal runs 4.1 to 9.8; the bootstrap CI reaches 17.3. Safer to say aloud: 'The mixed model puts the painting at 0.1 to 1.5%, and a one-way check at most 3.3%; the bootstrap interval is wide, so the cohort shows the share is small but cannot pin it down.' The same '3.3%' appears again in Future Work.

The jackknife on retro arousal ([4.1, 9.8]) does not contain the point estimate (0.1): dropping any single painting raises the share. That is odd and an examiner may ask. Honest answer: it is an optimiser artefact. The jackknife refits use lbfgs only, which stopped early; refitting the same five drops with powell gives 0.0 to 0.1%, in line with the full-data 0.1% (see the Exp 4 Results variance card). Either way the share is small.
'With the painting held fixed' is loose wording: the decomposition does not hold the painting fixed; it estimates a painting component on attended rows. Just say 'on the attended rows'.

visuals.title: Scoping moves visitors up and down about equally, on both streams
visuals.caption: Each line is one visitor's CCC on their attended seconds, whole-session model versus attended-trained model. 9, 9, 5 and 9 visitors improve and no test survives.

cards.key: Discussion > Predictability, Stability, and Shared Signal
cards.gist: Binning adds no signal: the two ordinal arms tie, and ordinal scores move with the level mix. Stable within a person, shared across people and carrying affect are three different things: HRV is the most person-locked signal and gave the top unimodal cell, but does not lead on average. The rating scale behaves as person-relative; response types and engagement stay untested.
steps: 'Two ways of producing levels cannot be told apart' <- Exp 3: arms differ 0.0123 vs resolution 0.21.
'HRV most locked to the person' <- Exp 4 per-feature decomposition: cardiac person share 66.2% and 56.9%.
'Single highest score' <- Exp 1 table: HRV retro valence +0.0841 (SD across visitors 0.164). HRV mean over four slices = (-0.0086 + 0.0374 + 0.0841 - 0.0718)/4 = +0.010; EDA mean = +0.015 leads.
'At most 1.5%' <- REML painting share maximum.

qa.q: Why does HRV give the single highest score yet is 'person-locked'?
qa.a: The high score is one cell, retro valence, 16 visitors, with a large spread across visitors (SD 0.164). The same sensor also gives the lowest cell, -0.072 on retro arousal, and its four-slice mean is only about +0.01, behind EDA. 'Person-locked' is a separate fact from the feature decomposition: most of HRV's variation is between people. A person-locked feature can line up with person-level rating differences in one small slice by chance. It does not travel to a new person.

qa.q: What does 'person-relative scale' mean?
qa.a: Two people looking at the same painting do not give comparable numbers. Each person uses the scale around their own level. So a 6 from one visitor is not the same as a 6 from another.

qa.q: Why doesn't binning help?
qa.a: Binning changes what is scored, not what information is there. And part of any change in an ordinal score comes from how the levels are filled, not from better prediction.

qa.q: What is the engagement idea?
qa.a: Gaze, dwell and revisits measure engagement directly, without asking. A guide could predict engagement first and link it to affect later.

traps: **'HRV produced the single highest score in the thesis'.** Not literally true: Exp 5's 180 s warm-up reaches CCC +0.0902 (retro arousal) and +0.0739 (rcea arousal), and pooled QWK/BA figures are larger still; individual visitors reach +0.70 (M08). Safer: 'HRV gave the highest single-sensor score without personalisation, +0.084 on retro valence.'
'a stable trait of the individual' - the person component is a stable offset over one visit, which could be scale use or mood that day, not necessarily a trait. Say 'stable across the visit'.
'The painting moves a rating by at most 1.5%' - point estimate only; CI reaches 17.3%. Say 'the estimate is at most 1.5%'.

visuals.title: Cardiac features are the most tied to the visitor, on both streams
visuals.caption: Look at the blue bars: cardiac is 66.2% visitor on rcea and 56.9% on retro (stored values). That fits 'stable within a person' without being 'shared across people'.

cards.key: Discussion > Reliable Inputs for an Adaptive Guide
cards.gist: A guide cannot rely on second-by-second affect decoding for a new visitor. More sensors do not help (best combination +0.0822 = best single sensor), so the number of sensors is a cost choice. Personalisation is the obvious remedy, but no lever survived correction: the warm-up came closest and needs ratings, and the label-free baseline moved scores less consistently.
steps: '+0.0822 exactly' <- Exp 2 combination mechanisms: pupil + HRV weighted averaging on retro valence and HRV alone, same slice.
'None survived correction' <- Exp 5 Verdict (0/48, min q 0.138).
'Gain increases with each additional second' <- Exp 5: pooled QWK monotone on 3 of 4 slices only.
'Baseline moved pooled figures less consistently' <- baseline raised pooled QWK and BA in 3 of 4 each and lowered CCC in 3 of 4, vs warm-up 180 up on all 4 for all three metrics.

qa.q: What should a museum guide use instead?
qa.a: Signals that are directly observable and reliable: where the visitor looks, how long, whether they return, whether they talk. Those measure engagement, and a guide can adapt to engagement without decoding affect.

qa.q: Is 'number of sensors is a cost decision' justified?
qa.a: On this data, yes: no combination beat the best single sensor. With a larger cohort or stronger stimuli fusion might help; I only claim it for this collection.

qa.q: Could the warm-up gain be obtained without labels?
qa.a: That is the open question. Options are passive baselines from the unlabelled stream, behavioural signals like dwell in place of ratings, or placing a new visitor relative to the cohort without any labelled second.

traps: **'Its gain increases with each additional second it is given'.** Overstated. Pooled QWK rises monotonically on 3 of 4 slices only (rcea valence dips from 0 to 60 s), CCC is not monotone (rcea valence 0.0368, 0.0412, 0.0287, 0.0400), and durations are 4 points, not 'each second'. Safer: 'its pooled agreement rises with the length of the warm-up on three of the four slices.'
'the warm-up's apparent gain' is the right word; keep 'apparent'. The 180 s CCC gain on rcea arousal is carried by two visitors.

visuals.title: The warm-up came closest, on both streams
visuals.caption: Look at the top row: by 180 s pooled QWK is up in every slice, though not at every step. None of it survives a paired test.

cards.key: Conclusion and Future Work
cards.gist: Two conclusions: a measured ceiling (nothing beat the chance-corrected floor for a new visitor) and its cause (ratings are mostly the visitor, barely the painting). Future work: an event-anchored collection with more contrasting, repeated stimuli, label-efficient personalisation, and a bigger cohort with better labels and covariates, starting with the variance split on pilot ratings.
steps: Backed by Summary of Findings (4.7) and the Exp 4 variance table; Future Work's 3.3% is the eta-squared maximum.

qa.q: What should the next study do?
qa.a: First, compute the person-painting split on pilot ratings before building any sensor pipeline. Then choose stimuli for contrast, use more of them, and show each one to every visitor more than once, so the person part can be estimated and removed. Size the cohort for a paired test, roughly 35 to 120 per stream by my rough estimate. Use one validated rating instrument, and record covariates like personality, art familiarity and scene luminance.

qa.q: What is your contribution if nothing worked?
qa.a: A careful measured ceiling under a leakage-free protocol with a stated noise floor, and an explanation of it from the ratings alone. Plus a reusable check, the variance split, that tells a project early whether shared signal exists.

cards.key: Conclusion and Future Work > Conclusions
cards.gist: Reliable prediction for unseen visitors was not achieved, because the response is mostly individual. The sensors are not the limit on this cohort: fusion, the target, scoping and personalisation do not move results past the resolution. Personalisation's direction is an underpowered null; the warm-up came closest but needs labels.
steps: 'No sensor ... personalisation mechanism ... predicted above the chance-corrected floor' <- Exp 1 to 5 findings.
'0.1 to 1.5% shared ... 36.4 to 64.5% carried by a stable trait' <- Exp 4 variance table.
'21 of the 24 cells' <- Exp 5 pooled QWK count.

qa.q: You say nothing predicted above the floor, but warm-up gives BA 0.44 and QWK +0.27. Contradiction?
qa.a: Those are pooled figures for one arm, untested at that level. The paired per-visitor tests are what I pre-specified for a claim, and none survived. So nothing established a gain over the floor. I would phrase it that way.

qa.q: Is 'the sensors are not the constraint' justified?
qa.a: What I showed is that the sensors cannot be told apart, their gap is inside the resolution. That does not prove better sensors would not help. The stronger argument is the variance split: little shared signal exists in the ratings for any sensor to find.

qa.q: What is a 'stable trait' here?
qa.a: The person component: each visitor's consistent offset over the visit. It could be how they use the scale or their mood that day. It is stable within the visit; I did not measure it across days.

traps: **'No ... personalisation mechanism tested predicted above the chance-corrected floor'.** Some pooled figures are above it (warm-up 180 BA 0.364 to 0.437, pooled QWK +0.08 to +0.27). Safer: 'none established a gain that survives the selection resolution or correction.'
**'carried by a stable trait of that person'.** One visit only; the component is a stable offset within the visit, not a demonstrated trait. Say 'a stable difference between visitors'.

**'On this cohort the sensors are not the constraint, since the gap between the leading sensors falls inside the selection resolution'.** Non sequitur: a tie between sensors shows they are indistinguishable, not that sensing is not limiting. Safer: 'no sensor can be told apart from another, and the ratings carry little shared signal for any of them.'
'its gain increasing with each additional second' (last paragraph) - same overstatement as in 6.4; only pooled QWK on 3 of 4 slices is monotone.

'personalisation's consistent direction across 21 of the 24 cells' includes cells the thesis attributes to marginal shifts. Say 'the pooled figures mostly move up, but none of it survives a paired test.'

cards.key: Conclusion and Future Work > Future Work
cards.gist: Three directions. (1) An event-anchored collection: more, contrasting, repeated stimuli and comparisons around shared gaze events. (2) Label-efficient personalisation, such as passive baselines, behaviour, cohort-relative placement or a short rating step added to eye-tracker calibration; (3) a cohort sized for paired tests with one validated rating tool, covariates and light logging. Run the variance split on pilot ratings first.
steps: 'Painting share at or below 3.3%' <- eta-squared maximum 3.33 (see 6.2 card trap).
'Gaze log already resolves sub-painting regions' <- AOI figure in Methodology 3.6.1 (B3 object AOIs) and Data Characterisation.
'Two annotation streams do not converge' <- van der Kaaden finding (Lit Review 2.6).
'Cohort sized for a paired per-participant test' <- my rough power estimate: about 35 to 60 per stream uncorrected, 70 to 120 corrected, for the strongest Exp 5 effect.

qa.q: How many visitors should the next study recruit?
qa.a: A rough estimate from my strongest personalisation effect: about 35 to 60 per stream for an uncorrected paired test at 80% power, and 70 to 120 once correcting for many tests. The effect is probably smaller than observed, so I would plan toward the upper end. That is an estimate, not a formal power analysis.

qa.q: Why repeat each stimulus for every visitor?
qa.a: If each person sees each stimulus more than once, the person effect and the stimulus effect can be separated cleanly, and the person part removed rather than just held out.

qa.q: Why is the variance split a good first step?
qa.a: It needs only ratings and a stimulus label, so it runs on pilot data before any sensor pipeline. It tells you whether there is a shared response worth predicting.

traps: **'The ceiling reported here belongs to the data, not to the analysis'.** Strong. Safer: 'The ratings carry little shared signal, which no analysis can add; approaches outside the set I tested remain open.'
'yielded a painting share at or below 3.3%' - same issue as 6.2; the REML estimate is 0.1 to 1.5, the CI reaches 17.3.
The eye-tracker calibration idea is a design suggestion, not tested.

cards.key: Experiment 5 Tables
cards.gist: Every Experiment 5 arm on all metrics, the per-lever changes, all 48 paired tests, and per-visitor CCC and QWK for each slice of both streams. Generated by `make_exp5_appendix.py` from `results/exp1_v2/exp5/`.
steps: Summary table: mean, population SD (ddof=0), range of per-visitor CCC; pooled QWK; BA (`make_exp5_appendix.py:45-50`).
Delta table: lever minus reference, on mean CCC and **pooled** QWK (`make_exp5_appendix.py:76-95`).
Tests table: from tests.csv; Reference/Lever/Delta columns are **per-visitor means**, for QWK the mean of per-visitor QWK (e.g. rcea arousal reference +0.0057), not pooled QWK (-0.1233).
Per-visitor tables: one per slice per metric (8 tables); a dash = too few rows or single-level QWK.

numbers.what: Per-visitor CCC range, reference rcea valence

qa.q: Why does the tests table show QWK reference +0.0057 but the body shows -0.1233?
qa.a: The body shows pooled QWK over all predictions. The test is paired per visitor, so it uses each visitor's own QWK, and the table shows their mean. They differ because pooled QWK also counts between-visitor level differences.

qa.q: Why is one visitor at +0.70 on rcea valence?
qa.a: M08. For that visitor the model tracks the rating well in all arms except baseline. One visitor like that lifts the mean by about 0.03 on its own, which is why I report the spread and the improved counts.

traps: **Tests table caption says the columns are in units of 'CCC or pooled QWK'.** Wrong for QWK: the values are means of per-visitor QWK (they match tests.csv, e.g. +0.0057, not pooled -0.1233). Say: 'the tests are on per-visitor QWK; the caption's word pooled is a slip.'
The same caption contains `$\\Delta$` and `\\ac{CCC}` (double backslashes, from `make_exp5_appendix.py:190`), which may render oddly in the PDF. Cosmetic.
The caption correctly says BH is 'within that metric's own family', which contradicts the Methodology's 'within that lever's own family'. The appendix matches the code.

visuals.title: The tests-table caption mislabels its QWK column
visuals.caption: Look at the caption string: it says 'CCC or pooled QWK', but the QWK values are means of per-visitor QWK (they match tests.csv). The raw string also prints `\\Delta` and `\\ac` with double backslashes.

cards.key: Declaration on the Use of Generative AI
cards.gist: Declares three AI tools. **Claude** helped discuss methods, draft code and text that the author then read, ran, revised and edited, find faults (including checking numbers against stored results), and search and summarise literature he then read in the original. **ChatGPT** was a conversational aid to understanding and **NotebookLM** helped work through single papers; the author's own judgement decided what stands.
steps: What it states: hybrid approach, idea or problem put to the model, options discussed, something tried, result brought back, many iterations; 'what stands in this thesis is what survived that exchange and the author's own judgement of it'.
Claude: 5 uses listed (method implementation and planning, drafting code, drafting text, fault finding and number checking, literature search and summary).
ChatGPT: talking through topics, questions about the field and methods, testing his own understanding.
NotebookLM: locating relevant passages, explaining a paper's method and findings, comparing papers.
What it does not state: percentages, which chapters, which scripts. Do not invent these.

qa.q: How did you use AI?
qa.a: As a discussion partner and a drafting tool. I discussed how to implement methods on this data, had it draft code and text, and used it to find faults and check numbers against the stored results. I read, ran and revised the code, edited the text, and read every cited paper in the original. ChatGPT helped me understand concepts, NotebookLM helped me work through papers.

qa.q: What did you do yourself?
qa.a: The research questions, the decisions about which analysis to run and which result to carry forward, reading and running the code, checking results, and judging what stands in the thesis. The declaration says what survives is what passed my own judgement. The fact that I can explain each step and each number today is the test of that.

qa.q: How do you know AI-drafted code is correct?
qa.a: I read it, ran it, and checked outputs against the data: row counts, per-visitor numbers, and cross-checks like the variance split by two methods. Numbers in the thesis were checked against the stored result files.

qa.q: Did AI choose the conclusions?
qa.a: No. Ideas went both ways, but the conclusions rest on results stored in files that anyone can recompute. The decisions were mine.

qa.q: Did AI write the literature review?
qa.a: It helped search and summarise, and drafted passages. I read each paper in the original before citing it, and edited the text for content and accuracy.

traps: Answer only from what the declaration says plus honest general framing. Do not give percentages or claim a split per chapter that is not in the text.
If asked 'could you rebuild this without AI', the honest answer is about understanding: you can explain every step, number and choice; speed would differ.
The strongest defence is fluency: being able to explain the code-level details on these cards is itself the evidence of ownership.

cards.key: Methodology
cards.gist: Five experiments run in a chain on one cohort under one protocol, each settling one choice and handing it on. Exp 1 and 2 predict the 0 to 10 rating (**regression**, scored by **CCC**); Exp 3 to 5 predict ordered levels (**ordinal classification**, scored by **pooled QWK** plus balanced accuracy).
steps: **Shared first (3.1, 3.2):** data, the four slices (rcea/retro x valence/arousal), LOSO, metrics, in-fold median imputation + scaling, Wilcoxon + BH testing, and the **selection resolution** (0.08 CCC, 0.21 pooled QWK) used to break ties.

**Exp 1 (unimodal) decides:** each sensor's configuration and the standard model. Carried: pupil `P_vt30_c0_t0` (30 deg/s fixation rule, no gaze correction, trailing, 0 s delay, 8 s window), EDA `E_nk_k5_w3` (NeuroKit, 5-MAD motion mask, 3 s trailing), HRV `H_m3_t0` (interbeat multiplier 3, trailing, 0 s delay, 60 s window), speech per utterance (88 eGeMAPS + 1 VADER). Standard model: **ExtraTrees**, 300 trees, max_depth tuned over {None, 8, 4}. Passes on: a 114-column matrix and the model.

**Exp 2 (fusion) decides:** how sensors are combined. Carried: fixed windowing (no learned alignment), the cross-sensor block at a 5 s window (8 columns), and **early fusion of all five sensors + the block** = 122 columns. Passes on: that matrix and the early-fusion regressor's stored predictions.

**Exp 3 (binning) decides:** target representation and level count, per condition and axis. Equal-width levels on the fixed 0 to 10 scale (edges never fitted). Carried: the **trained-on-levels arm** (a classifier fitted on levels) and **3 levels in every slice** (all counts tied inside 0.21, so the coarsest wins). Passes on: the 3-level target and the classifier.

**Exp 4 (localisation) decides:** whether scoping to seconds a visitor attends a painting helps, and bounds what any model could recover through a **variance decomposition** of the ratings (crossed person x painting random effects, REML). Attended rows: 7,986 rcea (63.1%), 4,134 retro (58.9%). M04, M07 (rcea) and M28 (retro) contribute no attended second.

**Exp 5 (personalisation):** tests three levers (baseline-window calibration, labelled warm-up, person-relative target) against a fresh no-personalisation reference on the whole-session Exp 2 pipeline. It carries nothing forward.
Appendix B (`app:alt-supplementary`) lists the final configuration each pipeline component ends up carrying.

qa.q: Walk me through the whole pipeline in one minute.
qa.a: I first fixed each sensor's preprocessing and the model on the continuous rating, because CCC separates candidates more finely. Then I chose how to combine the sensors: early fusion of all five plus a small cross-sensor block. Then I moved to an ordinal target and picked the level count: three levels, trained directly on levels. Then I asked whether restricting to painting-viewing seconds helps, and how much of the rating variance is shared across people at all. Last, I tried three ways of personalising to the visitor.

qa.q: Why regression first and classification later? Isn't that inconsistent?
qa.a: It is deliberate. A continuous score separates candidate pipelines more finely than three to ten levels, so I use it to choose features and models. The ratings are person-relative and carry reaction lags, so the final target is ordinal. The task changes at Exp 3, and the metric changes with it.

qa.q: Does a choice made in Exp 1 get revisited later?
qa.a: No. Each experiment takes the previous decision as fixed. That keeps later comparisons clean but means an early choice is never re-tested under the ordinal target. Since every Exp 1 difference is inside the resolution, a different early choice would most likely change nothing.

qa.q: What does Exp 5 hand on?
qa.a: Nothing. It is the end of the chain. It only tests whether personalising helps.

qa.q: Which model is used where?
qa.a: Configuration votes in Exp 1 use Ridge(alpha=1) because it is cheap. The standard model from Exp 1 on is ExtraTrees (regressor for CCC, ExtraTreesClassifier for the level arm). The selection resolution was measured with a random forest.

traps: The chain means early choices are made under CCC regression and never re-checked under QWK classification. Honest answer: yes, and every Exp 1 and Exp 2 difference was inside the 0.08 resolution, so there was no strong winner to lose.

Three different models appear: Ridge for the configuration vote, ExtraTrees as the standard model, RandomForest for the resolution repeats. Know which is which (see the Data and Shared Protocol card).

`predictions.py` docstring still says CatBoost; the grid actually builds ExtraTrees. CatBoost had the highest family mean but was tied with ExtraTrees (gap 0.0007) and the tie went to the family with the smaller spread.

cards.key: Methodology > Data and Shared Protocol
cards.gist: The rules every experiment shares. The two streams (rcea rated live, retro rated afterwards) are never pooled; every score is per **slice** (stream x axis) under **LOSO**, and anything that learns, including median imputation and scaling, is fitted on training visitors only. Scores: **CCC** for ratings, **pooled QWK** plus balanced accuracy for levels, **Wilcoxon + Benjamini-Hochberg** for tests, and the **selection resolution** (0.08 CCC) for ties.
steps: **Data:** eye tracker (headset), EDA and BVP wristband (with accelerometer and skin temperature as auxiliary channels), push-to-talk speech, and the VR engine's gaze-and-behaviour log (`neo_data/`). Five paintings: B1, B2, B3, C5, C6.

**Auxiliary channels, never predicted from:** accelerometer drives the EDA motion mask; temperature is only a reference for reading the tonic EDA level; engine floor position drives teleport detection and Exp 4's attended-painting labels.
**Rows:** one row = one second of one participant's analysed window on a 1 Hz label grid. Feature matrix: rcea 12,660 rows / 22 participants, retro 7,022 rows / 16 participants.

**Labels:** 0 to 10. rcea joystick at 4 Hz reduced to 1 Hz by per-second **median**, no fixed delay (`features.py` `labels_v2`: `load_rcea_aligned(pid, valence_delay_s=0, arousal_delay_s=0, reducer='median')`). retro native 1 Hz. Labels are never normalised.

**LOSO:** for each visitor, train on everyone else, test on them. A fold is skipped if the held-out visitor has < 5 rows or the training set < 50 rows (`families.py:113`). Inner tuning: ridge uses inner LeaveOneGroupOut, others GroupKFold(5), choice by mean inner CCC.
**CCC** (Exp 1, 2): computed per held-out visitor, then averaged over visitors (`exp4_localisation.py` `score_cell`: 'CCC is the mean of the per-visitor values').

**Pooled QWK** (Exp 3 to 5): `cohen_kappa_score(all_true, all_pred, weights='quadratic', labels=range(B))` once over the concatenated held-out predictions of every fold. **Balanced accuracy**: `balanced_accuracy_score` on the same pooled predictions, chance = 1/B (`chance=1/LEVELS`).

**Chance-corrected floor:** 0 on both CCC and QWK means no usable information about the held-out visitor. A constant prediction gives CCC exactly 0; QWK 0 means agreement equal to what the marginals alone would give. Both can go negative.

**Missing values:** every model is `Pipeline([SimpleImputer(strategy='median'), StandardScaler(), model])`, refitted per fold on training rows only, applied unchanged to the held-out visitor. Applied to all eight families, including HistGB, XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost which could handle NaN natively (`families.py:124,131`).

**Row rule:** a row is not dropped for a partly missing feature vector. Inside a single-sensor cell a row needs a finite label and at least one finite feature of that sensor (`families.py` `run_cell`). Late fusion renormalises averaging weights over sensors that produced a prediction.
**Seeds:** `RANDOM_SEED = 42` (`scripts/utils.py:39`) for every stochastic model; SVR is deterministic.

**Wilcoxon + BH, form 1 (Exp 1):** one-sample Wilcoxon on each feature's per-participant within-visitor Spearman r (at least 30 paired seconds per participant, at least 8 participants per cell), BH over all **436** tests at once (`relations.py:60-95`). 0 survive.

**Wilcoxon + BH, form 2 (Exp 4, 5):** paired Wilcoxon over per-participant scores (per-participant CCC and per-participant QWK), BH applied separately within each metric's family (`exp4_localisation.py:278-316`, `exp5_personalisation.py:255-282`). A difference is credited only if it survives q < 0.05 on **both** CCC and QWK.

**Selection resolution:** `selection.py` `measure_resolution`: cell rcea / `H_m4_t0` (HRV, starting multiplier 4) / arousal; `RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=42+r)`; 20 repeats; each repeat reruns full LOSO with each fold's training participants drawn with replacement (`rng.choice(..., replace=True)`); statistic = mean per-visitor CCC; resolution = ceil((p95 - p5) x 100)/100 = ceil(7.83)/100 = **0.08**.

**QWK resolution:** `resolution_qwk.py`: same cell, same repeats and resampling, `RandomForestClassifier(300)`, 5 equal-width levels, statistic = pooled QWK per repeat; p95 - p5 = 0.204 -> **0.21**. Robustness only: 3 levels 0.22, 10 levels 0.24.

numbers.value: 4 (rcea valence, rcea arousal, retro valence, retro arousal)
96 (48 per metric); 2 significant on CCC, 0 on QWK -> 0 credited

qa.q: What is a slice?
qa.a: One annotation stream crossed with one axis. rcea valence, rcea arousal, retro valence, retro arousal. Every score is reported per slice.

qa.q: Why are rcea and retro never pooled?
qa.a: They measure affect in different ways: one live with a joystick that rests at 5, one drawn afterwards from a replay. Their distributions differ (rcea valence mean 6.28, retro 5.52; 20% of rcea seconds sit exactly on 5, none in retro). Pooling would let the model learn which stream a row came from. They are also different people.

qa.q: Is the data normalised?
qa.a: The features, yes: every model is median imputer, then StandardScaler, then the model. Both are fitted on the training participants only and applied to the held-out visitor. The labels are not normalised; they stay on the raw 0 to 10 scale.

qa.q: Is the imputer also used for boosted trees that handle NaN themselves?
qa.a: Yes. All eight families get the same imputer and scaler pipeline, so they see identical inputs. A difference between models is then a difference between models, not between missing-value strategies.

qa.q: Why median and not mean imputation?
qa.a: Physiological features are skewed and have outliers. The median is robust to those, so one bad visitor does not shift the filled value much.

qa.q: Is anything fitted on the test visitor?
qa.a: No. Imputer, scaler, model and hyperparameter choice are all fitted inside the training fold. The configuration vote also runs on training participants only. The only thing computed on the held-out visitor is the score.

qa.q: What is the difference between pooled QWK and per-participant QWK?
qa.a: Pooled QWK concatenates every visitor's held-out predictions and computes one kappa. Per-participant QWK computes one kappa per visitor. Many visitors sit on one or two levels, where per-visitor kappa is unstable or undefined, so the headline is pooled. The paired Wilcoxon tests use per-participant QWK, because they need one number per visitor.

qa.q: How is CCC aggregated across folds?
qa.a: I compute CCC for each held-out visitor and take the mean across visitors. It is not pooled. The per-visitor values are also what the Wilcoxon tests use.

qa.q: What does chance-corrected floor mean?
qa.a: Zero. For CCC, zero means the predictions carry no linear agreement with the truth; a constant prediction scores exactly zero. For QWK, zero means agreement no better than the level marginals alone would give. Both can go below zero, which is worse than knowing nothing.

qa.q: Why is balanced accuracy chance 1/B?
qa.a: Balanced accuracy is the mean recall across levels. A model that always predicts one level gets recall 1 on that level and 0 on the others, so the mean is 1/B. Random guessing also gives 1/B on average. With 3 levels that is 0.333.

qa.q: What does credited only where both metrics agree mean?
qa.a: In Exp 4 and 5 I run the paired test on per-participant CCC and on per-participant QWK separately, each with its own BH correction. I only claim a difference if it survives q < 0.05 on both. In Exp 4, two comparisons survived on CCC and none on QWK, so none is credited.

qa.q: How exactly was the selection resolution measured?
qa.a: On one fixed cell: HRV features at their starting configuration (multiplier 4) against rcea arousal. I ran the full LOSO twenty times with a random forest of 300 trees. Each repeat changes the seed and resamples each fold's training participants with replacement. For each repeat I take the mean per-visitor CCC. The gap between the 5th and 95th percentile of those twenty numbers is 0.078, rounded up to 0.08.

qa.q: Why that cell and not the selected model?
qa.a: To avoid circularity. If I calibrated the margin on the thing I then choose, the margin would depend on the choice. The HRV starting configuration exists before any comparison and does not change whatever the selection decides.

qa.q: Why a separate QWK resolution?
qa.a: QWK is on a different scale with its own run-to-run noise. The same procedure with a random-forest classifier on five equal-width levels gives a gap of 0.204, so 0.21. At 3 and 10 levels it would be 0.22 and 0.24, which I report only as a robustness check.

traps: **The resolution model is a RandomForest, not the standard ExtraTrees**, and the thesis never names it (it says only 'one invariant reference cell under the starting configuration'). RandomForest is one of the eight families compared in Exp 1. Honest answer: it was chosen before the family comparison as a generic default; it was not the family carried forward, so the margin does not depend on the selection.

**The 'bootstrap' collapses duplicates.** The code draws training participants with replacement, then uses `np.isin(g, boot)`, so a participant drawn twice is used once. Each fold actually trains on a random subset of about 64% of the training visitors (about 13 of 21). This makes the measured noise larger than simple retraining, so the margin is conservative (it makes ties more likely, not fewer).

**19 of the 20 QWK repeats are negative (one is +0.0034)** (median about -0.13). The reference cell is below chance on pooled QWK. The margin measures spread between repeats, not the level, so this does not invalidate it, but be ready.
The thesis says 'the twenty means'; for QWK each repeat gives one pooled value, not a mean. Only the CCC version is a mean (over visitors).

**The protocol never states that CCC is averaged per visitor**, while QWK is pooled. The paragraph defining 'pooled' sits next to CCC. Say clearly: CCC = mean over held-out visitors; QWK and balanced accuracy = pooled.

**'Each slice carries one fold per visitor'** is not true for every cell: EDA-gated visitors have no EDA features, so their fold is skipped in single-sensor EDA cells (retro EDA scores only 7 of 16 visitors; rcea EDA 18 of 22).

**'Rows are never dropped for a missing feature'** holds for partly missing rows. In a single-sensor cell a row whose every feature for that sensor is missing is dropped (`ok = isfinite(y) & isfinite(X).any(axis=1)`).

**'Usability is established by the coverage audit'** overstates it. Cohort membership comes from whether a non-empty annotation file exists (22 rcea, 16 retro). The coverage audit excludes nobody: M18, M37, M28 all stay in.

**BH family in Exp 5:** thesis says correction is 'within that lever's own family'; the code corrects within each metric across all levers and slices together (`t.groupby('metric')`). Result is the same here (0 of 48 significant), but the family definition differs.

**Condition is confounded with collection wave.** rcea is 21 first-wave visitors (Nov 2025) + M42; retro is 3 first-wave (M14, M15, M17) + 13 second-wave (Jan-Feb 2026). The EDA failures cluster in the second wave, which is why retro EDA is so thin. A stream difference could partly be a wave difference.

cards.key: Methodology > Data Characterisation
cards.gist: Three checks on the data before any model. **Coverage** is the share of analysed seconds with at least one raw sample, per sensor and visitor. **Signal quality** asks whether rates, timestamps, ranges and completeness match the instrument; **visiting behaviour** reads order, dwell, revisits and guide use from the engine log.
steps: **Coverage** (`scripts/thesis_v2/raw_coverage.py` `_seconds_present`): floor every raw sample timestamp to the second, take the unique seconds, then coverage = share of the participant's analysed grid seconds that appear in that set. No cleaning, no validity flags (the pupil valid-flag variant exists in the script but is not in the thesis table).

Analysed grid = `_analysed_grid`: read from the cached `results/thesis_v2/features/{pid}_{stream}.parquet` index (annotation grid after the pre-session trim). Totals 12,654 rcea + 6,880 retro = 19,534 seconds.
Raw sources: pupil `raw_data_from_sensors/Pupil_120hz_UTC/*_eye120hz.csv` (`dt_utc_index`), EDA `load_eda`, BVP `load_bvp`, speech `load_speech_audio(pid)['utc']` (silence-removed audio frames).

**Signal quality** is computed in the notebooks `notebooks/characterisation_{pupil,eda,hrv,speech}.ipynb` over the full cohort's raw files (47 eye files, 47 EDA files, 48 BVP folders), not only the analysed 38.
**Annotation check** on the same pass: share of rated seconds exactly at the midpoint 5 (joystick rest), which matters for level boundaries in Exp 3.
**Visiting behaviour** is computed in `notebooks/characterisation_behaviour.ipynb` from `neo_data/viewing_events.csv`, `observings.csv`, `verbal_communication.csv`, `participants.csv`.

numbers.value: a second is covered if >= 1 raw sample falls in it

qa.q: How exactly is coverage computed?
qa.a: For each participant and sensor I take every raw sample's timestamp and floor it to the whole second. A second of the analysed grid counts as covered if at least one raw sample falls in it. Coverage is covered seconds divided by analysed seconds. It is measured before any cleaning.

qa.q: Why measure coverage before cleaning?
qa.a: So that a low figure means only one thing: the sensor did not record. Measured after cleaning, a gap could be either the sensor or my own rejection steps. Cleaning losses are reported separately, like the EDA gate.

qa.q: Why is the denominator the analysed window and not the whole annotation?
qa.a: rcea's joystick starts several minutes before any sensor, during a practice phase. Counting those seconds would make coverage look low for a reason that has nothing to do with the sensors.

qa.q: One sample in a second counts as covered? Isn't that generous?
qa.a: Yes, it is a presence measure, not a density measure. The eye tracker shows why that matters: coverage is about 0.99 but the tracker delivers a median 23 Hz, not 120. I report the density separately in Signal Quality.

traps: The coverage grid is the **old thesis_v2 grid** (19,534 s), not the Exp 1 feature matrix (19,682 rows). See the Coverage and Usability Audit card for the exact reason.

The characterisation numbers are computed **inside notebooks**, against the project's own rule that notebooks never compute. If asked 'where is the code', say `notebooks/characterisation_*.ipynb`, which import helpers from `scripts/thesis_v2/raw_coverage.py` and `scripts/preprocessing/`.
Coverage near 1 does not mean usable. EDA raw coverage is 0.99 / 0.98 while 20 of 47 EDA recordings fail the quality gate.

visuals.title: Coverage is one line: floor each sample to its second
visuals.caption: Look at the last two lines: each raw sample time is floored to the second, and coverage is the share of analysed seconds found in that set.

visuals.title: A second counts as covered if it holds one raw sample
visuals.caption: Look at the red boxes: rcea visitor M13's eye file starts 3 s after rating begins, retro visitor M17's about 4 minutes in, so those seconds are uncovered. After that every second counts, however bursty: coverage measures presence, not quality.

cards.key: Results > Data Characterisation
cards.gist: Three facts shape how every later result is read. Almost every second has pupil, EDA and BVP data but speech is sparse; the eye tracker runs far below spec, 20 of 47 EDA recordings are unusable, and BVP is perfect or absent. Visitors mostly start at B1, end at C5, and spend almost half their viewing time on text panels.
steps: Who exists: raw folders M01 to M48 (48 IDs). **M26** has no eye file, no EDA, no usable BVP, no transcript, no VR log: effectively 47 participants.
Annotation files: rcea 22 (M01-M13, M18-M25, M42); retro 20 (M14, M15, M17, M28-M31, M33-M38, M40, M41, M43, M45-M48). No annotation in either stream: M16, M26, M27, M32, M39, M44.

Retro files that load empty: **M33** (valence all NaN, arousal one constant value on 53 rows), **M36, M38, M47** (all NaN). `load_retro_aligned` drops rows missing valence or arousal, so they have 0 rows. 20 - 4 = **16 retro**.
Analysed cohort: 22 rcea + 16 retro = 38 participants, no participant in both.
Coverage, signal quality and behaviour then computed as in the three subsection cards.

qa.q: Why 22 and 16, not 45 or 47 or 48?
qa.a: 48 IDs exist, but M26 has no data at all, so 47. Only 42 have an annotation file: 22 rcea and 20 retro. Four retro files are empty after cleaning, M33, M36, M38 and M47, so 16 retro. Six people have no annotation file in either stream: M16, M26, M27, M32, M39, M44.

qa.q: Van der Kaaden had 45 visitors. Where are the other retro ones?
qa.a: He reports 22 real-time and 23 retrospective. In the data I received there are 20 retro annotation files, and four of them contain no ratings. I cannot tell from the files which three of his 23 are missing; that is a property of the data drop, not a filter I applied.

qa.q: Did you exclude anyone for bad signal?
qa.a: No participant is excluded for signal quality. Bad sensors become missing features for that participant: M18 and M37 have no HRV, EDA-gated recordings have no EDA, M28 has no pupil in its window. They stay in the cohort and the imputer handles the gaps.

traps: Van der Kaaden's 23 retro vs my 20 retro files cannot be reconciled from the files I have. Say so plainly; do not guess.
No participant-specific exclusions exist anywhere in `scripts/exp1_v2/` (grep finds none), so M19's hallucinated transcript and M38's noisy pupil are modelled as-is.

visuals.title: From 48 folders to 38 analysed visitors in two streams
visuals.caption: Look at the last row: 22 rcea and 16 retro, nobody in both. Signal-quality figures use all 47 recordings, including the 9 without usable ratings.

cards.key: Results > Data Characterisation > Coverage and Usability Audit
cards.gist: Raw coverage is near complete for pupil, EDA and BVP (means 0.894 to 0.993) and sparse for speech (0.230 rcea, 0.144 retro), because speech exists only when a visitor talks. Three visitors have zero on one sensor: **M18** (rcea) and **M37** (retro) have empty BVP files, and **M28** (retro) has an eye recording that starts after the rating window ends.
steps: Grid: `_analysed_grid(pid, stream)` reads the index of `results/thesis_v2/features/{pid}_{stream}.parquet`. Sum = 12,654 rcea (22) + 6,880 retro (16) = 19,534 (`notebooks/characterisation_pupil.ipynb` cell 3; saved `results/data_characterisation/analysed_grid_counts.csv`).
Per sensor, per participant: `_seconds_present(raw_index, grid)`; saved to `coverage_{pupil,eda,bvp,speech}.csv`.
Table 4.1 = mean, min, max over participants per stream; zero-coverage = count of participants at exactly 0.

**Why the feature matrix has 6 and 142 more rows** (12,660 and 7,022): the two grids are built by different rules. Old grid (`scripts/thesis_v2/build_features.py:144-152`): rcea labels with the loader default **2 s delay and modal reducer**, then drop every row where **all** sensor features are NaN, anywhere in the session. New grid (`scripts/exp1_v2/features.py:81` `analysed_index`): rcea labels at **0 s delay, median reducer**, then drop only the **leading** seconds before the first raw sample of any sensor.

Per-participant check (my comparison of the two indexes): rcea net +6 (M07 +5, M11 +1) but 320 seconds exist only in the new grid and 314 only in the old, because the 2 s delay shifts rcea timestamps. Retro net +142 = **M28 +113** (old grid stopped at 13:35:59 when all sensor features went NaN; new grid keeps labels to 13:37:52) + **M17 +35** (interior stretch with every sensor missing) - 2 each for **M14, M15, M30** (old grid kept 2 s before the first sample because the old pupil features used an 8 s forward window).
M28 detail: pupil file starts 13:40:55, annotation ends 13:37:52; so zero pupil coverage on either grid. EDA 0.777 reflects the gap between two restarted VR sessions.

qa.q: Why 19,534 here and 19,682 in the experiments?
qa.a: The coverage audit uses an earlier build of the grid. That build shifted rcea labels by 2 seconds and dropped any second where every sensor was empty. The experiment matrices use no delay and only trim the seconds before the first sensor sample. Net that adds 6 rcea rows and 142 retro rows, mostly M28 (113) and M17 (35), whose sensors drop out while they are still rating.

qa.q: Which participants have zero coverage and why?
qa.a: M18 (rcea) and M37 (retro) have empty BVP files: their wristband recorded that day but no second overlaps the session window. M28 (retro) has an eye file that starts about three minutes after its annotation ends.

qa.q: M18 has no BVP but its EDA is fine. Same wristband, how?
qa.a: The trimmed BVP file has zero rows inside the session window while the EDA file covers it. I report it as recorded; I did not find the device-level cause. It is channel-specific, not a missing visit.

qa.q: Why is speech coverage so low?
qa.a: Speech is push-to-talk and the audio is silence-removed, so there are samples only while a visitor talks. That is sparse by design, not a fault.

qa.q: What is M19's 0.990 speech coverage?
qa.a: M19's transcript is a Whisper hallucination: the word 'you' 24 times over near-silence, and silence removal kept 99% of the visit. Without M19 the rcea mean is 0.194 instead of 0.230.

qa.q: Speech coverage is 0.23 but speech features exist on 71% of rows. Why?
qa.a: Each utterance's features are copied onto every second of its transcript segment, and Whisper segments include pauses. So the feature is present over the whole utterance span, not only over voiced frames.

qa.q: Did low coverage remove anyone?
qa.a: No. The zero-coverage sensors just become missing features for that visitor. Everyone with a non-empty annotation stays in.

traps: **Appendix C's 'Analysed (s)' per participant is the old grid**, so it disagrees with the feature-matrix rows for M07 (423 vs 428), M11 (465 vs 466), M14 (606 vs 604), M15 (501 vs 499), M17 (760 vs 795), M28 (265 vs 378), M30 (259 vs 257). The BRIEF's 'M17 795' is the matrix count; 760 is the coverage grid.

The thesis says only 'assembled at a later stage'. The honest reason is that two different row rules were used (2 s delay + drop-all-NaN rows vs 0 s delay + leading trim). Coverage fractions were not recomputed on the new grid.

M28 contributes 378 rows to the retro matrix with **no pupil samples at all, EDA gated, and a near-empty transcript**. Its pupil 'features' are only the always-numeric sample count (0). It is a weak visitor to be scored on.
rcea pupil min prints 0.978 in the notebook and 0.979 in the thesis; the stored value is 0.9785 (rounding). Not a real disagreement.
M31 retro BVP is 0.627 while its EDA is 1.000; not investigated.

visuals.title: Pupil, EDA and BVP are recorded almost every second; speech rarely
visuals.caption: Look at the bottom row: speech covers a mean 0.230 of rcea and 0.144 of retro seconds; the three zeros are M18 and M37 BVP and M28 pupil. M19's 0.99 speech is a hallucinated transcript over near-silence.

cards.key: Results > Data Characterisation > Signal Quality
cards.gist: Recorded is not the same as usable. The eye tracker delivers a median **23 Hz** against a nominal **120** and slows to about 18 Hz at paintings; BVP is a perfect 64 Hz clock or absent; **20 of 47 EDA recordings are unusable**, including 9 of the 16 retro ones. rcea ratings rest at 5 for about 20% of seconds, retro never, and visitors spoke in a median 6.9% of seconds.
steps: **Midpoint:** share of rated seconds with value exactly 5.0 on the feature-matrix labels: rcea valence 0.200, arousal 0.2047; retro 0 and 0.

**Eye tracker** (`characterisation_pupil.ipynb` cell 5, all 47 eye files): burst rate = 1000 / median inter-sample gap in ms (median 45.5 Hz); session rate = samples / span (median 23.3 Hz); pause share = sum of gaps > 100 ms / span (median 57%, range 16-83%); valid = mean of `valid_combined` (92.5%); L-R r = Pearson on samples where both eyes valid and > 0 (median 0.92, M38 0.12).

**Density at paintings:** eye samples inside `observings.csv` intervals (unity clock) / total observing duration vs outside. Needs > 10 s both inside and outside: 45 participants qualify (M04 no log, M07 clock does not overlap). Slower inside for 44 of 45 (exception M28); median 18.3 vs 46.7 Hz.

**Teleports** (`scripts/preprocessing/teleport_detection.py`): floor positions from `observings.csv` (`location`, `distance` columns = x, z). Pairs with 0 < dt <= 0.5 s: 98,675; 99.81% below 2 m/s; 24 pairs in 2-4 m/s; 163 above 4 m/s, max 67 m/s. Jump rule: dt < 0.5 s and speed > **3 m/s** -> 172 jumps. Gap rule: dt >= 0.5 s and endpoint speed > **1.5 m/s** -> 130 gaps, whole gap masked. Pad 0.5 s either side.
Teleport mask use: in `features.py:190` it sets saccade/fixation classification to NaN for teleport-adjacent eye samples. Pupil diameter is not masked.
**BVP** (`characterisation_hrv.ipynb`): 100% of inter-sample gaps exactly 15.625 ms (64 Hz) in all 45 usable files. No in-session record: M18, M26, M37.

**EDA gate** (`eda_processing.py:43-55` `eda_quality_ok`, applied per whole recording in `features.py:250`): fail if share of negative samples >= 0.50, or P95 - P5 < 0.02 uS. Result: 20 of 47 fail (18 at least half negative, 2 flat only: M14, M44). Failed recordings produce all-NaN EDA features.
**Wave:** recording start before 2026-01-01 = first wave. First 5 of 25 fail (M05, M12, M14, M16, M25); second 15 of 22 fail (M27, M28, M30-M33, M39-M44, M46-M48).

**Temperature coupling:** for passing recordings with temperature and >= 300 overlapping seconds (25), resample EDA and temperature to 1 s means; Spearman on levels (median 0.89) and on first differences (median 0.00). Within-visit temperature range median 0.46 C.

**Speech presence:** kept-audio duration (frames x frame period) / analysed seconds; median 6.9% over 38 analysed participants, 1.2-23.0% without M19 (99.4%). Transcripts near-empty if < 35 words or <= 2 unique words: 8 of 47 (M16, M19, M28, M31, M35, M38, M44, M47).

qa.q: The tracker is 120 Hz. Why do you say 23?
qa.a: 120 Hz is the device spec and the folder name; it never reached the files. The logger writes one sample per rendered frame, so it runs at about 45 Hz while writing. It also pauses often: gaps over 100 ms cover a median 57% of a session. Over a whole session that averages to a median 23 Hz.

qa.q: Why does it slow down at the paintings?
qa.a: Because sampling is tied to rendering. Standing at a painting the headset renders a demanding scene, frames take longer, and fewer eye samples get written: 18 per second against 47 elsewhere, for 44 of 45 visitors. I inferred the rendering mechanism from that pattern; I did not measure frame times directly.

qa.q: If 57% of the session is pauses, how is coverage 0.99?
qa.a: Coverage only asks whether a second has at least one sample. The pauses are short, typically around 116 ms, and scattered, so almost every second still has some samples.

qa.q: Does that density effect contaminate your features?
