qa.a: Yes, and I show it. Saccade frequency tracks the window's sample count at a within-person r of about 0.9, and the strongest near-miss feature on retro arousal is the sample count itself. The apparatus carries scene information.

qa.q: M38's eyes correlate at 0.12. Why keep it?
qa.a: Both eyes have normal means and spread; they just carry independent noise. Averaging two noisy eyes reduces noise, so averaging is the right call. I expect M38's pupil features to be weak, and I kept the participant.

qa.q: How do you detect teleports?
qa.a: From the engine's floor positions. Between records less than half a second apart, a speed above 3 m/s is a jump. Across a longer gap between viewings, an average speed above 1.5 m/s means a teleport happened inside, so I mask the whole gap. Walking stays under 2 m/s in 99.8% of 98,675 record pairs, and teleports are 4 to 67 m/s, with only 24 pairs in between.

qa.q: What do you do with a teleport?
qa.a: I exclude eye samples within half a second of it from the fixation and saccade classification, because a teleport causes a reflexive re-orientation that is not viewing behaviour. Pupil diameter is not masked.

qa.q: What is the EDA gate exactly?
qa.a: A whole recording is unusable if at least half its samples are negative, since conductance cannot be negative, or if its 5th to 95th percentile range is under 0.02 microsiemens, smaller than one small response. 20 of 47 fail: 18 on negativity, 2 only on flatness. Their EDA features become missing.

qa.q: Why do you blame electrodes and not wear?
qa.a: The failures cluster in time: 5 of 25 in the first wave, 15 of 22 in the second. And the failing recordings show normal wrist temperature, so the band was worn. That points to electrode contact or channel wear, not visitors taking the band off.

qa.q: What does the EDA-temperature result mean?
qa.a: Within a visit, the slow conductance level correlates with skin temperature at a median Spearman 0.89. Their second-to-second changes correlate at 0.00. So the tonic level partly reflects warming and electrode contact, while the fast phasic responses do not.

qa.q: What about M26?
qa.a: M26 has no eye file, no EDA file, no in-session BVP, no transcript and no VR log. It is not in any stream.

qa.q: Why does the rcea midpoint matter?
qa.a: 20% of rcea seconds sit exactly on 5, where the joystick rests. With an even level count 5 falls on a boundary; with an odd count it falls inside a level. That is part of why three levels is attractive for rcea. Retro has no resting position.

traps: **Median 0.89 hides a spread**: the 25 level correlations have mean 0.57, IQR about 0.40 to 0.97, and a minimum of -0.63. The direction differs between people. Say 'typically strong, not always the same sign'.

**'Walking < 2 m/s, a teleport 4 to 67 m/s'**: the jump threshold is 3 m/s, so the 172 jumps include 163 pairs above 4 m/s plus about 9 in 3-4 m/s. Also, position records exist only while a painting is being viewed, so between-painting teleports can only be caught by the gap rule.
**Small code inconsistency:** the notebook counts pairs with dt <= 0.5 s, the detector uses dt < 0.5 s. Negligible.
**Teleport mask coverage:** M04 has no observings and M07's engine clock does not overlap its eye file, so neither gets any teleport masking.

**Signal Quality opens with 'measured on the raw recordings of the full cohort'**, but the midpoint shares and speech presence are over the analysed participants (22 rcea for the midpoint, 38 for speech). The eye, BVP, EDA and transcript figures are full-cohort.
**The rendering-load mechanism** is an inference from density inside vs outside viewing intervals, not a frame-time measurement.
**EDA coverage 0.99 vs 20 of 47 dead**: coverage counts samples, the gate judges values. Both are true.
**Temperature coupling uses 25, not 27, passing recordings**: the notebook requires a temperature channel and >= 300 overlapping seconds.
An older DATA_FACTS note says 13 negative + 7 flat, and 24 + 22 waves; those are superseded by 18 + 2 and 25 + 22.
The speech range 1.2 to 23.0% excludes M19, but the median 6.9% includes it (6.86% without, same rounding).

**M13 passes the EDA gate with 41% of its samples negative**, just under the 50% cut. A threshold rule always has near-misses. **If asked:** 'The rule was fixed in advance; M13 passes it, and a conductance recording that is negative 41% of the time is still questionable, which is one more reason the EDA results are read cautiously.'

visuals.title: The eye tracker slows to about 18 samples a second at a painting
visuals.caption: Look at the gap between blue and orange dots: a median 18.3 samples/s while viewing vs 46.7 elsewhere (rcea 18.6 vs 47.4, retro 19.3 vs 46.2). Only retro M28 is faster inside; the nominal rate is 120.

visuals.title: Most retro EDA recordings fail the gate
visuals.caption: Look at the red circles: a recording fails if half its samples are negative or its P95 - P5 range is under 0.02 uS (shaded). 4 of 22 rcea and 9 of 16 retro recordings fail, 20 of 47 in all.

cards.key: Results > Data Characterisation > Visiting Behaviour
cards.gist: A descriptive read of the engine log, separate from any sensor. 46 of 47 visitors have a usable log and 44 of those saw all five paintings; most start at **B1** and end at **C5**. **B3** is the most fragmented (revisit ratio 6.7), and the median visitor sent the guide 7 messages.
steps: `neo_data/participants.csv`: 47 participants (M26 absent). `viewing_events.csv`: 46 participants (M04 has 0 observings, so no log).
Paintings viewed per participant = number of unique `painting_code`; fewer than five: M17 (4), M28 (3).
Dwell per viewing = `n_samples x mean_sample_dur_s`. Visit order = rank of `t_start_unity` within participant (`rank(method='first')`); first-viewed = order 1.
Per painting: viewed by = unique participants (% of 46); mean order; mean dwell over viewing rows; revisit ratio = mean of `span_s / dwell_s`, where span is first-to-last look.
Guide engagement: rows per participant in `verbal_communication.csv`, over the 46 with a log, missing = 0: median 7, mean 9.2, range 0 to 42.

qa.q: Who has no movement log?
qa.a: M04. Its record in the engine export has zero observings. M26 is not in the engine export at all, so the base is 47 and 46 have a log.

qa.q: How is dwell computed?
qa.a: For each viewing event, the number of gaze samples on the painting times the mean sample duration. Mean dwell is averaged over the viewing events of that painting.

qa.q: What is the revisit ratio?
qa.a: The time from the first to the last look at a painting, divided by the time actually spent looking at it. A value of 1 is one continuous look; higher means the viewing was broken up with returns.

qa.q: Why does B3 have the highest revisit ratio?
qa.a: I report it, I do not explain it with data. B3 is the painting with three named objects inside it, and visitors went back to it more. It also has the lowest mean dwell of the B paintings.

qa.q: Why does this section matter for affect?
qa.a: It uses the same log that Exp 4 turns into attended-painting intervals. It shows that the visit order is not fixed, so painting and time in the visit are not the same thing, and that almost everyone saw every painting.

qa.q: Does the order follow the room layout?
qa.a: The table shows B paintings first and C paintings later, which is what a walk through the room would give. The methodology says the order is compared to the layout, but the results give only the mean orders; I did not compute a formal layout-order statistic.

traps: The Methodology promises a comparison of visiting order against the room's physical layout. The Results only report mean orders and first views; no explicit layout comparison is computed in the notebook.

Revisit ratio is a mean over visitors of span/dwell; `viewing_events.csv` has exactly one row per visitor x painting (227 rows), so each visitor counts once per painting. A single very fragmented visitor can pull the mean up; a median is not reported.
DATA_FACTS says '46 participants (M26 absent)' for the teleport log. The missing one out of 47 is actually M04 (0 observings); M26 is not in the 47 at all.
The per-painting table uses 46 visitors; the eye-density figure in Signal Quality uses 45 (M07 excluded for its clock offset). Different bases, both correct.

visuals.title: Both streams tend to start at B1 and end at C5
visuals.caption: Look at the darkest bar in each C5 row: C5 was last for 18 of 21 rcea and 9 of the 14 retro visitors who saw it. B3 gets the shortest dwell in both (80 s rcea, 44 s retro); visitors without usable ratings are left out.

cards.key: Raw Coverage per Participant
cards.gist: Two tables. The first gives each visitor's raw coverage for pupil, EDA, BVP and speech; the second gives every eye file's burst rate, session rate, valid-sample share and left-right pupil agreement, for all 47 recordings.
steps: Table 1 rows come from `results/data_characterisation/coverage_{sensor}.csv`, with 'Analysed (s)' from `analysed_grid_counts.csv` (the old thesis_v2 grid).

Table 2 rows come from `results/data_characterisation/pupil_quality_per_participant.csv`: burst rate = 1000 / median gap (ms); session rate = samples / span; Valid = mean of `valid_combined`; L-R r = Pearson on samples with both eyes valid and > 0 (requires > 100 such samples).
Burst rate is 45.5 Hz for almost everyone (a 22 ms frame), 43.5 for M03, M22, M25, and 47.6 for M42.

qa.q: What does 0.000 for M18 BVP mean?
qa.a: Not one raw BVP sample falls inside any of M18's analysed seconds. The wristband's BVP record does not overlap the session window.

qa.q: Why is M17's pupil coverage only 0.73?
qa.a: M17 has two restarted VR sessions, and part of its analysed window has no eye data; its session also has 71% pauses and one of the lowest valid-flag shares (77.6%). I did not trace the exact gap second by second.

qa.q: What is the difference between burst rate and session rate?
qa.a: Burst rate is the rate while the logger is writing, from the median gap between samples: about 45 Hz. Session rate is total samples over total time, pauses included: median 23 Hz.

qa.q: Why are the EDA-gated people at coverage 1.000?
qa.a: Coverage counts samples, not whether their values are plausible. M40 or M48 record the whole visit, but the values are negative or flat, so the gate removes their features later.

traps: 'Analysed (s)' here is the old grid, not the feature-matrix row count (e.g. M17 760 vs 795 rows, M28 265 vs 378).
Table 2 covers all 47 eye files, including the 9 people not in either analysed stream (M16, M27, M32, M33, M36, M38, M39, M44, M47); table 1 covers only the 38 analysed.
The caption says 'L-R r' agreement; it is Pearson r over valid sample pairs, not an ICC.

visuals.title: Eye files run at a median 23 samples a second, not the nominal 120
visuals.caption: Look at the bars: the whole-session rate has a median of 23.3 Hz, lowest 14.0 (rcea M25 and M22). The orange ticks, the rate inside a burst, sit at 45.5 Hz for almost every file, so the tracker pauses rather than runs slowly.

cards.key: Visiting Behaviour Detail
cards.gist: Viewing time inside each painting, split into artwork and text panel, and for B3 into three named objects. The **text panel takes 43.5 to 49.9%** of viewing at every painting, and in B3 the **ivory tusk** draws more viewing than the portrayed man, Pedro Sunda.
steps: Source: `neo_data/observings.csv` (one record per gaze sample on an AOI, about 10 per second while viewing).
Region mapping: AOI ending `_Text` -> Text panel; ending `_Background` -> Artwork; any other AOI kept by name (B3's Pedro Sunda, Cloth, Ivory tusk).
Per painting x region: viewers = unique participants; cohort dwell = sum of `duration_s`; share = region dwell / painting total dwell.
Saved to `results/data_characterisation/behaviour_aoi.csv`.

numbers.what: B3 ivory tusk vs Pedro Sunda

qa.q: Why does the text panel matter for your affect models?
qa.a: Almost half the time at a painting, visitors are reading. Exp 4 treats the whole painting, text panel included, as attended. So 'attending the painting' is partly reading about it, which may not carry the same affect as looking at the image.

qa.q: Why not model at the region level?
qa.a: The rows are thin already at painting level. Splitting further would leave too few seconds per visitor per region to train or score. I report the regions descriptively only.

qa.q: Do the region dwells add up to the per-painting dwell in the Results table?
qa.a: Yes, to rounding. B1's regions sum to 3,844 s, and the per-painting table's 46 viewers x 83.6 s mean is the same 3,844 s. The region table sums `duration_s` over observing records; the painting table uses samples x mean sample duration from the viewing events. Same log, two routes, same total.

traps: Viewers per region differ from viewers per painting (e.g. B2 text panel 45 vs B2 46): a visitor can view a painting without ever landing gaze on one of its regions.
'Artwork (other)' for B3 is the background surface outside the three named objects, so B3's artwork share is split four ways and not directly comparable with the other paintings' single artwork row.

visuals.title: The text panel takes close to half the viewing at every painting
visuals.caption: Look at the green bars: 45 to 52% for rcea and 41 to 53% for retro (whole cohort 43.5 to 49.9%, as in the thesis). In B3 the ivory tusk (rcea 18%, retro 22%) beats Pedro Sunda (7% and 10%).

viva.q: Can you summarise your thesis in two minutes?
viva.a: I asked whether wearable sensors can track an unseen museum visitor's valence and arousal second by second. Across five experiments (single sensors, fusion, ordered levels, scoping to the painting, personalisation) nothing beat the chance-corrected floor. The reason is in the ratings: 36 to 65% of a rating is the person, only 0.1 to 1.5% the painting.

viva.q: What is your research gap?
viva.a: Van der Kaaden collected this data to compare two rating methods, and prediction was a side result that fell near chance for new visitors. His future work names multimodal fusion, finer features and clearer affective events. I make prediction for an unseen visitor the main question, test those steps, and explain the ceiling.

viva.q: Where did the idea for this thesis come from?
viva.a: From van der Kaaden's future work. His models learned visitors they had seen, about 0.84, but not new ones, 0.20 to 0.24, and he recommended fusion, temporally finer features and settings with clearer affective events. Those became my Experiments 1, 2 and 4.

viva.q: What is your main research question?
viva.a: How well can moment-to-moment valence and arousal be recovered for a visitor the model has never seen, and what limits or improves that? It splits into five sub-questions: sensors and fusion, target form, scoping to the painting, sources of variance, and personalisation.

viva.q: What is the answer in one sentence?
viva.a: On this cohort, not above chance: every sensor, combination, target and scoping sits at the floor, because most of a rating belongs to the person and almost none to the painting.

viva.q: Why does this problem matter?
viva.a: A museum guide that adapts to how a visitor feels would have to read affect from sensors, for someone it meets for the first time. My result tells designers that with calm art and wrist and eye sensors, that decoding is not reliable, so a guide should adapt to engagement instead.

viva.q: What is new in your work?
viva.a: Van der Kaaden classified k-means regions. I predict the continuous rating under strict leave-one-subject-out, search the open preprocessing choices instead of fixing them, and add fusion, scoping, a variance decomposition and personalisation, none of which he ran.

viva.q: What is your main contribution?
viva.a: A measured ceiling with a stated noise floor, plus its explanation from the ratings alone. The variance decomposition shows the painting explains 0.1 to 1.5% of a rating, so little is shared across people, and any future project can run that check on pilot ratings first.

viva.q: Walk me through the five experiments in order.
viva.a: Experiment 1 fixes each sensor's settings and the model on the continuous rating. Experiment 2 combines sensors and carries early fusion plus a cross-sensor block. Experiment 3 moves to three ordered levels. Experiment 4 scopes to attended paintings and splits the variance. Experiment 5 tries three personalisation levers.

viva.q: How do you know the ceiling is in the data and not in your pipeline?
viva.a: Three reasons. The variance split uses only the ratings, no pipeline, and finds the painting explains 0.1 to 1.5%. Van der Kaaden's independent pipeline also collapsed to near chance on new people. And my search over settings, eight model families, alignment, fusion, targets and scoping never separated. I cannot prove no method could do better.

viva.q: Experiment 1 was already null. Why keep going?
viva.a: Because one null can be blamed on one choice: the single sensor, the fusion, the target, the scoping, or missing personalisation. Each later experiment removes one of those excuses. Together they show the null is not a tuning accident.

viva.q: What is the best score anywhere in the thesis?
viva.a: Without personalisation, +0.084 CCC for heart-rate variability on retro valence, barely above the 0.08 resolution, and the same sensor scores -0.072 on retro arousal. With the 180 second warm-up, which uses the visitor's own ratings, +0.090. Nothing was credited as a gain.

viva.q: Does 'the ratings set the ceiling' mean no sensor model could ever do better?
viva.a: No, that would be too strong. The split bounds what knowing the painting can add. Sensors could still track the within-visit part, 35 to 62% of the variance. In my data they did not: 0 of 436 feature correlations survive, and every leave-one-out score sits near zero.

viva.q: Isn't a null result just a failed project?
viva.a: No. The question was whether a guide can rely on these sensors for a new visitor, and the answer is a measured no across a wide search. I also show why: the rating is mostly the person. A failed project would be one that cannot say why it failed.

viva.q: Why should anyone care about a thesis where nothing works?
viva.a: Because the null is useful. It tells a museum not to build on second-by-second affect decoding with these sensors, and it gives the next study a cheap pilot check, the variance split, that shows whether shared signal exists before anyone builds a pipeline.

viva.q: What would you do differently?
viva.a: I would run the variance split on the ratings first, before building any sensor pipeline. I would also fix the RCEA timestamp parse, add a speaking-now indicator, leave a gap between warm-up and scored rows, and push for logged scene luminance and repeated, contrasting stimuli.

viva.q: Did you just keep searching until you could explain away the null?
viva.a: No. The candidate sets, the 0.08 resolution, the tie rules and the both-metrics rule were fixed before comparing. The search was wide to rule out explanations, not to find a winner, and every difference stayed inside the resolution.

viva.q: Your conclusion says the sensors are not the constraint. Can a tie show that?
viva.a: Not on its own, and I would word it more carefully. A tie shows the sensors cannot be told apart. The stronger argument is the variance split: the ratings carry little shared signal for any sensor to find.

viva.q: Warm-up gives balanced accuracy 0.44 and QWK +0.27. Doesn't that contradict 'nothing beat the floor'?
viva.a: Fair point on wording. Those are pooled figures for one arm, and they were never tested at that level. My pre-set claim rule was the paired per-visitor test, and none survived correction. So the accurate sentence is: nothing established a gain over the floor.

viva.q: What is the circumplex model?
viva.a: It places affect as a point on two continuous axes: valence, from unpleasant to pleasant, and arousal, from calm to excited. Both annotation tools in this dataset record exactly that, on a 0 to 10 scale.

viva.q: Why valence and arousal and not discrete emotions?
viva.a: Both annotation tools record a point on the valence-arousal plane, so the data are dimensional from the start. A dimensional rating can also change gradually through a visit, which suits per-second prediction.

viva.q: What are RCEA and RetroSketch?
viva.a: RCEA is live: the visitor moves a joystick on both axes during the visit, logged at 4 Hz. RetroSketch is retrospective: afterwards the visitor watches a replay of their own session and sketches valence and arousal over it, at 1 Hz.

viva.q: Why did you never pool the two streams?
viva.a: They are different instruments and different people. RCEA rests at 5 for about 20% of seconds, RetroSketch never does and is smoother and memory-based. Van der Kaaden found they do not converge; his cross-method models reached only 0.17 to 0.18 balanced accuracy. Pooling would mix two targets.

viva.q: Why subject-independent evaluation?
viva.a: A museum guide meets each visitor for the first time and cannot collect their ratings first. So I hold out each visitor in turn. A within-person split lets the model learn that person's level; that is how van der Kaaden reached 0.84 within people but 0.20 to 0.24 across.

viva.q: Why CCC and not accuracy or Pearson r?
viva.a: The target is a continuous 0 to 10 rating, so accuracy does not apply. Pearson r ignores bias: a prediction always two points too high can still get r = 1. CCC drops when the mean or spread is wrong, and it is the standard for continuous affect.

viva.q: What did van der Kaaden do?
viva.a: He built the VR museum, collected eye, skin conductance, pulse and speech from 45 visitors under two annotation methods, and classified seven k-means regions of the valence-arousal plane. Within people he reached about 0.84 balanced accuracy; on a new person 0.20 to 0.24, against chance of 0.14.

viva.q: How does your thesis extend his?
viva.a: Four ways. I predict the continuous rating, then fixed ordered levels, instead of k-means classes. I report only leave-one-subject-out, with every choice inside the training fold. I rebuilt the pipeline from raw files and searched five open settings. And I add fusion, scoping, variance decomposition and personalisation.

viva.q: Why these sensors?
viva.a: They are what the dataset has: the headset's eye tracker, the wristband's skin conductance and pulse, and the microphone. I did not choose the hardware. Each reads a different system: pupil for arousal, EDA for sympathetic sweating, pulse intervals for heart control, speech for how and what is said.

viva.q: How do your numbers compare with Marin-Morales and other published results?
viva.a: They are not comparable. Their 71 to 77% is two-class accuracy, where 50% is chance, on one rating per room or artwork, with EEG and ECG. My CCC tracks a per-second trace, where 0 is chance. Both are subject-independent; the target and sensors differ.

viva.q: Why tree ensembles and not deep learning?
viva.a: With 16 to 22 people and tabular features, tree ensembles beat deep networks in comparisons like Grinsztajn 2022, and FEEL 2025 found handcrafted features generalise to new people better than networks trained from scratch. In any case, all eight families I tried tied within 0.0124 CCC.

viva.q: Why not a pretrained foundation model like NormWear?
viva.a: It is a fair alternative that I did not test, and it would bring knowledge from large external data. But it would not change the variance split, which comes from the ratings: if about 1% of a rating is shared, a bigger model has little shared signal to find.

viva.q: Why move away from van der Kaaden's k-means classes?
viva.a: K-means regions are fitted to the data, so their meaning depends on the cohort, and they leak if fitted outside the fold. They also merge valence and arousal into one label and ignore order. A continuous per-axis target keeps full information, and fixed equal-width levels keep the order.

viva.q: What is the difference between an ICC and your variance decomposition?
viva.a: An ICC asks whether raters agree on the same targets. The decomposition splits all rating variance into person, painting and residual shares. At one mean per visitor per painting the painting share is the ICC, but I also get the person share, which is the key number for an unseen-visitor model.

viva.q: What does Szymanska 2025 tell you?
viva.a: In a headset with standard pictures, pupil and gaze gave F1 0.73 for binary arousal but only 0.31 on nine levels. So coarse pupil prediction in VR can work but falls apart as targets get finer. It was seated, static images, and probably not subject-independent, so it is an upper bound.

viva.q: How did you check your citations?
viva.a: I kept a citation audit: for each key, the claim it carries, what the paper actually says, and a verdict. Several were corrected or removed, for example Wang2022, which had no museum content, and Wass2015, which contradicted the original claim and is now used only as a caution.

viva.q: His leave-one-out was 0.20 to 0.24 against chance 0.14. Isn't that some signal, and yours worse?
viva.a: It is modestly above chance, with fold SDs of 0.12 to 0.20, and balanced accuracy on k-means classes can pick up a person's typical region. My CCC asks whether second-by-second movement is tracked, which is harder. His simplest retro model scored 0.10, below chance. The two results agree.

viva.q: Many of your sources come from infants or seated labs. Isn't your literature a poor fit?
viva.a: Some sources come from other settings, and I flag each one: Wass is infants, Bradley is seated picture viewing, the synchrony papers are between people. I use them only for what transfers, a caution or a method, never a parameter. Museum sensor studies at this grain barely exist.

viva.q: You reviewed networks and methods like CORAL but did not use them. Why review them?
viva.a: To show the alternatives and why they do not fit here. The network review argues that trees suit this data size. For personalisation I tested the simplest members of each family; baseline subtraction is a mean-shift special case of CORAL. The fuller methods are future work.

viva.q: Describe your data.
viva.a: 38 visitors of a VR museum: 22 rated their feelings live with a joystick and 16 rated afterwards from a replay. Each second of a visit is one row, with pupil, skin conductance, heart-rate variability and speech features, and a valence and arousal rating from 0 to 10.

viva.q: Why 22 and 16 participants?
viva.a: There are 48 folders, and M26 has no data at all. 22 have a joystick file, all usable. 20 have a replay file, but four, M33, M36, M38 and M47, have every rating empty. That leaves 16. Nobody was excluded for signal quality.

viva.q: Van der Kaaden reports 23 retro visitors. Where are the others?
viva.a: The data I received holds 20 retro annotation files, and four of them are empty. I cannot tell from the files which three of his 23 are missing. It is a property of the data drop, not a filter I applied.

viva.q: What is one row?
viva.a: One UTC second of one visitor's analysed window. It carries that second's rating and each sensor summarised over a window ending at that second: 8 seconds of pupil, 3 of skin conductance, 60 of heartbeats, and the utterance covering that second.

viva.q: How many rows and columns?
viva.a: 12,660 rows for rcea and 7,022 for retro. 114 feature columns: pupil 7, EDA 10, heart-rate variability 8, speech acoustics 88 and speech sentiment 1. Experiment 2 adds eight cross-sensor columns, which gives 122.

viva.q: Is the data normalised?
viva.a: The features yes, the labels no. Every model is a pipeline of median imputation, then z-scoring, then the model, fitted on the training visitors only and applied unchanged to the held-out visitor. Ratings stay on the raw 0 to 10 scale, and later become fixed equal-width levels.

viva.q: How did you handle missing data?
viva.a: Each gap is filled with that column's median over the training visitors of the fold, inside the model pipeline, so the held-out visitor never shapes it. From Experiment 2 on no row is dropped. In Experiment 1 a row is dropped only when that sensor's whole block is empty.

viva.q: What do the labels look like?
viva.a: rcea valence averages 6.28 and arousal 3.76; retro 5.52 and 5.23, with SDs around 2. About 20% of rcea seconds sit exactly on 5, the joystick's rest position; retro never does. At three levels the middle level holds roughly half of every slice.

viva.q: The eye tracker is 120 Hz. Why do you say 23?
viva.a: 120 Hz is the device specification. The logger writes one row per rendered frame, about 45 Hz while writing, and pauses often, so over a session the median is 23 Hz, and about 18 Hz at the paintings. The Results chapter reports the real rate.

viva.q: What is the EDA gate, and how many recordings failed?
viva.a: A whole recording is rejected if at least half its samples are negative or its 5th to 95th percentile span is under 0.02 microsiemens. 20 of 47 failed, 18 of them on negativity. That leaves EDA for 18 of 22 rcea and only 7 of 16 retro visitors.

viva.q: Why did EDA fail so often?
viva.a: The failures cluster in the second collection wave, 15 of 22 against 5 of 25 in the first, and the failing recordings show normal wrist temperature, so the band was worn. That points to electrode contact or channel wear, not visitors taking the band off.

viva.q: Visitors talk about 6% of the time, yet speech features sit on 71% of rows. How?
viva.a: Each utterance's features are computed on its voiced audio only, then copied onto every second of the Whisper segment's real-time span, and those spans include pauses. So voiced audio is about 6% of a visit, but 71% of rows carry the surrounding utterance's summary.

viva.q: Why the median to go from 4 Hz to 1 Hz for rcea?
viva.a: The median of a second's joystick samples is robust to one jumpy sample and keeps the rest value 5 exact. Van der Kaaden used the mode. I applied no fixed delay; the searched window delay was meant to absorb the reaction lag.

viva.q: What was the RCEA timestamp problem?
viva.a: The raw file's column called timestamp_utc_plus1 is tagged as UTC but holds Dutch local time, one hour off. Parsed as UTC, no rating overlapped the sensors for any visitor. I parse the correctly tagged timestamp_cet column instead, and M01's session ends then agree within about 65 ms.

viva.q: Which data quality problems did you find?
viva.a: Several. The timezone column, an accelerometer loader that overflowed so the motion mask was random, an EDA double filter, and an HRV filter too wide to flag anything. All were fixed before the submitted run. Raw gaps remain: M18 and M37 have no pulse, and M19's transcript is a Whisper hallucination.

viva.q: Isn't broadcasting utterance features over silent seconds a bug?
viva.a: No, it is a design choice I should have stated more clearly. Filling only voiced seconds would leave about 6% of rows and make speech almost useless per second. The cost is that the model cannot tell 'not speaking' from median speech, because I added no speaking indicator.

viva.q: Is your pipeline bug-free now?
viva.a: No, one small issue is still in the submitted labels. The RCEA parser drops samples that fall on whole seconds, so each second's median uses three samples, or one for six visitors. I measured it: no second lost, mean label change 0.003 to 0.12 points. I expect no conclusion to change.

viva.q: M45 gave one constant rating for the whole visit. Why keep them?
viva.a: M45 passed the inclusion rule, a non-empty annotation file. A constant target gives CCC exactly zero whatever the model predicts, so M45 pulls retro means slightly toward zero. It is a property of the ratings, and removing people after seeing results would be selective.

viva.q: Retro EDA is scored on seven visitors. Can you trust those numbers?
viva.a: Not much, and I report the fold count beside it. One of the seven is M45, who scores exactly zero. I read every such cell against the 0.08 resolution, and none separates from zero anyway.

viva.q: Are annotation stream and collection wave confounded?
viva.a: Yes. rcea is almost all first wave, November 2025, and retro mostly second wave, early 2026, where EDA failed most. So a difference between streams could partly be a wave difference. That is one more reason I never pool the streams or read their differences as method differences.

viva.q: How does your leave-one-subject-out work?
viva.a: For each visitor I train on everyone else in the same stream and test on that visitor: 22 folds for rcea, 16 for retro. Seconds from one visitor never appear on both sides. A fold is skipped if the held-out visitor has under 5 rows or training under 50.

viva.q: What does CCC measure?
viva.a: Agreement between predicted and true ratings in both shape and level: twice the covariance, divided by the two variances plus the squared mean difference. It is 1 for perfect agreement, 0 for no information, and it can go negative.

viva.q: What does QWK measure?
viva.a: Chance-corrected agreement between ordered levels, where each disagreement is weighted by the squared distance between levels. Predicting level 1 when the truth is 3 costs four times as much as predicting 2. Zero is chance agreement, one is perfect.

viva.q: Why also report balanced accuracy?
viva.a: QWK depends on how unevenly the levels are filled, so I do not rely on it alone. Balanced accuracy is the mean recall per level, read against its chance value of 1 over the number of levels, which is 0.333 at three levels.

viva.q: What is the chance-corrected floor?
viva.a: Zero on both CCC and QWK: the score of a model with no usable information about the held-out visitor. A constant prediction gets CCC exactly zero. Both scores can go negative, which is worse than knowing nothing.

viva.q: What is the selection resolution?
viva.a: How much the same pipeline's score moves by luck alone: 0.08 CCC and 0.21 pooled QWK. I measured it before comparing anything. A difference smaller than that is not one I can trust, and ties go to a rule fixed in advance.

viva.q: How exactly was the 0.08 measured?
viva.a: On one fixed cell, heart-rate variability at its starting configuration against rcea arousal, I reran the full leave-one-out 20 times with a 300-tree random forest, changing the seed and resampling each fold's training visitors. The 5th to 95th percentile gap of the 20 mean CCCs was 0.078, rounded up to 0.08.

viva.q: Why that cell and a random forest, not your selected model?
viva.a: To avoid circularity. If I measured the margin on the model I then choose, the margin would depend on the choice. The HRV starting configuration exists before any comparison, and the random forest was a generic default, not the family carried forward.

viva.q: Why 0.21 for QWK?
viva.a: QWK has its own scale and noise. The same 20-repeat procedure with a random forest classifier on five equal-width levels gave a 5th to 95th percentile gap of 0.204, rounded up to 0.21. At three and ten levels it would be 0.22 and 0.24.

viva.q: What does nested tuning mean in your thesis?
viva.a: Two choices are made inside each training fold only. The preprocessing configuration is picked by a rank vote of the training visitors, scored with ridge. Hyperparameters are picked by an inner split grouped by visitor: leave-one-out for ridge, five folds for the rest. The winner is refitted and scored once on the held-out visitor.

viva.q: Pooled or per-participant: which do you use where?
viva.a: CCC is computed per held-out visitor, then averaged. QWK and balanced accuracy are pooled once over all held-out predictions, because many visitors sit on one or two levels, where a per-visitor kappa is unstable. The paired tests use per-visitor scores, since they need one number per visitor.

viva.q: Why can pooled and per-visitor QWK differ in sign?
viva.a: Pooled QWK also counts differences between visitors. The model gets visitors' average levels wrong, sometimes backwards: for rcea valence the correlation between a visitor's mean rating and mean prediction is -0.55. Within one visitor that offset does not count, so per-visitor kappas sit near zero while pooled goes negative.

viva.q: Why Wilcoxon signed-rank with Benjamini-Hochberg?
viva.a: Seconds from one person are not independent, so each test uses one score per visitor. The Wilcoxon uses ranks, so one extreme visitor cannot drive it. Benjamini-Hochberg then controls the false discovery rate across the many tests in a family.

viva.q: What is your both-metrics rule?
viva.a: In Experiments 4 and 5 I run the paired test on per-visitor CCC and on per-visitor QWK, each with its own correction. I only credit a difference that survives q below 0.05 on both. That stops a shift in level shares, or a noisy continuous score, from counting on its own.

viva.q: How do you know there is no leakage?
viva.a: Everything that learns is fitted inside the training fold: imputer, scaler, model, hyperparameters, configuration vote, and the DCCA and DCTW projections. Level edges are fixed on 0 to 10, never fitted. The held-out visitor only provides its score. The one deliberate exception is the Experiment 5 levers that use the visitor's opening seconds.

viva.q: Your Methods say the Experiment 3 classifier was tuned per fold. Was it?
viva.a: No. That sentence in the submitted version was wrong: the classifier used fixed settings, 300 trees, unrestricted depth, seed 42, refitted every fold. The conclusion does not change, because every Experiment 3 difference is far inside the 0.21 resolution, so tuning could not change what was carried. I have corrected the text.

viva.q: The thesis says the two B2 losses are established. Under your own rule, are they?
viva.a: No. That wording in the submitted version was wrong. They survive correction on CCC only, q = 0.019 and 0.035; on QWK q is 0.55 and 0.95, so my both-metrics rule does not credit them. The conclusion does not change: scoping still shows no gain anywhere.

viva.q: p = 0.0066 is below 0.05. Why is it not significant?
viva.a: It is one of 24 CCC tests in its family, and after Benjamini-Hochberg it becomes q = 0.138. I also checked other groupings, per lever or all 48 together, and the smallest q stays between 0.092 and 0.275. The null does not depend on how I cut the family.

viva.q: Your resolution bootstrap collapses duplicate visitors. Doesn't that distort it?
viva.a: Yes, a visitor drawn twice is used once, so each fold trains on roughly 64% of the training visitors. That makes the measured noise larger than plain retraining, so the margin is conservative: it makes ties more likely, not false wins.

viva.q: All 20 QWK repeats were negative. Doesn't that invalidate the 0.21?
viva.a: No. The resolution measures the spread between repeats, not their level. The reference cell sits below chance on pooled QWK, but the question is how far two runs of the same pipeline differ by luck, and that gap was 0.204.

viva.q: The 0.08 comes from one cell and one model. Does it hold for everything else?
viva.a: It was assumed to transfer, which is a limitation, and Experiment 2's repeats showed the averaging fusion rules vary more. But the observed differences between options were far smaller: families span 0.0124, alignment methods 0.006, and the largest settings gap 0.036.

viva.q: What are the main limitations?
viva.a: Three. A calm, natural setting where affect is weak and mixed up with walking and light. A small cohort, 22 and 16, which limits power. And sensors that measure bodily correlates, not feelings, with no questionnaire or person-level covariates.

viva.q: Is your cohort too small?
viva.a: For small personalisation effects, yes. By my rough estimate the best effect would need about 35 to 60 visitors per stream uncorrected, 70 to 120 with correction. For the main conclusion less so: the painting share is small in the ratings themselves.

viva.q: Why was luminance not controlled?
viva.a: The study was designed as a natural visit, and scene luminance was not logged, so I cannot regress it out of the pupil. Pupil size responds strongly to light, so any pupil-affect link here is confounded with what is on view.

viva.q: How does the calm paradigm limit you?
viva.a: Paintings are calm and static, so the affect they evoke is weak compared with lab elicitation, where states are provoked and well separated. Weak stimuli give a small stimulus-driven share, which is what I found: 0.1 to 1.5%.

viva.q: How good are the labels?
viva.a: Noisy. rcea rests at 5 for a fifth of seconds, which may mean neutral or that the visitor stopped rating. RetroSketch relies on memory of a replay. The two methods do not converge, and one retro visitor gave a constant rating throughout.

viva.q: Would more data fix it?
viva.a: More visitors would estimate the person share more precisely and give the tests power. They would not turn a person-specific response into a shared one. What would change that is different stimuli that provoke stronger, contrasting, repeated responses.

viva.q: What should the next study do?
viva.a: Run the person-painting split on pilot ratings first. Then use more, contrasting stimuli, show each to every visitor more than once, size the cohort for paired tests, use one validated rating tool, and log covariates like art familiarity, personality and scene luminance.

viva.q: How would the variance decomposition work as a pilot tool?
viva.a: It needs only ratings and a stimulus label, no sensors. Collect ratings in a small pilot, fit the crossed person-by-stimulus model, and read the stimulus share. If it is near zero, as here, an unseen-visitor model has little shared signal to find, and the design should change first.

viva.q: Do your results generalise beyond this dataset?
viva.a: The numbers do not. They belong to five calm paintings, wrist and eye sensors, and 38 visitors. What transfers is the method: the leakage-free protocol, the measured resolution, and the variance split, which runs on any dataset with stimulus labels.

viva.q: Why repeat each stimulus for every visitor?
viva.a: If each person sees each stimulus more than once, the person effect and the stimulus effect separate cleanly, so the person part can be estimated and removed rather than only held out.

viva.q: How precise is your painting share?
viva.a: Not very. The point estimates are 0.1 to 1.5%, but the bootstrap interval reaches 17.3% on retro arousal, because the share rests on only five paintings. So the fair claim is that the share is small, not that it is exactly 0.1%.

viva.q: Which limitations are missing from your Limitations chapter?
viva.a: A few I would add: one fixed seed; the Experiment 5 models held at one setting; the rcea rest value at 5; the annotation delay absorbed by a searched window rather than measured; and the RCEA timestamp parse that thins each second's samples.

viva.q: Could label-free personalisation work?
viva.a: That is the open question. Options are passive baselines from the unlabelled stream, behaviour like dwell and revisits in place of ratings, placing a new visitor relative to the cohort, or a short rating step added to eye-tracker calibration. I only tested the simplest baseline offset.

viva.q: Your Limitations open by saying the labels set the ceiling. Isn't that too strong?
viva.a: Yes, I would soften it. The ratings bound what painting identity can add, 0.1 to 1.5%. They do not bound what a sensor could learn about the within-visit part, 35 to 62%. The fair statement: the labels leave little shared signal, and the sensors did not find the rest.

viva.q: With this little power, isn't your personalisation null meaningless?
viva.a: It is an underpowered null, and I say so. I cannot claim personalisation fails; the pooled figures mostly move up. I can only say no gain survived correction at 12 to 22 visitors, and the lever that came closest needs the visitor's own ratings.

viva.q: Almost half of viewing time is on text panels. Does that undermine Experiment 4?
viva.a: It changes what attended means. Text panels take 43.5 to 49.9% of viewing at each painting, and I count the whole painting, panel included, as attended. So attending is partly reading, which may carry different affect. Splitting further would leave too few seconds per visitor.

viva.q: Isn't the eye-tracker density effect a flaw in your pupil features?
viva.a: Yes, and I report it. The tracker slows at paintings, and saccade frequency tracks the window's sample count at a within-person correlation of about 0.9. So part of the pupil block encodes where the visitor stands, not how they feel.

viva.q: How did you work?
viva.a: I started from van der Kaaden's raw files and rebuilt the processing myself, then fixed a protocol before comparing anything: leave-one-subject-out, a measured resolution and pre-set tie rules. Each experiment settled one choice and handed it on. I checked numbers against stored result files throughout.

viva.q: What did you learn?
viva.a: That a careful null takes as much work as a positive result, and that checking data is most of the job: the timezone column and the accelerometer overflow would each have silently broken everything. I also learned to separate what a number shows from what I hoped it would show.

viva.q: What was the hardest part?
viva.a: The data. Every sensor had its own clock, rate and failure mode, and some bugs looked perfectly fine: the RCEA timezone column made the ratings miss the sensors entirely. Second, staying honest when results were null and not hunting for a positive.

viva.q: How did you use generative AI?
viva.a: As a discussion partner and a drafting tool. With Claude I discussed how to implement methods, had it draft code and text, and used it to find faults and check numbers against stored results. I read, ran and revised the code, edited the text, and read every cited paper in the original.

viva.q: What were ChatGPT and NotebookLM used for?
viva.a: ChatGPT was a conversational aid: talking through concepts, asking about methods, and testing my own understanding. NotebookLM helped in the literature phase to find the relevant passages in a paper, explain its method, and compare what several papers say.

viva.q: What are you proudest of?
viva.a: The protocol: everything fitted inside the fold, a noise floor measured before any comparison, and rules fixed in advance. And the variance decomposition, because it turns 'nothing worked' into 'here is why', using only the ratings.

viva.q: How do you know AI-drafted code is correct?
viva.a: I read it, ran it and checked outputs against the data: row counts, per-visitor numbers, cross-checks. The reported numbers were checked against the stored result files. Being able to explain every step and number today is part of that check.

viva.q: Did AI choose your conclusions?
viva.a: No. Ideas went both ways, but what stands is what survived my own judgement, as the declaration says. The conclusions rest on stored result files that anyone can recompute.

viva.q: Which parts are your own?
viva.a: The research questions, the decisions about which analysis to run and what to carry forward, reading and running the code, checking the results, and judging what stands in the thesis.

viva.q: What would you change in the thesis text?
viva.a: Three sentences in the submitted version were wrong, and I have corrected them. The Experiment 3 classifier used fixed settings, not per-fold tuning. The Experiment 4 distance bound was each visitor's own 95th percentile, not one pooled 2.81 m. And the B2 losses survive on CCC only, so they are not credited. No conclusion changes.

viva.q: Anything else you would reword?
viva.a: I would soften a few strong lines: 'the ceiling belongs to the data' should say the ratings carry little shared signal, and 'the sensors are not the constraint' should say they cannot be told apart. I would also state plainly that eye tracking delivered 23 Hz, not 120, and describe the speech broadcasting.

viva.q: Why rebuild the pipeline instead of using van der Kaaden's features?
viva.a: To control every step. I needed to search open settings such as windows and filters inside the training folds, which precomputed features do not allow. Rebuilding also exposed real problems, like the RCEA timezone column.

viva.q: If you started again, what would you change in how you worked?
viva.a: Look at the ratings first: the variance split would have shown early how little is shared. And write data checks as tests from day one; the timezone and accelerometer bugs were caught by looking at numbers, not by the code failing.

viva.q: You declare a lot of AI use. How much of this is really yours?
viva.a: The questions, the design decisions and the judgement of what stands are mine. AI drafted and checked, and I read, ran and revised everything. The honest test is whether I can explain every step, number and choice, and that is what I am here to show.

viva.q: Could you have done this without AI?
viva.a: Yes, but more slowly. The understanding is mine: I can explain every step, number and choice. What AI changed was the speed of drafting code and text and of checking numbers, not who made the decisions.

viva.q: You found slips after submitting. Doesn't that worry you about other errors?
viva.a: It is a fair worry. I checked every reported number against the stored results, and the slips were mostly descriptions of what the code did. None changes a conclusion, because each affected difference is either inside the resolution or not credited anyway.

viva.q: What does Experiment 1 test, in one sentence?
viva.a: Whether any single sensor can predict the valence or arousal of a visitor the model never saw. Five sensors, two axes, two streams gives 20 cells, each scored by leave-one-subject-out CCC.

viva.q: What is the main result of Experiment 1?
viva.a: No sensor predicts an unseen visitor. All 20 cells sit between -0.072 and +0.084 CCC, where zero means no information, and every one is inside the 0.08 noise band.

viva.q: How did you clean the pupil signal?
viva.a: I dropped samples the tracker flags as invalid and diameters outside 1.5 to 9 mm, averaged the two eyes, bridged gaps up to 0.5 seconds, and subtracted a trailing 30 second mean for drift.

viva.q: Where do the pupil thresholds come from?
viva.a: 1.5 to 9 mm is the plausible range in Kret's preprocessing guideline, and 0.5 seconds is the standard blink ceiling in Mathot's methods paper. Longer gaps stay missing rather than being invented.

viva.q: How did you clean the EDA?
viva.a: First I removed recordings without skin contact: half the samples negative, or a 5 to 95 percentile span under 0.02 microsiemens. That removed 20 of 47. Then I masked wrist motion from the accelerometer and split tonic and phasic parts.

viva.q: Why 0.02 microsiemens for the flat-recording gate?
viva.a: The smallest deflection that counts as a skin-conductance response is conventionally 0.01 to 0.05 microsiemens. A recording that never moves more than 0.02 over the whole visit cannot contain a real response.

viva.q: How did you clean the heartbeat intervals?
viva.a: I removed intervals outside 40 to 180 beats per minute, then flagged jumpy intervals against a rolling spread over 45 beats, times a multiplier of 3, and interpolated over them. So the beat count is kept.

viva.q: How was speech processed?
viva.a: Each utterance from the Whisper transcript was cut out of the audio. openSMILE gave the 88 eGeMAPS acoustic features per utterance, and VADER gave one sentiment score for the text. Both are copied onto every second the utterance covers.

viva.q: How many features per sensor, and over what windows?
viva.a: Pupil 7 over 8 seconds, EDA 10 over 3 seconds, HRV 8 over 60 seconds, speech acoustics 88 and speech content 1 per utterance. That is 114 columns, and a single-sensor model only sees its own.

viva.q: Why 8, 3 and 60 seconds?
viva.a: A pupil episode lasts three to four seconds, so 8 holds one even if it starts off the rated second. EDA 3 seconds won the searched window through the tie rule. 60 seconds is the shortest where my HRV indices stay valid, per Castaldo.

viva.q: Which model families did you compare?
viva.a: Eight: ridge and SVR as references, then random forest, ExtraTrees and four boosting libraries, HistGradientBoosting, XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost. Each had a three-value grid on its main knob, tuned in an inner loop on training visitors only.

viva.q: Why ExtraTrees?
viva.a: CatBoost led ExtraTrees by 0.0007, a hundredth of the 0.08 resolution, so they tied. My pre-set tie rule takes the family whose cell scores vary least, and ExtraTrees has SD 0.034 against 0.043. On this cohort the choice is arbitrary.

viva.q: Why trailing windows and not forward ones?
viva.a: Trailing windows only use signal before the rated second, so a live system could run them. Forward was a candidate too. Every difference sat inside 0.08, so the declared tie rule, with trailing listed first as simpler, carried trailing.

viva.q: What are the five searched parameters?
viva.a: The fixation rule, gaze-angle correction, window direction and delay for pupil and HRV, the interbeat multiplier, and the EDA decomposition with its motion mask and window. They are the settings where the literature validates several values rather than one.

viva.q: Walk me through the rank vote.
viva.a: Inside each outer fold, every training visitor scores every candidate by ridge CCC, trained on the other training visitors. I rank candidates within each visitor and average the ranks. Then the tie rule: the first-listed candidate within 0.08 mean CCC of the rank winner wins.

viva.q: Why decide one parameter at a time?
viva.a: All pupil settings at once would be 112 combinations, and picking the best of 112 on about 21 visitors mostly picks noise. The pupil steps act on separate parts of the signal. EDA decomposition and mask are decided together because both shape the responses.

viva.q: What did the correlation analysis find?
viva.a: Nothing survives. Of 436 within-person tests, none passes FDR correction, lowest q 0.67. 14 are nominally significant, 3.2%, which is less than the 5% chance gives.

viva.q: Where does 436 come from?
viva.a: 114 features times 2 axes times 2 streams is 456. Retro EDA has only 7 usable visitors, below my minimum of 8, so its 20 tests are not run. 456 minus 20 is 436.

viva.q: Why correlate within each participant?
viva.a: Pooling lets differences between people pose as a relation. Someone with bigger pupils who also rates higher creates a pooled correlation even if nothing moves together within a visit. Within-person correlation asks what the model needs.

viva.q: Saccade frequency correlates -0.37 with retro arousal. Isn't that a finding?
viva.a: No. The tracker writes one sample per rendered frame and slows at paintings, 18 against 47 per second. Saccade frequency correlates 0.90 with the window's sample count, so it tracks where the visitor stands, not arousal.

viva.q: Did the features move in the directions the literature predicts?
viva.a: Only 12 of 28 times, which is a coin flip, binomial p 0.57. Pupil diameter rose with arousal and HNR, jitter and shimmer went the predicted way, but interbeat interval, pitch and loudness went the opposite way.

viva.q: Why is CCC near zero if the model isn't random?
viva.a: CCC is computed within each visitor and averaged. The model mostly predicts the population level with little movement, prediction SD about 0.5 against a within-visit rating SD of 1.4 to 1.9. It does not follow the ratings inside a visit.

viva.q: The tie rule decided every choice. Wasn't the search a formality?
viva.a: Yes, in effect. Every candidate sat within 0.08, so the first-listed won in all 38 folds. That is the finding: the largest span was 0.036, so the null is not caused by a bad preprocessing setting.

viva.q: Didn't the rank vote actually prefer forward windows?
viva.a: Yes. On rcea the forward pupil window had the best mean rank in all 22 folds. But rank and mean CCC disagreed and every gap was inside 0.08, so the declared tie rule picked trailing, listed first as simpler.

viva.q: Your SDNN is around 237 ms. Is that plausible?
viva.a: No. Normal short-term values are tens of milliseconds, and the filter still repairs a median 23% of intervals. On walking wrist PPG these indices mostly measure beat-detection noise, which fits the null result. I should have reported the magnitudes.

viva.q: You subtract a 30 second baseline. Is pupil_mean baseline-corrected?
viva.a: No. Only the dilation slope uses the corrected series. pupil_mean and pupil_std use the absolute diameter in millimetres, so they carry drift and between-person level. The mean of a corrected series would sit near zero and lose the level.

viva.q: The Methods say you swept the SCR threshold from 0.02 to 0.2. Where is that?
viva.a: That sweep ran during pipeline calibration, before the experiments, against the origin pipeline's output. The detected counts did not change across that range, so the experiments use the inherited 0.1, relative to each recording's largest phasic peak.

viva.q: What does Experiment 2 test?
viva.a: Whether combining sensors beats the best single sensor. It chooses an alignment method, builds 8 cross-sensor columns, and compares four ways of combining sensors, all with one fixed ExtraTrees model on the same rows.

viva.q: What did Experiment 2 find?
viva.a: Combining sensors does not beat the best single sensor. The four alignment methods span 0.006, the cross-sensor block beats its shifted copies in 1 of 12 cells, and the combination methods all tie inside 0.08.

viva.q: How are the sensors aligned?
viva.a: By fixed windowing. Every sensor is summarised over a window ending at each rated second, so all sensors land on the same 1 Hz label grid. Early fusion then just joins the 114 columns row by row.

viva.q: Why fixed windowing and not warping?
viva.a: Sensor and rating come from the same person on the same clock, so only a lag separates them, and a searched shift absorbs a lag. In the test all four methods tied within 0.006, and fixed windowing is the simplest.

viva.q: What is DTW, in plain terms?
viva.a: Dynamic time warping stretches two signals in time to line up their shapes. For each second I warped 12-second windows of pupil, phasic EDA and heartbeat intervals against each other and kept the cost, the lead or lag, and the amount of stretching: 9 columns.

viva.q: What are DCCA and DCTW?
viva.a: DCCA trains two small networks that project two sensors' features so they correlate as much as possible. DCTW does the same but first lines up the rows with warping during training. Each adds 12 columns, refitted inside every fold.

viva.q: What is early fusion versus late fusion?
viva.a: Early fusion joins all sensors' columns into one model. Late fusion trains one model per sensor and averages their predictions, either equally or weighted by each sensor's CCC on the training visitors.

viva.q: What is the cross-sensor block?
viva.a: Eight columns measuring whether pupil, phasic EDA and heart rate move together just before each rated second. Three plain correlations, three lag-searched correlations up to 5 seconds, and two counts of skin responses starting 0 to 3 seconds after a pupil dilation.

viva.q: What does Experiment 3 inherit from Experiment 2?
viva.a: Early fusion with the block: the 114 sensor columns plus the 8 cross-sensor columns at 5 seconds, 122 columns, with the same ExtraTrees model.

viva.q: How does the surrogate work?
viva.a: I rotate the EDA and heart-rate series in time, each by its own random offset of at least 5 seconds, wrapping the end round. Each signal keeps its rhythm; only the timing between signals breaks. I rebuild and score the block 20 times per window.

viva.q: The block is positive in 8 of 12 cells. Isn't that signal?
viva.a: Not against the right reference. The shifted copies also score above zero, +0.005 to +0.014. Against their 95th percentile only 1 of 12 cells passes, and 0.6 would pass by chance.

viva.q: Why do the shifted copies score above zero?
viva.a: Rotation only breaks timing. Each correlation still reflects how smooth or variable each signal is locally, and the two event columns are not rotated at all in my code. The trees can use that without any real coupling.

viva.q: Why is the best combination exactly the best single sensor?
viva.a: It is the same prediction. On retro valence every other sensor has a training CCC of zero or below, so weighted averaging floors them to zero weight and returns the HRV prediction unchanged: +0.0822.

viva.q: Why does simple averaging get worse with more sensors?
viva.a: Equal weights mix the one sensor that works in a slice with four that do not, which drags the prediction toward noise. Early fusion and weighted averaging can ignore a useless sensor, by not splitting on it or by flooring its weight.

viva.q: Why carry early fusion plus the block if all four tie?
viva.a: The Methods fixed the highest four-slice mean as the criterion, and early plus block had it, +0.0271 against +0.0199. I say plainly the order is not established; early fusion also had the smallest run-to-run spread.

viva.q: Why decide on the full five-sensor set only?
viva.a: The question is whether combining beats the best single sensor. Picking the best of 31 subsets would answer a different question and inflate the result by multiple comparisons, so the subset table is description only.

viva.q: Why no tuning in Experiment 2?
viva.a: So that differences between arms come from the alignment or combination rule, not from how hard each arm was searched. ExtraTrees is fixed at 300 trees, unlimited depth, seed 42.

viva.q: Why do the single-sensor numbers differ slightly from Experiment 1?
viva.a: Experiment 2 scores every labelled second and imputes a missing sensor, with fixed depth. Experiment 1 dropped rows without that sensor and tuned depth. So retro HRV valence is +0.0841 in one and +0.0822 in the other.

viva.q: DCCA scored highest. Why not carry it?
viva.a: It led by 0.004, a twentieth of 0.08, and it flips from worst on rcea valence to best on rcea arousal. With all four tied, I took the simplest, which learns nothing and adds no columns.

viva.q: Why is the DTW block missing on an eighth of retro rows?
viva.a: A DTW value needs two usable signals in the same 12-second window. Nine of 16 retro visitors failed the EDA gate, leaving only pupil and heart. M28 and M31 alone account for about three quarters of the 849 missing rows.

viva.q: Doesn't the block's lead flip in your repeats?
viva.a: Yes. Over five bootstrap repeats plain early fusion averages +0.0235 and early plus block +0.0212. The block was carried on a single-run margin of 0.007, far inside 0.08, because the rule said highest mean, not because it is better.

viva.q: Alignment ties went to the simplest, combination ties to the most complex. Isn't that inconsistent?
viva.a: It is a fair point. The combination criterion was stated as highest mean, and the block costs little. Under a simplicity rule plain early fusion would have been carried; nothing downstream would change, since the two are inside 0.08.

viva.q: The Methods say late-fusion weights come from Experiment 1. Do they?
viva.a: No. The code recomputes each sensor's weight inside every fold, from a pooled CCC of its out-of-fold predictions on the training visitors. The Results describe it correctly; the Methods sentence is a simplification.

viva.q: Do the held-out visitor's labels leak into the late-fusion weights?
viva.a: Slightly, at second order. A training visitor's out-of-fold prediction came from a model that included the held-out visitor. It touches at most five weights per fold, likely negligible, but a nested refit would remove it.

viva.q: Is 'SCR after a dilation' really a coupling measure?
viva.a: Not much. A 0.05 mm pupil peak happens about 2.5 times a second, so almost every skin response has one just before it: 1,627 of 1,798 rcea onsets. The column behaves like a plain SCR count.

viva.q: Does the lag search look into the future?
viva.a: Yes, up to 5 seconds. It uses no labels, so it is not leakage, but those three columns are not strictly trailing. A live system would need negative lags only or accept a 5 second delay.

viva.q: Two combinations did beat the best single sensor. Why dismiss them?
viva.a: They gained +0.016 and +0.021, each picked as the best of 78 cells in its slice, so they are selection-inflated, and both are far inside 0.08.

viva.q: Why turn the rating into levels at all?
viva.a: Ratings are person-relative: one visitor's 6 is not another's 6. A few ordered levels keep the order and drop fine distinctions that probably don't compare across people. Experiments 1 and 2 stayed continuous because CCC separates pipelines more finely.

viva.q: What is the headline of Experiment 3?
viva.a: Levels do not help. Pooled QWK is negative on every slice except retro valence, balanced accuracy is at chance, and no level count beats another inside the 0.21 margin.

viva.q: How are the bin edges set?
viva.a: Equal width on the fixed 0 to 10 scale, np.linspace from 0 to 10. They are never fitted to data. At 3 levels the edges are 3.33 and 6.67.

viva.q: Why equal-width and not quantile bins?
viva.a: Quantile edges would have to be learned inside every fold, so a level's meaning would shift. One rcea second in five sits exactly at 5.0, so quantile cuts would collapse. And equal width means the same thing to everyone.

viva.q: What are the two arms?
viva.a: The trained arm fits an ExtraTrees classifier on the binned labels. The post-hoc arm fits nothing: it cuts the continuous Experiment 2 predictions with the same edges as the truth. Same rows, features and folds.

viva.q: What is the 1% occupancy rule?
viva.a: Every level must hold at least 1% of rated seconds in every slice. A level almost nobody occupies cannot be learned or scored. It was fixed before any score, and it leaves 3 to 7 levels usable.

viva.q: Why three levels?
viva.a: Because no count could be told apart: within each slice the five usable counts span at most 0.110 QWK against a 0.21 margin. With all tied, my rule keeps the coarsest, 3. It is odd too, so the joystick rest value 5.0 sits inside the middle level.

viva.q: Why read balanced accuracy against 1/B?
viva.a: Always predicting one level gives exactly 1/B, one third at 3 levels, 0.05 at 20. So an accuracy only means something against the chance on its own row. My best excess over chance is 0.041.

viva.q: Why is pooled QWK negative?
viva.a: Pooling puts all visitors in one table, and the model gets visitors' average levels backwards. For rcea valence and retro arousal, a visitor's mean prediction correlates about -0.5 with their mean rating. That shows up as negative agreement.

viva.q: Experiment 2 was positive CCC, Experiment 3 negative QWK. How?
viva.a: Mostly aggregation, not the metric. The +0.0271 is a mean of per-visitor CCCs; QWK here is pooled over all rows. Pooling the same continuous predictions already gives negative CCC on the same three slices.

viva.q: Why do pooled and per-participant QWK differ in sign?
viva.a: Pooled QWK is dominated by differences between visitors, which the model gets wrong. Within one visitor that offset does not count, so per-visitor kappas sit near zero. At 5 levels, rcea arousal is -0.058 pooled but +0.013 per visitor.

viva.q: How were the arms compared?
viva.a: Mean pooled QWK over the 5 usable counts and 4 slices: trained -0.0387, post-hoc -0.0510. The gap, 0.0123, is far inside 0.21, so they tie, and my rule keeps the trained arm because it optimises what it is scored on.

viva.q: Balanced accuracy is below chance at three levels. Is that a problem?
viva.a: No, it means no information, like slightly above would. The middle level holds more than half the seconds, and an unweighted forest drifts toward it, so the small levels get poor recall.

viva.q: How does the jackknife work?
viva.a: I drop one visitor at a time from the stored per-visitor QWK scores and re-rank the counts by the mean of the rest. The same count comes first in 91, 100, 75 and 100% of drops. No refitting.

viva.q: How was the 0.21 QWK resolution measured?
viva.a: The same 20-repeat procedure as for CCC: one HRV reference cell at 5 levels, a random forest classifier, new seed and bootstrapped visitors each time. The 5 to 95 percentile gap was 0.204, rounded up. At 3 and 10 levels it gives 0.22 and 0.24.

viva.q: Which level breaks the 1% rule first?
viva.a: The top of retro arousal. At 8 levels, 8.75 to 10 holds only 31 seconds, 0.44%. At 7 levels the emptiest anywhere is 1.72%, which still passes.

viva.q: Where does a rating exactly on an edge go?
viva.a: To the level above, since np.digitize is closed on the left. At even counts 5.0 is an edge, so every rcea resting second goes up a level. At the carried 3 levels that never happens.

viva.q: The thesis says the classifier was tuned per fold. Was it?
viva.a: No. That sentence in the submitted version was wrong: it used fixed settings, 300 trees, full depth, seed 42, refitted each fold. The conclusion stands, because every Experiment 3 gap is far inside 0.21. I have corrected the text.

viva.q: Your jackknife is stable, so is three levels stable?
viva.a: No, the jackknife says something else. It ranks on mean per-visitor QWK, and its winners are 5, 4, 7 and 5, never 3. It shows that ranking isn't driven by one visitor. Three was carried on pooled QWK, where all counts tied.

viva.q: You show the sign flip at five levels. What about the carried three?
viva.a: At 3 levels only rcea arousal flips, -0.084 pooled against +0.013 per visitor. Rcea valence and retro arousal stay negative both ways. The three-of-four flip holds at 5 levels on the trained arm.

viva.q: Why didn't you fit a proper ordinal model?
viva.a: I didn't, and the thesis names it as a gap. The classifier ignores order; the post-hoc arm keeps it by construction. Both sit at chance on predictions with near-zero CCC underneath, so an ordinal loss is unlikely to fix a missing signal, but I can't rule it out.

viva.q: You say ratings are person-relative, then use the same absolute edges for everyone. Isn't that a contradiction?
viva.a: Partly, yes. Coarse levels reduce fine distinctions but do not remove a visitor's personal offset. Per-person edges would need the held-out visitor's ratings, which is what Experiment 5's warm-up explores.

viva.q: Is a 0.21 margin sensible when scores are around -0.05?
viva.a: It is wide, and it was measured, not chosen: 20 repeats of a reference cell spread by 0.204. It means this cohort cannot resolve QWK differences smaller than that, which is itself a finding.

viva.q: Would a constant predictor do as well as your model?
viva.a: Yes. Predicting one level always gives QWK 0 and balanced accuracy 1/B exactly. My QWK is mostly below zero and the best accuracy excess is 0.041, so the sensors don't separate from that.

viva.q: What does Experiment 4 ask, in plain words?
viva.a: Two things. Does it help to train and score only on the seconds a visitor looks at a painting? And how much of a rating belongs to the painting, to the visitor, or to neither? The second answer explains the first: the painting holds 0.1 to 1.5 per cent, so scoping has almost nothing to find.

viva.q: How do you decide which painting a visitor is attending at a given second?
viva.a: From the VR engine's log of ray hits on the paintings. I keep a hit only if the visitor stood within their own 95th percentile viewing distance, merge back-to-back hits of the same painting into looks, and drop looks under one second. A second inside a kept look gets that painting; every other second gets none.

viva.q: How many seconds end up labelled with a painting?
viva.a: About sixty per cent. 7,986 of 12,660 rcea seconds, 63.1 per cent, and 4,134 of 7,022 retro seconds, 58.9 per cent. The rest is walking, teleporting, looking elsewhere, or glances shorter than a second.

viva.q: What are the three quantities you compare?
viva.a: Whole-session: the normal model scored on every second. Whole-on-attended: the same predictions, scored only on attended seconds. Attended-trained: a new model trained and scored on attended seconds only. Each step changes one thing at a time.

viva.q: So does localising to the painting help?
viva.a: No. On identical seconds, training on attended rows is never credited as better. Pooled QWK falls in all four slices, CCC rises slightly in two, and none of the 48 headline tests survives correction. The smallest raw p is 0.053, so nothing is significant even before correction.

viva.q: What are the variance shares?
viva.a: The painting explains 0.1 to 1.5 per cent of a rating, the visitor 36 to 65 per cent, and the rest, 35 to 62 per cent, moves within the visit. So a rating is mostly about who is rating, barely about what they look at.

viva.q: Explain the mixed model in plain words.
viva.a: Each rating is split into three parts: a fixed offset for the visitor, a fixed offset for the painting, and whatever is left. The model estimates how much each part varies. Visitor and painting are crossed, because every visitor could see every painting and no painting belongs to one visitor.

viva.q: Why is whole-on-attended against attended-trained the headline, not attended-trained against whole-session?
viva.a: Because those two are scored on exactly the same seconds of the same visitors. The only difference is what the model learned from. Attended-trained against whole-session would mix that with a change of scored rows, and QWK's chance correction moves when the scored rows change.

viva.q: How do you get 96 tests, and how is the correction done?
viva.a: Two comparisons, times six scopes, the pooled set plus five paintings, times two streams, two axes and two metrics: 96. Benjamini-Hochberg runs separately per metric, so 48 CCC tests in one family and 48 QWK tests in the other. A change counts only if it survives on both metrics.

viva.q: Why correct per metric and then demand both metrics agree?
viva.a: So one metric's tests do not dilute the other's, and then agreement on both is a stricter bar than a single pooled correction. For the headline it makes no difference anyway: nothing is below 0.05 even uncorrected.

viva.q: Why REML and not ordinary maximum likelihood?
viva.a: Plain maximum likelihood underestimates variance components because it ignores that the mean was also estimated. REML corrects for that, and it is the standard choice for variance components. I fitted it with statsmodels MixedLM.

viva.q: What does the painting share bound, and what does it not bound?
viva.a: It bounds how much knowing which painting is on view can explain: at most 1.5 per cent, a correlation of about 0.12. It does not bound what a sensor model could learn about the within-visit part, the 35 to 62 per cent residual. The sensors would have to find that, and here they did not.

viva.q: Why can a leave-one-visitor-out model not use the 36 to 65 per cent person share?
viva.a: The held-out visitor has no rows in training, so the model never sees their personal offset. It can only predict the typical level of other people. Recovering the offset needs some data from the new visitor, which is exactly what Experiment 5 tries.

viva.q: Why is the bootstrap interval so wide, up to 17.3 per cent?
viva.a: The painting share rests on only five painting offsets, and it cannot go below zero, so resampling visitors swings it to the right. I also found the optimiser sometimes stopped early at a worse fit with a bigger painting share, which stretches the top. With a better optimiser the upper end shrinks, so the true interval is narrower.

viva.q: Why is the ICC 0.000?
viva.a: On one mean rating per visitor per painting, the painting variance sits at the zero boundary: visitors do not agree on which paintings feel better or more arousing. REML cannot go below zero, so it reads 0.000 to 0.002. With five paintings I cannot tell that apart from a small positive value.

viva.q: Why do the sensors track the paintings more than the ratings do?
viva.a: Because a sensor responding to a painting is not the same as a shared feeling. Pupil size follows the painting's brightness, and EDA and heart rate follow the walk between paintings. Luminance was not logged, so I cannot remove it. That is painting-locked physiology, not painting-driven affect.

viva.q: Why a per-visitor distance bound and a one-second dwell?
viva.a: The per-visitor bound adapts to how close each person habitually stood, 1.58 to 6.31 metres, median 2.47, and cuts off rays crossing a painting from across the room. One second is the resolution of the labels, so a shorter glance cannot fill a second.

viva.q: Your text says one pooled 2.81 metre cut. Is that what the code did?
viva.a: No. That sentence in the submitted version was wrong; the code used each visitor's own 95th percentile. The attended-row totals, 7,986 and 4,134, always came from the per-visitor rule, and a pooled cut would give nearly the same, 7,975 and 4,178. The conclusion does not change, and I have corrected the text.

viva.q: You call the two B2 losses established. Under your own rule, are they?
viva.a: No, and that submitted wording was wrong. They survive correction on CCC only, q 0.019 and 0.035, but on QWK q is 0.55 and 0.95, so my both-metrics rule does not credit them. They are losses from narrowing the scored rows, not from training on them, and nothing shows a gain from scoping.

viva.q: The retro arousal jackknife runs 4.1 to 9.8 per cent around a point estimate of 0.1. Isn't that a bug?
viva.a: It is an optimiser artefact. Those refits used lbfgs only, which reported convergence but stopped at a worse likelihood. Refitting the same five drops with powell gives 0.0 to 0.13 per cent, in line with the full fit. Correcting it only makes the painting share smaller, so the conclusion strengthens.

viva.q: Is 'attended' really attention?
viva.a: It is looking, not attention in the cognitive sense. It is a ray hit filtered by distance and a one-second dwell, so it cannot tell whether the visitor was thinking about the painting. It is the standard overt-attention proxy and the best the engine log supports.

viva.q: Your text says dwell removes far more than proximity. Is that true?
viva.a: For looks, yes: the one-second rule removes about 37 per cent of episodes. For time, no: by seconds proximity removes about 14 per cent and dwell under 2 points, because short glances hold little time. I should have said 'episodes'. The labels are unaffected.

viva.q: The attended model trains on fewer rows. Isn't any loss just less data?
viva.a: Partly, yes, it could be. The attended model has about 60 per cent of the rows. But the question was whether attended rows carry extra signal that outweighs that, and they do not: CCC barely moves and wins 10 of 20 painting cells, which is what no effect looks like.

viva.q: With five paintings, how can you say anything about painting variance?
viva.a: I can say it is small, not pin it down. Five paintings is the weakest part of the design, and the bootstrap width shows it. But the point estimate, the ICC of 0.000, the eta-squared check and the cell-mean refit all agree the painting share is small, and none points the other way.

viva.q: What are the three personalisation levers, in plain words?
viva.a: Baseline calibration subtracts each visitor's own median feature values from the minutes before their first painting. Warm-up adds the visitor's first 30 to 180 rated seconds to training.
