The person-relative target sets the level edges from each visitor's own ratings. Each is compared with a fresh reference on the same seconds.

viva.q: What does each lever ask of the visitor?
viva.a: Baseline asks nothing: it uses only their unlabelled sensor data. Warm-up asks for up to three minutes of moment-to-moment ratings. The person-relative target asks for the same opening 180 seconds of ratings, used only to place their level edges.

viva.q: Did any lever work?
viva.a: None earned a credited gain. No test of 48 survives correction, the smallest q is 0.138. The pooled numbers move the expected way in 21 of 24 cells, so I read it as a null at 12 to 22 visitors, not as proof that personalisation fails.

viva.q: How is the common set of scored seconds built?
viva.a: For each visitor I sort their rows in time and cut at the larger of the end of their baseline window and 180 rows. Only rows after the cut are scored, for every lever and the reference. That gives 8,700 rcea and 3,980 retro rows, and warm-up rows are never scored.

viva.q: Why is the reference different from the Experiment 2 number?
viva.a: It is a fresh no-personalisation model on the same folds but only the scored rows, which drop the opening three minutes of every visit. So it is not the whole-session figure; rcea valence reads +0.0257 here against +0.0067 in the whole-session run.

viva.q: How can a lever raise QWK while lowering CCC?
viva.a: They come from two different models and measure different things. CCC is per visitor and continuous, from the regressor. Pooled QWK is on three levels over all visitors, from the classifier, and its chance correction moves when the predicted level shares shift. So QWK can rise with no second tracked better.

viva.q: Why is CCC identical to the reference for the person-relative target?
viva.a: By construction. That lever only changes the level edges, which only the classifier sees. The regressor is trained on the raw 0 to 10 rating with the same rows and seed, so its predictions are exactly the reference. Those four identical tests get p equal to 1.

viva.q: Then what does the person-relative QWK gain of up to +0.17 mean?
viva.a: That the target changed, not the prediction. Levels now mean high or low for that person, which is easier to agree with. I report it but do not count it as better prediction.

viva.q: What does the warm-up curve show?
viva.a: Pooled QWK rises with warm-up length on three of four slices, up to +0.30 at 180 seconds on retro arousal. It is not monotone everywhere: rcea valence dips early, and CCC is not monotone. So the ordering is suggestive, not evidence.

viva.q: How do you get 48 tests, and what is the correction family?
viva.a: Six levers against the reference, baseline, person-relative and four warm-up lengths, in four slices on two metrics: 48. The code corrects per metric, 24 CCC tests and 24 QWK tests. Four of the CCC tests are identical by construction.

viva.q: The best case has p equal to 0.0066. Why is it not significant?
viva.a: It is one of 24 CCC tests, and with 24 tests small p-values appear by chance. After Benjamini-Hochberg it becomes q 0.138. The second smallest p, 0.0115, gives the same q, because the step-up never lets a smaller p get a larger q.

viva.q: Is that 180-second warm-up gain real or a few visitors?
viva.a: Mostly two visitors, M10 and M02, who gain about 0.4 to 0.5. The median visitor gains only 0.013, though 16 of 22 move up, which is why the rank test gives a small p. And M10 has only 293 rows, so 180 warm-up rows are most of their visit.

viva.q: Why subtract the median over the opening window?
viva.a: The window is short, one to three minutes, and one motion spike would drag a mean. The median ignores it. It uses no rating and nothing from other visitors, so it is the one lever a museum could run on a stranger.

viva.q: How many visitors would you have needed?
viva.a: This is a rough estimate from my own per-visitor differences, not a formal power analysis. For the strongest effect, about 35 to 60 per stream uncorrected and 70 to 120 with correction. It is the best of 48 comparisons, so the real effect is probably smaller and the number higher.

viva.q: Isn't this null just evidence that personalisation does not work?
viva.a: No. A negative result would show it does not help. The direction is mostly positive and the test is weak at 12 to 22 visitors, with power I estimate needs roughly 35 or more. So I can only say I could not establish a gain, not that there is none.

viva.q: Your methods say correction is within each lever's family. The code corrects per metric. Did you pick the family that kills the result?
viva.a: No. The methods wording was loose; the code corrects per metric, and the appendix caption says so. I recomputed other groupings: per lever the smallest q is 0.092, all 48 together 0.275, without the four identical tests 0.115. Nothing crosses 0.05 under any grouping.

viva.q: There is no gap between warm-up rows and scored rows. Isn't the gain partly leakage from neighbouring seconds?
viva.a: I cannot rule that out. Features use trailing windows up to 60 seconds and ratings are autocorrelated, so the first scored seconds resemble the warm-up. I did not insert a buffer. That is one more reason I do not claim the gain.

viva.q: 21 of 24 cells go up. Isn't that consistent evidence?
viva.a: Not independent evidence. They share one reference per slice and the same visitors, the warm-up lengths are nested, and seven of them are baseline and person-relative cells I explain as shifts in level shares. So I use it as description; the paired tests are the claim, and none survives.

viva.q: The only label-free lever lowered CCC on three slices. So what could a museum actually deploy?
viva.a: Nothing from this experiment as an affect decoder. Baseline calibration is deployable but did not help; the warm-up came closest but needs three minutes of ratings, which defeats the point. A museum could deploy engagement signals like dwell and revisits, and test label-free personalisation in a larger study.

viva.q: Are your person-relative levels really tertiles?
viva.a: Nominally. With many tied ratings, like the rcea joystick resting at 5, the two cut points can coincide and a visitor gets two levels, not three. That happened for 6 of 22 rcea valence visitors on the opening slice. It only strengthens my point that this lever changes the target, not the prediction.

viva.q: Why did you not tune the models in Experiment 5?
viva.a: On purpose. Tuning per arm would add a second source of difference between lever and reference. So the regressor stayed at 300 trees with no depth limit and the classifier at defaults, and only the lever changes.

viva.q: Give me one line per research question.
viva.a: RQ1: no sensor or combination beats the chance floor, all between -0.072 and +0.084 CCC. RQ2: ordered levels do not help. RQ3: scoping to the painting does not help. RQ4: the person holds 36 to 65 per cent, the painting 0.1 to 1.5. RQ5: personalisation is not established at this size, smallest q 0.138.

viva.q: What is the single most important finding?
viva.a: The rating is mostly the person: 36 to 65 per cent belongs to who is rating, 0.1 to 1.5 per cent to which painting. A model for an unseen visitor needs signal shared across people, and there is very little.

viva.q: What is the answer to RQ1?
viva.a: No sensor separates from the floor. The twenty sensor-by-slice scores sit between -0.072 and +0.084 CCC, and the best combination, +0.0822, equals the best single sensor. Sensors, model families and alignment methods each span less than the 0.08 selection resolution.

viva.q: What is the answer to RQ2?
viva.a: Ordered levels do not lift agreement above chance. Balanced accuracy is at most 0.041 above chance, and the two ways of making levels differ by 0.0123 against a resolution of 0.21, so they are indistinguishable.

viva.q: What is the answer to RQ4's second part, which sensors carry the painting-shared component?
viva.a: On retro every sensor category tracks the painting more than the ratings' 0.1 per cent, and on rcea pupil does too. But that is most simply light and movement, not shared affect. Cardiac features are the most person-locked, about 57 to 66 per cent person share.

viva.q: Isn't this just a failed project?
viva.a: No. The question was whether a guide can rely on these sensors for an unseen visitor, and the answer is a measured no across a wide search. I also explain why, from the ratings alone, and give a check the next study can run first. A failed project would be one that cannot say why.

viva.q: What is your contribution, then?
viva.a: A careful measured ceiling under a leakage-free protocol with a stated noise floor, 0.08 CCC. An explanation of it from the ratings alone. And a reusable first step: the person-painting variance split, which tells a project early whether shared signal exists.

viva.q: Discussion 6.1 says a model trained on others can only use the painting part. Isn't that too strong?
viva.a: Yes, as written it is too strong. The split bounds what knowing the painting can add. A sensor model could still in principle track the within-visit part or a person's level. The fair version: little is shared across people, and in my data the sensors did not find the rest, 0 of 436 correlations survive.

viva.q: You say the painting part is at or below 3.3 per cent. Is that consistent with 0.1 to 1.5?
viva.a: 3.3 is the largest value of the one-way eta-squared check, not the main estimate. The mixed model gives 0.1 to 1.5. It is not an upper bound on the uncertainty: the bootstrap reaches 17.3 per cent. The safer line is: the estimate is 0.1 to 1.5 per cent, and the cohort shows it is small but cannot pin it down.

viva.q: You say HRV gave the highest score in the thesis. Did it?
viva.a: Not literally. HRV gave the highest single-sensor score without personalisation, +0.084 on retro valence. The warm-up reaches +0.090, and HRV's four-slice mean is only about +0.01, behind EDA. So I should say 'highest single-sensor cell'.

viva.q: You call the person component a stable trait. Is it?
viva.a: Stable across the visit, not a proven trait. I only have one visit per person, so it could be how they use the scale or their mood that day. I would say 'a stable difference between visitors'.

viva.q: The RQ4 summary says the split holds for any pipeline. Does it?
viva.a: The split itself does, because it uses only the ratings and the painting label, no model. What it bounds is what the painting identity can explain. It does not by itself bound what any sensor pipeline could learn about the within-visit residual.

viva.q: So should a guide just use behaviour, like dwell time, instead of affect?
viva.a: Not as the goal. Behaviour is what existing guides already use; my aim is affect. The results say affect needs different data: contrasting artworks seen more than once, shared moments like a first look, a short labelled warm-up, and the variance split run first on a pilot.

viva.q: What transfers from this study to others?
viva.a: The method, not the numbers. The person-painting variance split runs on pilot ratings before any sensor pipeline, and the selection resolution tells you which differences to trust. Lab studies with strong stimuli would likely show a larger stimulus share.

viva.q: What should the next study do differently?
viva.a: Run the variance split on pilot ratings first. Then pick contrasting stimuli, more of them, shown to every visitor more than once, so the person part can be removed. Use one validated rating tool, log luminance and covariates, and size the cohort for a paired test, roughly 35 to 120 per stream by my rough estimate.

viva.q: You say nothing beat the floor, but the warm-up gives balanced accuracy 0.44 and QWK +0.27. Isn't that a contradiction?
viva.a: Those are pooled figures for one arm, untested at that level. The paired per-visitor tests are what I set as the claim, and none survived. So the right phrasing is: nothing established a gain over the floor that survives the resolution or correction.

viva.q: You say the sensors are not the constraint. Does a tie between sensors show that?
viva.a: No, that is a non sequitur as written. A tie shows the sensors cannot be told apart, not that better sensing would not help. The stronger argument is the variance split: little shared signal exists in the ratings for any sensor to find.

viva.q: Your Limitations say the ceiling is set by the labels themselves. Can you claim that?
viva.a: Too strong as stated. The ratings bound what painting identity can add, 0.1 to 1.5 per cent. They do not bound the within-visit part, 35 to 62 per cent. The safer claim: the labels leave little signal shared across people, which is what an unseen-visitor model needs.

viva.q: How do you know the ceiling is in the data and not your pipeline?
viva.a: Three reasons. The variance split uses no pipeline and finds almost no painting share. Van der Kaaden's independent pipeline also fell to near chance for new visitors. And my own search, eight model families, alignment, fusion, targets, scoping, personalisation, never separates. Approaches outside that set remain open.

viva.q: You say the warm-up gain grows with each additional second. Does it?
viva.a: Overstated. Pooled QWK rises with warm-up length on three of four slices, over four durations, and CCC is not monotone. The safe line: pooled agreement rises with warm-up length on three of the four slices, and none of it survives correction.

viva.q: Would more participants have changed your conclusion?
viva.a: They would give the personalisation tests the power they lacked and estimate the shares more precisely. They would not turn a person-specific response into a shared one, because the painting share is small in the ratings themselves. Different, more contrasting stimuli would matter more.

viva.q: Could deep learning or a foundation model have done better?
viva.a: Possibly on other data, but it does not change the variance split, which is computed on the ratings. If about 1 per cent of a rating is shared, a bigger model has little shared signal to find. With 22 and 16 visitors, tree ensembles on handcrafted features are the sensible family.

viva.q: Are there places where the submitted text and the code disagree?
viva.a: Yes, a handful, and I have listed them. Three I corrected on 23 September: the Experiment 3 classifier tuning, the Experiment 4 distance bound, and calling the B2 losses established. The rest are wording slips. None changes a conclusion, because every affected difference is inside the resolution or already non-significant.

viva.q: Was the distance bound one pooled 2.81 metre cut?
viva.a: No, the submitted sentence was wrong. The code used each visitor's own 95th percentile, 1.58 to 6.31 metres. The attended totals always came from that rule, and a pooled cut gives nearly the same rows, 7,975 against 7,986 on rcea.

viva.q: Were the two B2 losses established?
viva.a: Not under my own rule, and that submitted wording was wrong. They survive on CCC only; QWK gives q 0.55 and 0.95, so the both-metrics rule does not credit them. The conclusion stands: scoping shows no gain.

viva.q: Your introduction says the eye tracker runs at 120 Hz. Is that right?
viva.a: 120 Hz is the device specification. The delivered rate is about 23 Hz over a session, 45 in bursts, because the logger writes one sample per rendered frame. I measured it and report it in Data Characterisation; the introduction should say 'nominal'.

viva.q: Which model measured the selection resolution? The thesis does not say.
viva.a: A random forest of 300 trees on one fixed cell: HRV at its starting configuration, H_m4_t0, rcea arousal, 20 bootstrap repeats. The thesis only says 'one invariant reference cell'; it should name the model. I chose it before the family comparison so the margin could not depend on what was selected.

viva.q: How were the late-fusion weights really set?
viva.a: The methods say each sensor's Experiment 1 CCC. The code recomputes a pooled CCC from out-of-fold predictions on the training visitors, inside every fold, which is what the Results say. The methods sentence is a simplification. Negative weights floor to zero, and if all floor out, the weights fall back to equal.

viva.q: You write that rows are never dropped for a missing feature. True?
viva.a: True from Experiment 2 on, and true for partly missing rows. But in an Experiment 1 single-sensor cell, a row with every feature of that sensor missing is dropped. Pupil and HRV rows are effectively never dropped, because sample count and HRV count are always numeric; EDA and speech rows can be.

viva.q: You say each slice carries one fold per visitor. Always?
viva.a: Not in every cell. A visitor whose EDA failed quality control has no EDA features, so their fold is skipped in the single-sensor EDA cell: retro EDA scores only 7 of 16 visitors, rcea EDA 18 of 22. Elsewhere it holds.

viva.q: Speech is intermittent, yet speech features exist on 71 per cent of rows. How?
viva.a: Each utterance's features are copied onto every second of its transcript segment, and Whisper segments include pauses. So speech columns sit on about 71 per cent of rows while voiced audio is only about 7 per cent of a visit. The thesis line 'the seconds an utterance covers' is literally true, but it should mention that.

viva.q: In Experiment 5 your methods say correction within each lever's family. What did the code do?
viva.a: It corrected within each metric across all levers: 24 CCC tests and 24 QWK tests. The appendix caption matches the code; the methods wording is a slip. Under every other grouping I tried, the smallest q stays between 0.092 and 0.275.

viva.q: You cite Mariooryad for a one-to-three second annotation delay. Is that what the paper says?
viva.a: The paper says one to six seconds, depending on annotator and dimension. One to three is the typical figure I carried over. My delay search covers 0 to 6 seconds, so the method matches the paper's full range.

viva.q: Your text says dwell removes far more than proximity. Check that.
viva.a: True for episodes, about 37 per cent of looks, but not for time: proximity removes about 14 per cent of seconds, dwell under 2 points. The sentence should say 'episodes'. The labels themselves are unaffected.

viva.q: Why do some retro visitors score exactly 0?
viva.a: Two structural zeros. M45 drew perfectly constant ratings, so CCC has no covariance and is 0 in every retro cell. M28 has no eye data in its window, so its pupil features are constant and the prediction is constant, CCC 0. Both passed the inclusion rules and are counted, pulling retro means slightly toward zero.

viva.q: Is there a bug still live in your submitted labels?
viva.a: One small one. The rcea timestamp parser drops 4 Hz samples stamped on exact whole seconds, so each second's median is usually of three samples, for six visitors of one. I measured it: no second is lost, labels change 0.003 to 0.12 points on a 0 to 10 scale. I expect no conclusion to change, but I have not re-run.

viva.q: How do I know the rcea timestamps are even on the right clock?
viva.a: An earlier bug taught me to check. The column labelled UTC actually holds Dutch local time, which put ratings an hour off the sensors. I parse the correctly tagged CET column instead, fixed before the submitted results. After the fix, rating and pupil session ends agree within about 65 milliseconds.

viva.q: Did you verify the Marín-Morales 2019 figures you quote?
viva.a: Not to the same standard. My citation audit covers their 2018 paper; the 2019 figures were taken from the paper but are not in my audit. I would re-check them before quoting exactly. They are context, not evidence for any of my results.

viva.q: If the resolution came from a random forest on HRV, why apply it to ExtraTrees, ridge and fusion?
viva.a: Fair point: that transfer was assumed. It is a noise yardstick measured before any selection, on a cell that no choice could change. Experiment 2 checked it for fusion and found it fails for the averaging rules, which I report. For the main comparisons the gaps are so small that no reasonable resolution would separate them.

viva.q: With this many slips, why should I trust the numbers?
viva.a: Because every number in the thesis was checked against stored result files, and I found these slips myself by reading the code line by line. They are descriptions that were wrong, not results that were wrong. Each one sits inside the resolution or among tests that were already non-significant, so no conclusion moves.

viva.q: Why keep M45 and M28 if you knew they score exactly zero?
viva.a: Because dropping them after seeing their scores would be selecting on the outcome. They passed the inclusion rules I set before. Each pulls a retro mean toward zero by one sixteenth of the gap, which does not change any comparison.
